The Ash in the corner is the shape of that decision and she has lived beside it for a year. \emph{Ch 2:} she keeps his seat empty and his coat on its peg, will not let anyone sweep the ridge, and touches the widow’s mark only before she opens the kiln. The house keeps a roll of its own in which he is entered, and does not show it to a man from Slate Row.

\textbf{Ch 4.} The boy was carried to the Drawing and back like a pot filled that must not be slopped; she placed him where he could see and not join and stood a half-pace off, her burn shut on nothing, and would not be the one to tell him what the room was doing. She did not answer Jorra’s \emph{the back room’s cold}; she shifted the damper. With Alda, a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement, and neither asked what the other had written. Dessa at her threshold got no look from her and no word, and the barley between the two houses went on being unentered. Garl’s mark was touched before the kiln and not at the bank, and his coat, seat, ridge and proverb kept the house in his shape while the debt stayed uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 5.} The rule of the mark held exactly: touched before the opening on Stone 13 and at no other time, not at the bank that night or on Stone 15. She fed him barley gruel from the house’s own dish, holding his head with two fingers behind the ear, and gave every instruction to the fire, the pot and the wool --- \emph{keep it off his ears; it’s the river wind} --- never to the basket. She carried him down to the Fishstairs twice and to the market’s edge once, kept her half-pace from every open slate, laid marks for two pair of eels and counted them with her eyes, and said nothing about the collector’s cuff, the cord or where they had been. At dusk on Stone 15 her hand did not go to the mark; she counted loaves and bits with her lips and came back to the same place twice, keeping the shape of the days to Kindling without giving the number. She neither saw nor refused the crust Mira put in the fold, and where she is concerned these are the same thing.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 she touched the mark before the lid and at no other hour, moved her lips along the loaf shelf so the days to Kindling stood as a shape, and told the neighbour at the threshold to ask the pot. She carried him down to the Cross on Stone 20 and back, kept her half-pace from every open slate, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and did not look into it; at dusk she put the fold right without his face, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a reading is not an opening. On Stone 19 she slid the basket a hand’s breadth out of the draught and would not have called it love, measured the ridge with her thumb --- near two thumbs here, a finger more two doors down --- and said leave it until the Last Day. The crust Mira put in the fold went from warm to cold and she neither took it out nor named it. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again; Berr read his figure over the basket and went around Garl’s uncalled debt another year; Jorra moved the damper before she had finished and did not say the back room was cold.

\textbf{Ch 7.} Through Days 15--24 she went to the fire before anything else and touched the widow’s mark before each opening and at no other hour --- not when she banked with the back of a broken pot, not at the reading on Stone 30. She counted fuel and bread into the last tend in loaves, glances and the space where a loaf should have stood, and answered the man who came back from the ice with a number in his fist by saying it was a cold and feeding the fire. She sent Tarn for a collector for a neighbour, carried the basket two doors down and set it at the edge of the light with her burn shut on nothing. On Stone 29 she laid her thumb in the Vail Ash ridge and then in the death-house ridge, near two thumbs here and a finger thicker there, and walked back without saying which was which. At the last market she kept her half-pace from every open slate, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and gave instruction to the wool, and at dusk put the fold right without looking at his face, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and banked the coals. She neither took out nor named either crust. With Alda a half-pace and a slate turned writing-down stood in for the arrangement again; she did not answer Jorra’s silence about the back room, let Berr go around Garl’s debt, and carried the keeping into Kindling without explaining any of it.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On Kindling she took the clay dish of fire up from the yard before first light, put her hand to the widow’s mark for one breath before she opened the kiln and tipped the coal in, and did not touch it again; nobody said where the flame came from or what it cost, and she gave the instruction to the fire and the wool and fed him from the house’s own dish, saying \emph{the house}. Through the Five the mark was touched before openings and at no other hour, never at the bank. At the Weighing she kept her half-pace from every open slate and did not repeat the name the officer read; the clean voice and the Court’s room reached the basket only as a sound through a doorway, and she did not turn toward it. On the Long Night she let the fire go out at dusk and sat with the others telling the Return in the dark, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would have said \emph{I} and going around Garl’s name as she went around Ash. On the Remembering she did not say Garl’s name and let Alda put dates where it should have stood. On the Last Day she would not let anyone sweep the Ash early, laid her thumb flat in the Vail ridge and then the neighbour’s, near two thumbs here and a finger’s width thicker two doors down, and left both where they lay. On Ilmen 1, with the grey burned in the morning and called dealt with by a neighbour and not by her, the coals were still banked under ash so there was no opening and she did not touch the mark; she put the fold right without looking at his face, fed him from the house’s own dish, and said nothing about where any of the warmth came from or who had paid for it.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the keeping went on without an entry. At the well she drew with her free hand, the little-door burn closing on the rope and then on nothing, spoke \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and gave the instruction to the bucket, the fire and the wool and never to the basket; she did not say where the warmth in the household dish came from. On Ilmen 3 she fed him from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear and sat with the mark untouched at the bank, because a dusk is not an opening. On Ilmen 5 she stood a half-pace off while Alda laid dates and wrote what she turned down, and did not ask. On Ilmen 6 she touched the mark before the opening, held it one breath and let go, and did not touch it for a pot, a note or a nearly full sound. On Ilmen 8 she set him in the shade of the nineteen steps three doors down, carried him up the yard at dusk, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a bank was not an opening. She has said nothing about the payer of any warmth.

\textbf{Ch 10.} On Day 38 she holds the basket on the higher ground at the Slip Brook and turns the boy’s face toward the bank, as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it; she does not set him down. She goes to the fire, not down the road for a collector, and sends nobody; the omission is not entered and she does not name it. On Day 42 she fetches a clay jar from House Silt and sets it on the shelf by the wall, without turning the errand into a walk to a bank or opening a slate. On Day 43 and Day 44 she leaves the boy in shade at the Weir and carries him home at dusk, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face. She still says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the wool, the fire and the pot, touches the mark only before openings, and has named neither the payer of the warmth nor the woman in the brook.

\textbf{Ch 11.} She carried him down to the Fishstairs before light and set him below the north bridge where a pot would be set, out of the draught, then up the Clay Yard and onto his bed at dusk, never into the Debt Loft; the fold went right at his ear without a look at his face. Every instruction went to the fire, the pot and the wool, and she said the house where another woman would have said I. She touched the widow’s mark once before the opening on Day 45 and not at any bank or on any other day. She fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish, two fingers behind his ear, spoon wiped on her sleeve and his mouth not wiped. At the well she went at a half-pace from every open slate, went wide around a slate propped at the rack end and gave the instruction to the bucket. She said nothing about the payer of any warmth, did not name Dessa, and did not say that the smoky crust was gone. Her hand is one of the three the boy set on a tray as possible takers.

\textbf{Ch 12.} Through seven more days she gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and none to the basket, and said the house where another woman would say I. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again while the fifth note went under a floorboard and she did not ask; with Berr the debt against the tiles lay where it lay and one in twelve went over the basket unchallenged; with Jorra the dust out of the back room went unasked about and the damper went ahead of her sentence. She did not look toward the bed or into the basket, did not touch the mark at a well or a bank, and said nothing about the payer of the milk, the coal that went up with the bird or the crust that went out of the fold on Day 46.

\textbf{Ch 13.} She carried him three doors down into House Silt on Ilmen 27 and set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from every open slate; she opened no slate and turned the errand into no walk to Slate Row. Alda came and she stood a half-pace off with her burn shut on nothing and asked no question about the birth-slates or the fold pressed too long. At the well and at the last market she gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and said the house where another woman would say I. She fed the fire and told it the thaw when a man from Greybank spoke of a counting room shut in the war; if she connected any of it to her own roof she put the connection in the private roll nobody is shown, but she did not connect it. On Ilmen 29 she laid one thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, and fetched no broom for either. On Silt 1 she stood over a new hairline of grey in the corner with a broom in her hand and did not sweep, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it goes; she touched the widow’s mark before the opening and at no other hour, not for the new grey, not for a basket, not at a bank.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Through Silt 2–8 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and a half-pace kept from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the well. She told the fire it was the thaw when the brook came up clay-heavy behind the racks and again when the ice was called honeyed all through, and stood over the new grey in the corner without sweeping it, finer than the old clean dark line beside it. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark hung where it hung, untouched at a rack, a basket, a well, a door and a bed. On Silt 5 she carried him three doors down, set the basket inside the finger’s-width-open door away from any open slate, stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote, and asked nothing about the writing or the tin; the little-door burn shut on nothing. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and put the fold right without looking at his face, carrying one crust and an empty place through seven days without a name.

\textbf{Ch 15.} Through Silt 9–15 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace kept from every open slate at the Fishstairs, the Cross, the racks and three doors down in House Silt. She carried him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back, and when the water went around the clean dark line she stood over it and the new finer grey beside it with a broom in her hand and swept neither, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it went. A neighbour said the house had been saved and she did not. On Silt 14 she gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Round it / Go around}), went wide around the space under the lowest rack, and did not answer Jorra’s silence about the room off the shed. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark was not touched once, not at a rack, a shore, a step or a bed. It is told of her that she once sat up three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everybody was kind; she did not go toward the child in the yard whose foot stayed cold, and the boy did not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she carried him up at the half-pace, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. One brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold with the empty place beside it unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\textbf{Ch 16.} Through Days 75–77 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. The flood has gone out of the yard and left mud, and the sweeping goes around the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack; she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out.}), stands over the two lines with a broom in her hand and sweeps neither, and tells the fire it is the thaw. The yard counts what the water took in loaves, glances and a space at the row’s end that nobody calls a number, and when a woman asks for a figure she tells her to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. She keeps the half-pace from every open slate, goes wide around a slate set out to dry at the well’s edge and does not touch the widow’s mark, because a well is not an opening and a basket is not a door. At the well she does not look at the quick child in cast-offs or at the warm loaf in his pocket and does not connect the man from Slate Row with either; if she saw the passing she put it where she puts the other things she does not enter, in the private roll nobody is shown. No opening came in three days and the mark hung where it hung. At dusk each day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one brown-edged crust lies stiff in the fold with the empty place beside it unnamed and no third comes. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the mud, the half-beat, the loaf, the man from Slate Row, the two unswept lines and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

\textbf{Ch 17.} Through the lean week the keeping goes on in the same grammar: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace from every open slate at the well, the Cross, House Silt and the racks. She gives the broom its instruction before anybody — go around what the water left, it cost enough to come in and will cost more to take out — and sweeps neither the clean dark line nor the new finer grey. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, opens no slate and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and stands a half-pace off while Alda writes what she will not show. When the second man from Greybank repeats the story of the counting room at the well she tells the fire it is the thaw, makes nothing of it and does not connect it to her own roof; she has lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. \textbf{Ch 65 (bonds).} With Corin nothing was said and nothing was joined across Smoke 7–9: the half-pace from every open slate, every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, the bed under the roof and not the Debt Loft, the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen. She went to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, and sent every cost-question to the pot and the weather. The widow’s mark hung where it hung — two hundred and forty-six, forty-seven and forty-eight days since the opening before Smoke 1 — because the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour; the one opening stayed behind the household with no lesson, no mending named and no payer. The dressed grain was turned under wool, spread thin and gathered by the handful on all three mornings, changing state and gaining no figure. When the ownerless question came over the boards a fifth time on the afternoon of Smoke 8 she answered it as she answered everything that wanted a number, the weather first and the price of barley after it, and nobody leaned in to take the answer down and no row was named. With Jorra her unfinished sentence at the hearth still arrived at the pot behind his remembered finger and she asked nothing about the men who went low into the back room; with Tarn the two silences stayed unjoined, his ear-sentence stopped short of the calling word with nine stoppings and no tenth, and she asked about neither his seventh year nor his ear. Garl was kept in objects with his name unspoken two hundred and forty-eight days; Dessa’s cost stayed unentered, Alda’s writing unshown and the private roll hidden. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no opening made after the first.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
\textbf{Ch 123 (Days 420–422, Ilmen 26–28).} Keeper of the fire through three ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, intake/hold/letting-go with neither gap figured, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, clay jar glanced at with the hand half over nothing, twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, nineteen steps at the half-pace, seven walked-around places once and not twice, fold righted without a second fold, widow’s mark untouched because none of these days was an opening and seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule. Repair stayed apart from restoration: the second mending was the true one because it was done by a hand that had already handled the break, and the hairline was left showing. She said nothing of the figure offered at the well and gone back into the fist, of the woman who said \emph{Then it’s a stick} and went back to the round, of a note that was not a price or of the softening nobody owned, and did not repeat a previous day’s sentence to the fire on a day that had not earned it. Tarn’s sentence was found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the damper without a second holding. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

Feed it} to the fire and to no basket. Tarn’s sentence was found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the damper without a second holding. Tarn’s sentence was found where put and not made a habit and the loan stayed uncalled at the end of an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still reached the pot through the bent finger in the damper. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 120 (Days 411–413, Ilmen 17–19).} Keeper of the fire through three more ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing between staple and wire and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, charcoal unread, widow’s mark untouched, seven openings in seven months and not a rule. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, righted the fold without a second fold, and said nothing of the air that had turned on the nineteenth — she told the fire it was the thaw and did not tell the basket. Tarn spoke his sentence on the seventeenth, withheld it on the eighteenth and spoke it again on the nineteenth, and the loan stayed uncalled at the end of an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the damper. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 119 (Days 408–410, Ilmen 14–16).} Keeper of the fire and the house through three more ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told it was the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing between old-brass staple and tighter wire and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, seven openings in seven months and not a rule. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, righted the fold without a second fold, and said nothing of the word that came up at the well or of the figure the clerk entered before he looked up. Her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through Jorra’s bent finger in the damper, and Tarn’s six and seventh held unremarked at the kindling with the loan uncalled. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 118 (Days 405–407, Ilmen 11–13).} Keeper of the fire through three ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, seven opened in seven months and not a rule. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, righted the fold without a second fold, and said nothing of the word that came up at the well on Ilmen 12. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. Forward, not closed. \textbf{Ch 117 (Days 402–404, Ilmen 8–10).} Keeper of the fire through two ordinary tending days and the year’s first Account-day, three dated days lived one at a time with the old grammar unbroken: fire before basket, coals told the thaw, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, grain covered and unfigured, the half-beat at setting, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, seven opened in seven months and not a rule. On Ilmen 10 she set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home saying nothing; the arithmetic that began again up the road did not come under the roof as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. Forward, not closed. \textbf{Ch 116 (Days 399–401, Ilmen 5–7).} Keeper of the fire through the new year’s first working week, three dated days lived one at a time with the old grammar unbroken: fire before basket at both ends, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, the dressed grain turned under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and \emph{Lie down. You’ll keep better there}, the pot rim set two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, the seven walked-around places once and not twice. She carried the boy down and up at the half-pace and set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the wool was found where put on all three mornings and goings of the light and stayed a finding (T097/T060/T086 advanced, not paid). On Ilmen 6 she gave the men unnamed in the back room no name and the man from Slate Row at the yard’s edge no word, no loaf passing, no slate shown; her silence left the promise under the shed ungiven and Tarn’s ended term uncalled, and the boy filed the waiting on its own tray and made no cause of it (T035/T031/T080, T036/T076/T006 advanced, not paid). Garl stayed in his objects with his name unspoken 399, 400 and 401 days, the fire’s fifth unpaid the same number. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 115 (Days 396–398, Ilmen 2–4).} The turned year is taken up as an ordinary week: the house goes back to its grammar, the fire is fed before the basket, the coals are told it is the thaw, and the pot rim is set two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. A wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards on Ilmen 3 and takes it out again; a fist opens toward the pail and closes empty; word comes up of a runner going up the clay road with the writing turned to her sleeve and unread, and of the soft-cuffed clerk still set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing with his slate turned inward for a measure nobody called. She does not go near the landing or make a door of it, and no slate is opened within reach of the basket. Count \textbf{398 exact}, six months and two hundred and eighteen days told by nobody, \textbf{372 honest answers} on the sixth place; twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 remain behind one unsigned figure and Ilmen 10’s first arithmetic waits six mornings off as a reset and not a signing. The keeping at the fold is found where put and stays a finding; Tarn’s term ends with the loan uncalled and Jorra’s promise is neither given nor withdrawn; Garl stays in objects with her kept ridge unswept, his name unspoken 396, 397 and 398 days and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid the same number. No rank, power, growth or ending. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 114 (Days 393–395, the Remembering–Ilmen 1).} The keeper of the Vail fire carries the last two of the Five and the turn of a year in the same grammar in which she kept all that went before: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the pot lifted thumb-first with the crack showing, the grain covered and unfigured, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat, the charcoal unread and the widow’s mark untouched. On the Remembering she carries him to House Silt on an errand and neither opens the tin above the empty bed nor names the woman who lay there; the names of the dead go up the yard and she does not say the one that matters. On the Last Day she bakes bread, leaves the grey in the corners and will not say \emph{dealt with} after a neighbour calls the burning of it dealt with; on Ilmen 1 the yard burns its grey and she still says nothing, keeping the called-gone on its own place beside the left-in-place ridge. Her hand puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin at each going of the light and adds no second fold; the wool is found where she put it on the three mornings and goings and stays a finding, not a habit, way or payment. Twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 stand behind one unsigned figure and the year turns with nothing signed, and neither buys a teaching under this roof; the carried fire’s fifth stays unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 393, 394 and 395 days. No change of voice, no new scar or possession; she has still not said whose child he is, and the house goes on as a house goes when a pot is set down in its place and the fire kept.

On Kindling she sets the basket at the edge of the light two doors down while a collector takes the year’s first measure and says nothing of it afterward; on Weighing she carries him past the clean voice’s name in the yard without repeating it; on the Long Night she banks the coals early, turns them with the broken pot’s back, leaves no fire after dusk and sits in the dark with her hands in her lap and not still. Her hand puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin at each going of the light and adds no second fold; the wool is found where she put it on the three mornings and goings and stays a finding, not a habit, way or payment. The year’s fire comes up the Clay Yard from a source nobody names or prices; twelve arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure and buy no teaching under this roof; the carried fire’s fifth stays unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 390, 391 and 392 days. No change of voice, no new scar or possession; she has still not said whose child he is and the Five are not over.

No change of voice, no new scar or possession; she has still not said whose child he is, and the year ends without a boundary drawn.

\textbf{Ch 109.} Through Stone 19, 20 and 21 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the deep winter’s last tend brings no lesson under the roof. \textbf{Ch 108.} Through Stone 16, 17 and 18 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the deep winter’s middle tend is lived as three wholly ordinary days that bring no lesson under the roof. Ten arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure with no doctrine out of ten; the four rooms with the same gap stay held apart; the Drawing’s flat knock stays outside the six hearings; the river’s winter skin is found where put and not spent; Garl’s name is unspoken and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid 375, 376 and 377 days. The thread is left frozen and unwiped and she says nothing of where they have been. No new scar or possession, no change of voice. She has still not said whose child he is. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 107.} Through Stone 13, 14 and 15 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the three days after the Hearth Drawing are lived as ordinary tending days that bring no lesson under the roof. Fire before basket at both ends of every day, coals told the thaw and turned with the broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, twice-mended pot thumb-first at the wire with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, seven walked-around places gone around with a look and no number and widest around the returning-line place. Ten arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure with no doctrine out of ten; the four rooms with the same gap stay held apart with a finger between every pair; the Drawing’s flat knock stays outside the six hearings; the river’s winter skin is found where put and not spent; Garl’s name is unspoken and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid 372, 373 and 374 days. She has still not said whose child he is. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 106.} Through Stone 10, 11 and 12 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the month’s first Account-day and the year’s first Hearth Drawing pass through her hands without leaving a figure or a lesson under the roof. Fire before basket at both ends of every day, coals told the thaw and turned with the broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first with its hairline showing, dressed grain turned under wool and given no figure or handful, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, pot rim two inches out with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. Ten arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure with no signature on the space; the four rooms with the same gap stay apart with a finger between every pair; the Drawing’s flat knock stays on its own place outside the six hearings; the river’s winter skin is found where put and not spent on the reading or the Drawing; Garl’s name is unspoken and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid 369, 370 and 371 days. She has still not said whose child he is. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 105.} Through Stone 7, 8 and 9 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the month comes round to the deep-winter day a year before without a hand under any roof marking it. Fire before basket at both ends of every day, coals told the thaw and turned with the broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, twice-mended pot thumb-first at the wire with the hairline showing, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand. Nine arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure; Garl’s name is unspoken and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid 366, 367 and 368 days; the river’s winter skin is found where put and not spent on the birthday or the Drawing. The year finishes under this roof without one mark on any account, and nothing she does or does not do makes a lesson of it. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 104.} Through Stone 4, 5 and 6 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the deep-winter month holds without a boundary drawn. Fire before basket at both ends of every day, coals told it was the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say I, intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row unfigured, twice-mended pot thumb-first at the wire with the hairline showing, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand. She carries him down and up at the half-pace and goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and no number, sets him on his bed under the roof and never in the Debt Loft at every going of the light, and leaves the thread frozen and unwiped. \textbf{The chapter’s one change, advanced and NOT paid:} on the morning of Stone 5, before any instruction went to the basket, she carried him to the kiln mouth, set him level out of the draught where the heat came sideways, put her left hand to the widow’s mark at her throat for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot. The fire took in fours with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and sixty-four days; nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. Seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule, no eighth is made due, and the mark is not touched again at shelf, well, rack, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, going of light or bed. Nine arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure; Garl’s name is unspoken 363, 364 and 365 days and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid the same number; her hand rests the half-beat longer than the setting needed at the bed and she says nothing of where they have been. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 103.} Through Stone 1, 2 and 3 she keeps the hearth grammar at both ends of every day and the deep-winter month comes on without a boundary drawn; the river goes under its winter skin on the first afternoon and she tells the fire the thaw and banks it under blind ash against their coming back, and buys no opening, lesson, sign or payment from the ice. Fire before basket; coals told the thaw and turned with the broken pot’s back; \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say I; intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured; finger on top of the loaf shelf with the charcoal unread; lips on a two-gapped row unfigured; one glance at the clay jar cold under glaze with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air; twice-mended pot thumb-first where the wire crosses the crack with both proverbs to pot and fire and the hairline left showing; dressed grain turned under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and no figure or handful; pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. With Tarn the six and the seventh and the checked objects held unremarked; with Jorra the dust, the withheld note and the bent finger standing ahead of her unfinished sentence asked no question from her and the extra holding of Ash 26 was not made a second time; with Ilva at the well on Stone 2 the count stayed in wood; with Garl the objects kept his shape and his name went unspoken 360, 361 and 362 days. No bond changed hands and no change of voice. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 102.} Through Ash 28, 29 and 30 she keeps the Vail house in the old grammar and nothing under it is opened, named, called, paid or ended. She came to the fire before the basket at every morning and going of the light, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, kept her finger above the charcoal so the tally stayed unread, moved her lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its lead glaze and shut her hand half over nothing, turned the dressed grain beneath the wool with a progressively lighter touch and gave it no figure, set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number. On Bone 2, before she came to the basket, she touched the widow’s mark for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire took and answered four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and one days then three hundred and two, and nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. Five openings in five months are five and not a rule, the four behind are not looked at again as signs or menders, and she touched the mark at no other hour on any of the three days, because the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour. The stayed frost went off the well’s north lip while the trough kept its skin and the silt-clouded plate stood out of the path of feet, all called weather and entered nowhere; the Cold Acre hunter’s hare went toward the north gate road with its carrying answered by the weather; Ilva’s strip stayed in her sleeve; Frost’s three arithmetics stayed locked up the clay road; the Frost 14 saying stood at three shapings, the row at five askings, the burned slate at four, the shut-room tellings at two and the pot sayings at three with the Smoke 14 note apart; Garl’s name stayed unspoken three hundred and two days. No bond changed hands, no tin or box was opened and no secret was entered.

\textbf{Ch 80.} Through Frost 22–24 the keeping goes on in the same grammar and settles nothing: fire before basket at every morning and going of the light, instruction to the fire, the wool, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, her finger above the charcoal so the tally stays unread, the pot rim set two inches out with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, the dressed grain turned beneath the wool with a progressively lighter touch and no figure, the widow’s mark untouched because no morning and no going of the light is an opening. On Frost 23 she heard the ownerless voice over the boards and the well-roof give the Frost 14 saying a third shaping and went on with the house, bringing nothing under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment; by then the carried fire had gone four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should stand for two hundred and ninety-three days with its payer unnamed, and Frost’s first and second arithmetics were locked up the clay road with the figure read still not the figure paid. The stayed frost, the skinned trough and the clouded plate of ice were weather entered nowhere, and no figure or payer was taken off any of them. With Jorra the bent finger went into the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and the household straightened around his silence; with Tarn six were counted and the seventh held with the loan uncalled; Garl’s objects and his uncalled tile debt kept their places with his name unspoken two hundred and ninety-three days. Frost 30 (Day 299) stood six mornings ahead and was not made a sign.

\textbf{Ch 79.} Through Frost 19–21 the keeping goes on in the same grammar and settles nothing: fire before basket, instruction to the tools and never the basket, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace from every open slate, finger above the charcoal, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure given, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, mark untouched because none of these hours is an opening, dressed grain turned under wool with a lighter touch and no figure, stayed frost, skinned trough and plate of ice still called weather. On Frost 20 she carries him to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay and stands half a pace off while the figure goes twice over the basket and Berr takes the second arithmetic up the road in his locked box; nothing under the roof is settled by it. Nothing of the Frost 14 saying or its second shaping is brought under the roof. The fire’s fifth goes unpaid for two hundred and eighty-eight through two hundred and ninety days with its payer unnamed, and Frost 30 stands nine mornings beyond the close unbrought.

\textbf{Ch 78.} Through Frost 16–18 the keeping goes on in the same grammar and settles nothing: fire before basket, instruction to the tools and never the basket, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace from every open slate, finger above the charcoal, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure given, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, mark untouched because none of these hours is an opening, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure, stayed frost, skinned trough and plate of ice still called weather. She carries him up at the going of the light onto the bed under the roof and not into the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. Nothing of the Frost 14 saying is brought under the roof and no second shaping comes. The fire’s fifth goes unpaid for two hundred and eighty-five through two hundred and eighty-seven days with its payer unnamed, and Frost 20 stands two mornings beyond the close unbrought.

\textbf{Ch 72.} Through the last tend of Smoke she keeps the house by not-doings as much as by doings and gives no figure to the covered grain that three readings go over. On the third Account-day she carries the basket to the Cross and stands half a pace off while the arithmetic changes for the third time; nothing under the roof is settled by it. The fire keeps its four low pulls with the fifth missing, its payer unnamed for two hundred and sixty-nine days, and Frost comes on in the dark beyond the door with the first firing still far off.

In Chapter 1 she is a hand in a doorway and a shadow, not a speaking part. Woodsmoke and wet wool arrive ahead of her; then the burn shaped like a little door reaches for the heat at the child’s belly, finds none, hovers over the bundle and withdraws. In Chapter 2 she is inside the house for the first time on the page and is known by its objects before she is known by her words: the hollow seat, the salt coat, the Ash ridge a thumb and then two thumbs wide, the charred edge of a slate nobody picks up, the roll the house keeps and does not show. She announces the taking, is answered by her son, refuses the answer by getting quieter, and on the third day performs the taking with a hand that knows how much a thing will bear. She lays the boy on a bed and tells the fire what to do. In Chapter 3 she takes that keeping out of the house for the first time and into a market that explains him as a figure. She carries him in a basket, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, refuses to say whose house he is beyond \emph{the house}, refuses to answer Berr about the mark, and walks him home without a word about where they have been. The private roll and the Court’s slate are seen to be the same shape of account, both entering a child who has not agreed to either, and her little-door hand is at one end of it. She has not explained any of it. Her silence has stopped being a pause and become a wall, and the wall has acquired a second face in the district’s grammar of entered kindness. Through the middle tend of Grain she took the year’s first grain at the yard’s edge and set it near the hearth under wool with no figure, and went around the returning-line place with a look and no number, while the widow’s mark stayed untouched and the private roll unshown (T058/T079, T098 advanced and unpaid).

On Days 5 and 6 the keeping goes on without an entry. She touches the widow’s mark before the kiln on Stone 11 and at no other time, banks the coals with the back of a broken pot at dusk on Stone 12 and does not touch the mark then; she feeds the boy from her own dish and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She carries him to the Drawing and places the basket where he can see the work and cannot be part of it, never where a slate lies open, and stands a half-pace off with her little-door burn shut on nothing, refusing by her stillness to tell him what is being done. She says nothing about where they went, what was taken or from whom; when Jorra says \emph{the back room’s cold} she shifts the damper instead of answering. The wall has acquired a door she will not open and a room she will not enter, and the fire inside the rule of the mark goes on holding.

On Days 7, 8 and 9 the keeping goes on without an entry and adds no explanation. She opens the kiln under a hand that touches the mark and lets it go, feeds the foundling from the house’s dish and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She carries him down twice through the cold off the Slip Brook and sets him in the bridge’s shade on a patch no slate has reached, the same care she used at the edge of the light at the Drawing; she stands a half-pace from every open slate and buys eels without counting them with her fingers. At the bank she does not touch the mark, and at the end of Stone 15 she goes around the days to Kindling in the arrangement of loaves and bits and comes back to the same place twice, so that the number need never be said. The wall has grown a second face: it keeps out the woman at the eels, the crust in the fold, the cuff on the bridge and the count her son will not speak, and it keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 10 through 14 the keeping goes on without an entry and the shape of the number becomes a household’s whole arithmetic. She touches the mark only before an opening --- not at a bank, not at the reading on Account-day --- and moves her lips along the loaves so the days to Kindling are a shape no collector can take up. She stands a half-pace from every open slate in the yard and at the Cross, refuses a neighbour a number with \emph{the house} and \emph{ask the pot}, and carries the basket down and back saying nothing about where they have been or what was read over him. On Stone 19 she moves the basket out of a draught without looking at his face and calls it nothing; she measures the Ash by thumb and leaves both ridges for the Last Day. The crust in the fold goes cold and stays where it was put. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour with the slate, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure at the moot and the number her son will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 15 through 24 the keeping takes the measure of a tend and a year. The rule of the mark holds before each opening and at no bank or reading; the household’s number lives in loaves moved along a shelf, in the space at the end of the kindling and in a fist shut on a door-latch, and she will not say it even when the district gives out three and then two. She sends Tarn for a collector and carries the boy to the neighbour’s room, setting him where he can see and not join, with a half-pace kept from the open slate. At the Last Day’s sweeping she measures the ridge against the death-house’s with a thumb laid flat first, and lets the woman at the tubs say the grey will be left and burned and called dealt with. On Stone 30 she carries him down to the year’s last market for a reading and not an opening, stands a half-pace off with her burn shut, and brings him back under the roof to his bed, banked coals and two crusts in the fold she has neither named nor removed. The wall has acquired no door in ten days: it keeps out the neighbour with the fist, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure read over the basket and the number Tarn will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without entering the warmth.

On Days 25 through 30 the keeping takes the measure of the Five and crosses the turn of the year. The year’s fire comes into the house in a clay dish from hands along the yard, and she touches the mark once before the opening and at no other hour --- a rule that holds as exactly on Ilmen 1, where there is no opening, as it held inside Y.H. 812. She says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gives every instruction to the fire and the wool, and enters neither the flame nor its payer. At the Weighing she keeps her half-pace from the slates and does not repeat the name the clean voice reads; at the Long Night she banks the fire and keeps the dark with stories; at the Remembering she goes around Garl’s name as around Ash left in a corner; on the Last Day she measures both ridges with one thumb and will not let the grey be swept early. On Ilmen 1 a neighbour calls the burned Ash dealt with, and she does not; the coals stay banked, the mark stays untouched, the two crusts stay in the fold, and she carries the keeping into 813 without explaining any of it. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the warmth, the name read at the Weighing, the reading in the next room and the year the district has already entered on its slates, and keeps the boy warm without entering the warmth.

On Days 31 through 37 the keeping takes the measure of the first warm days of the new year and adds no explanation. She says \emph{the house} and gives every instruction to the fire, the bucket and the wool; the half-pace from Alda and the turned slate stand in for the arrangement again; the widow’s mark is touched before the opening on Ilmen 6 and at no other hour, not at the bank, not for a date, not for a nearly full sound. She feeds him from the house’s own dish, puts the fold right without looking at his face, neither takes out nor names either crust, and carries him three doors down to the shade of the nineteen steps and back up the yard at dusk. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the warmth, the fourth note under a floorboard, the number in a fist at the well and the cough three doors down that everybody calls weather.

On Days 38 through 44 the keeping takes the measure of a death the Court does not enter and adds no explanation. She holds the basket on the bank with her feet apart in the wet clay while the yard lifts Dessa Silt out with their hands, and turns the boy’s face toward what is being done rather than away. She does not send for a collector and nobody remarks on it; the household goes to the fire and to its buckets instead, and warmth left where it fell and the morning came. On Ilmen 11 she measures the clean dark line where the Vail Ash turned its corner against the ridge two doors down, lays one thumb in each and carries the knowledge back without saying which was which; she does not fetch a broom. On Ilmen 13 she fetches a clay jar from House Silt, sets the basket just inside a door standing a finger’s width open, opens no slate and turns no errand into a visit to a bank, then sets the jar on the shelf by the wall at home. On Ilmen 14 and 15 she carries the boy upriver and leaves him in shade where no slate lies, stands a half-pace off a woman with a slate under her arm on the way home, and sets him on his bed at dusk with the fold put right and no look at his face. The private roll stays unshown, the wall acquires no door, and she has said nothing about the payer of any warmth or the woman in the water.

On Days 45 through 47 the keeping takes the measure of three days after the blessing and adds no explanation. She carries him under the north bridge and back at a half-pace from every open slate and sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without a look at his face. The mark is touched once before the opening on Day 45 and at no other hour --- not at a dusk bank, not for a date, not for a nearly full sound, not for the carrying of a basket. The month’s days go around in loaves moved along a shelf, a glance at the clay jar on the wall shelf and the space where a loaf should stand; at the well she goes around an open slate as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it over, and tells a neighbour the house sent the number up the road. She feeds him from the house’s own dish and does not say who paid for the milk. She does not touch the mark when the smoky crust goes out of the fold on Day 46, does not say that it is gone, and does not go around it with a broom. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the coal that went up with a bird, the hand that took the crust, the number that passed from fist to mouth to shoulder, and a woman dead nine mornings with no collector called.

On Days 48 through 54 the keeping takes the measure of seven more days of thaw and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and says the house where another woman would say I; at the well and at the racks she goes at a half-pace from every open slate, goes around a slate propped at the rack end as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, and does not touch the widow’s mark, because a well is not an opening. On Account-day she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She stands a half-pace off while Alda writes and does not ask what was written, and says nothing about the payer of any warmth or about the woman dead sixteen mornings with no collector called. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the slack frame, the silence where an argument stood, the fifth note under a floorboard, the number that went from fist to mouth to shoulder, and the omission nobody will name.

On Days 55 through 60 the keeping takes the measure of the approach to Silt and the month named for what the river does, and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw when a stranger at the well speaks of a sealed counting room and men dead of the breath, and she does not join the story to the kiln under her own roof; whatever she would put away she puts in the private roll nobody is shown, and there is nothing to put away. On Ilmen 27 she carries the basket three doors down into House Silt, sets it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from any open slate, straightens a chipped cup and does nothing else; she stands a half-pace from Alda and the birth-slates and asks nothing. Her instruction goes to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and she says the house where another woman would say I. The stores go around in loaves and glances and a space at the row’s end that she does not call a number; the days to Silt are three, two, whatever the moot will say, and she gives the boy no figure. On Ilmen 29 she lays one thumb flat in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and fetches no broom for either, while the yard prepares a sweeping done a month ago. At the last market she keeps the half-pace, sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home at dusk. On Silt 1 she stands over a fresh hairline of grey beside the clean dark line with a broom in her hand and does not sweep, saying it is the thaw; the mark is touched before the kiln is opened and not for the grey, a basket or a bank, and the carried fire keeps four, four and a gap under blind ash. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the Greybank story, the new grey, the withheld number, the sixth note that was not written and the woman dead twenty-two mornings with no collector called.

On Days 61 through 67 the keeping takes the measure of a week in which the river rises and the district calls it weather, and adds no explanation. She gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, three doors down in House Silt and at the well. She tells the fire it is the thaw when the brook comes up clay-heavy and when the ice is honeyed all through, and the new hairline of grey in the Vail corner lies finer than the old clean dark line and is not swept because the house says it is the thaw. There is no opening in any of the seven days, so the widow’s mark is not touched once, not at a rack, a well, a door or a basket. In House Silt she stands a half-pace off while Alda lays the slates writing-down and writes what she will not leave lying, and asks nothing; the arrangement between the two women holds without a word, a wall with a door neither opens. Each dusk she carries him up at a half-pace, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. The private roll stays unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the higher water has given her nobody to answer. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the sixth page, the gone stone, the second cord, the clerk’s slate and the rising river, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 68 through 74 the keeping takes the measure of a flood that comes up around everything the house has left where it lies and then goes down again, and adds no explanation. She carries him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back at the half-pace, says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and tells the fire it is the thaw when a neighbour says the house was saved. The Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs, stands on the second step at the Cross on Account-day, and goes around both the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the burned line two doors down; she stands over the standing line and the new finer grey with a broom and sweeps neither, and gives the broom its instruction before anybody. No opening comes in seven days and the widow’s mark is not touched once. On Silt 13 she carries him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and no slate opened, and asks nothing about the sixth page or the tin; the arrangement with Alda holds without a word. She does not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stays cold, though it is told of her that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everyone was kind, and the boy does not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the flood, the cold foot, the two lines and the empty place beside the one crust, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 75 through 77 the keeping takes the measure of a recovery that is another kind of avoidance. The yard sweeps around what the water left and calls the new grey thaw, and she stands over both lines with a broom and sweeps neither; a figure goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere, and she answers a woman who wants it by sending her to the pot. A warm loaf passes from a man from Slate Row into a foundling’s pocket with no slate between them, and she neither looks nor connects the two. The half-pace, the unentered basket, the untouched mark and the private roll all hold exactly as they held before the flood; the wall has acquired no door, and the boy is still not written as Vail.

On Days 78 through 84 the keeping takes the measure of a lean week that changes nothing and adds no explanation. The flood has gone into mud that sets into a brown skin over the ruts, and she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody: go around what the water left, the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack, because it cost enough to come in and will cost more to take out. She sweeps none of them. The house keeps its number in loaves moved along a shelf, glances at the clay jar and a space at the row’s end nobody calls a figure, while she says \emph{the house}, sends every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom, and never to the basket. Three doors down she sets the basket at the edge of the light away from any open slate and stands a half-pace from Alda’s writing; at the well she goes wide around a slate set out to dry and does not touch the mark. When a second man come downriver from Greybank tells the bucket-round of a counting room shut in the war with the men inside dead of the breath, she tells the fire it is the thaw and lets it lie, joining nothing to her roof. No opening comes in seven days and the mark hangs where it hangs. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the gone board, the cold foot and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 85 through 90 the keeping takes the measure of a month turning on the same mud it came in on, and adds no explanation. The boy is eighty-five through ninety days old, three months at the close, and she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. On Silt 26 and Seed 1 she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody --- go around what the water left, it cost enough to come in, it will cost more to take out --- stands over the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, and sweeps none of them; when a woman asks what the month will cost she moves her lips along the loaf shelf, glances at the clay jar and tells her to ask the pot. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; she says the house where another woman would say I. When the second telling of the shut counting room goes over the bucket she tells the fire it is the thaw and joins nothing to her roof, though she lost a husband to that danger and has never once described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, stands a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show, and asks nothing. On Silt 30 she sets him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr reads one in twelve over fewer bodies and takes himself out of his own sentence, and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. No opening came in six days and a month’s turning is not an opening, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is. At the turn into Seed the first work is sweeping and the work after it lies east of Low Kiln in strips she has not gone to see. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the out-of-line landing, the foundling’s half-beat, the turned slate, the cold foot and the unnamed empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 91–93 the keeping takes the measure of the first planting week and adds no explanation. The house’s work moves east of Low Kiln into strips she goes around with a broom and a look, and her rule holds exactly: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the strips, House Silt and the Fishstairs. On Seed 2 she gives the broom its instruction before anybody, goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeps none of them, and at the well sends a woman asking the planting cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}, leaving the empty place at the row’s end with no figure. She tells the fire it is the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot; its payer has gone unnamed for ninety-three days. No opening came in three days --- not a strip, a broom, a basket, a well, a market, a door or a bed --- so the widow’s mark hung where it hangs; she has lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opens none and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, standing a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Mira’s cords, Berr’s box and Alda’s tin all stay as they were. At dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; the private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door.

Through Days 94 through 100 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become waiting and adds no explanation. The house’s arithmetic is now two empty places on the loaf shelf --- the old space at the row’s end nobody calls a number and a new gap that came in the night of Seed 5 --- and she moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar, gives the instruction to the pot, the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. To a woman at the well she says ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there, because \emph{the house has said it}, and leaves the space at the row’s end with no figure. She goes around the brown skin holding a boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and sweeps none of them, telling the fire it is the thaw each day and turning the coals with the back of a broken pot. The carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred days and the coal the gull took is entered in no slate. No opening came in seven days --- a strip, a shelf, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark stayed where it hung; she lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opened none and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the going of the light on Day 100 she set the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped; the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s four, four and a gap through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and nothing was joined, paid, explained or ended. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

Through Days 101 through 103 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become three ordinary days of two absences nobody joins. A neighbour at the loaf shelf reaches past the bare board, names the row’s old space as a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear as a child’s appetite in one breath, takes her loaf and goes with her pot; Sella moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar and leaves both gaps with no figure, and does not hear the two places as one. On Seed 13 she agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying; Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and the household straightens around his silence, and a neighbour at the bucket-round only mentions a room shut in the war with men dead of the breath, which she answers by telling the fire it is the thaw and joining nothing to her roof. On Seed 14 she sets the basket at the end of the fish-trade shade where no slate lies and then three doors down just inside a finger’s-width-open door, opens no slate and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the water, the pot and the broom and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, tells the fire the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot. No opening came in three days, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred and three days and the two lines in the corner stayed unswept. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen, carrying one crust and its unnamed empty place and two shelf gaps in another room that does not touch it.
