\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Did not enter the birth room and said nothing. Woodsmoke and wet wool came ahead of her, then the cold off the yard, then the hand with the little-door burn across its back --- lintel, threshold, two straight sides. It felt for heat at the child’s belly, found none, opened and shut once above the covered bundle and withdrew. She stepped back out into the Clay Yard without looking at child or women. The crust and the warmed stone had already come from her hearth, neither entered against anybody; the kiln breathed through the wall afterward. She still intends to take him on the third day.

\item Ch 2: Kept the fire and the house through Days 2 and 3. At first light touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, gave instruction to the pot and the fire, would not let anyone fill Garl’s seat or take his coat down, and said the house kept a roll of its own. Announced that the boy would come under the roof and was answered \emph{he’s not Vail}; got quieter and did not reply. On the third morning came for him, crossed to the bench first, lifted him with the little-door hand, said \emph{the boy} and \emph{the house}, carried him up the Clay Yard and laid him on fresh straw. Gave the bed to the foundling and the loft to Tarn without explaining either, told the pot it would pay for itself in the thaw, and left the charred slate in the kiln ash untouched.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Carried the boy out of the kiln-house in a basket under a fold of wool --- he left the house and its heat went out behind him --- and held him like a pot filled that must not be slopped. Did not touch the widow’s mark, since the coals were only being banked. Counted off the question of the mother with \emph{Account-day} and the question of the house with \emph{the house}; put the fold back over his face and ears without looking and spoke the instruction to the wool and the wind. Kept a half-pace from the slate on the block and did not set the basket where it lay open. At the Slate Row end refused to answer Berr about the confirmed widow’s mark, pulled the wool over the boy’s ear, and let the uncalled debt lie. Lifted the basket off the post in the late afternoon and turned back up the Clay Yard without a word about where they had been or what had been read over the top of him; the wool smelled of woodsmoke and the door did not quite shut.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. On Stone 11 touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, fed the household from her own dish, put the fold right without looking and gave the instruction about the draught to the fire. On Stone 12 carried the boy two doors down to a neighbour’s house for the Drawing, turned the basket with her knee and set it at the edge of the light, not where the slate lay open, and said \emph{a pot filled is a pot carried} to the girl at the hearth. Stood a half-pace from bench and bed with her burn shut on nothing and did not look toward the basket when the man gave. At dusk banked the coals under ash with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{that’ll hold} to the fire, put the fold right without looking at his face, and said nothing about where they had been, what had been taken or from whom. Did not touch the mark at the bank. Did not answer Jorra’s \emph{the back room’s cold}; shifted the damper instead. Fed the boy gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish and entered neither the spoon nor the boy.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. Touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln on Stone 13 and at no other time, held it a moment longer than the touch required, and gave the instruction to the fire. Fed the boy barley gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish, spoon wiped on her sleeve, and said \emph{the house}, never \emph{I}; put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and did not wipe the drool. At dusk banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark. Carried him down to the Fishstairs on Stone 8 and to the market’s edge on Stone 9, kept the half-pace from open slates and the shade where no slate lay, laid marks for two pair of eels and counted them with her eyes, and said nothing about the cuff, the cord, the crust or where they had been. On Stone 15 counted her loaves and bits with her lips twice and returned to the same place, keeping the days to Kindling as a shape and not a number; neither thanked nor refused the crust and did not take it out.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 touched the widow’s mark before lifting the kiln lid and at no other hour, moved her lips along the loaf shelf so the days to Kindling stood as a shape, and did not touch the mark when Alda came or at the dusk bank. Kept a half-pace from the neighbour’s slate at the threshold and told her to ask the pot; let Garl’s uncalled debt lie in the space where the sentence ended. On Stone 18 said \emph{the house} and gave the neighbour the pot instead of a number; at the yard well kept the half-pace and drew water; at dusk did not touch the mark. On Stone 19 turned the coals with the back of a broken cup, called the crack in the ice weather, slid the basket a hand’s breadth out of the draught without looking at his face, measured the ridge with her thumb --- near two thumbs here, a finger more two doors down --- and said leave it, it’ll be swept on the Last Day. On Stone 20, Account-day, did not touch the mark because a reading is not an opening, carried him down in the basket and set it in the moot-post’s shade, kept a half-pace from every open slate, did not look into the basket, and carried him home through the doors going shut. Put the fold right without looking at his face, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{that’ll hold}. Neither took out nor named the cold crust Mira had put in the fold.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Days 15--24. Touched the widow’s mark before each opening (Stone 21, 25, 27, 29, 30) and at no other hour, including the bank and the reading at the last market. Counted fuel and bread into the last tend with her lips and loaves, moving three here, two there and one set apart with its brown edge turned up, and came back to it twice; answered the man who brought a number from the ice in a shut fist with \emph{It’s a cold} and fed the fire. Sent Tarn for a collector for a neighbour two doors down, carried the basket there and set it at the edge of the light away from any open slate, standing a half-pace off with her burn shut on nothing. Kept the boy’s ears out of the draught off the brook by speaking to the wool, fed him from the house’s own dish with the spoon wiped on her sleeve, and entered neither. On Stone 29 laid her thumb in the Vail ridge and then the death-house ridge and came back without saying which was which; let the debt against the tiles be circled and not named, and said Garl’s sayings to the pot and the fire. On Stone 30 carried him down for the reading with the mark untouched because a reading is not an opening, set him in the moot-post’s shade, kept her half-pace, and at dusk set the fold right without looking at his face, put him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and banked the coals with the back of a broken pot. Neither took out nor named either crust, and said nothing about where they had been.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 25--30. On Kindling took the year’s fire in a clay dish from hands along the yard and tipped it into the kiln, touching the widow’s mark for one breath before the opening and at no other hour; nobody said where the flame came from or what it cost and she did not enter either. Fed him gruel from the house’s own dish and gave the instruction to the fire and the wool, saying \emph{the house}. Through the Five touched the mark before openings only, never at a bank; at the Weighing kept her half-pace from every open slate and did not repeat the name the clean voice read; on the Long Night let the fire go out at dusk and told the Return in the dark; at the Remembering went around Garl’s name as around Ash and let Alda lay dates where it should have stood; on the Last Day would not let anyone sweep early, measured the Vail ridge with her thumb and the neighbour’s a finger’s width thicker two doors down, and left both where they lay. On Ilmen 1 let a neighbour call the burned grey dealt while she said nothing, kept the coals banked so there was no opening and the mark stayed untouched, put the fold right without looking at his face, fed him from the house’s own dish and said nothing about where any warmth came from or who had paid.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Days 31–37. At the yard well on Ilmen 2 drew her bucket with the little-door burn closing first on the rope and then on nothing, said \emph{That’ll do} to the bucket and \emph{Keep it off him; it’s the river wind} to the wool, said \emph{the house} and did not say who paid for the warmth in the household dish. On Ilmen 3 fed him gruel from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, did not wipe his mouth, and at the bank turned the coals with a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a dusk is not an opening. On Ilmen 5 stood a half-pace off while Alda reached for the slate first, laid dates where a name should stand and turned a fourth note writing-down into her shawl, and asked nothing. On Ilmen 6 touched the widow’s mark before the opening, held it one breath, let go, and did not touch it again for a pot, a note or a nearly-full sound; moved the damper after Jorra. On Ilmen 7 answered the man with the figure in his fist by speaking to the fire --- \emph{It’s a cold. That’s all it is. Feed the fire} --- and did not ask what was in the fist. On Ilmen 8 carried him three doors down and set the basket in the shade at the end of nineteen steps without looking into it, then carried him up the yard at dusk; turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a bank was not an opening. Neither took out nor named either crust and no third came; said nothing about the payer of any warmth.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 38–44. On Ilmen 9 held the basket on the bank at the Slip Brook with the little-door burn shut on the wicker, turned the boy’s face toward the bank and did not set him down while the yard lifted Dessa from the clay; went to the fire afterward and sent nobody toward the road for a collector, and did not name the omission. Gave the instruction to the wool and the pot, said \emph{the house}, did not touch the widow’s mark because there had been no opening. On Ilmen 11 laid her thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash had turned and then in the ridge two doors down, brought it back without saying which was which and fetched no broom; fed him from the house’s own dish and left both crusts where they lay. On Ilmen 12 kept a half-pace from the eel-board and the writing at the gate. On Ilmen 13 carried a clay jar from House Silt, held the basket level inside the door a finger’s width open, opened no slate and set the jar on the shelf by the wall at home. On Ilmen 14 and 15 carried him upriver to the Weir, left him in the shade out of the draught, stood a half-pace from a slate under a woman’s arm on the way back, and at dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face. Still had not said who paid for the warmth or that the woman in the brook was the mother of the child under her roof.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Days 45–47. Carried him below the north bridge at dawn and up the Clay Yard at dusk, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face; every instruction to the fire, the pot and the wool, and the house where another woman would say I. Touched the widow’s mark once before opening the kiln on Day 45 and at no other hour, not at any bank. Went around the month in loaves and glances, moved a loaf along the shelf and came back to the same place, glanced at the clay jar on the wall shelf, and let nobody say the stores were thinner. Fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, wiped the spoon on her sleeve and did not wipe his mouth. At the well kept a half-pace from every open slate, went wide around a slate at the rack end and gave the instruction to the bucket; told a neighbour the house had sent the number up the road. Did not touch the mark at the dusk banks and did not name either the payer of the warmth or the crust that went out of the fold. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Days 48–54. At the well she told the fire it was the thaw and gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket, never to the basket, saying the house; she went at a half-pace from every open slate and around a slate propped at the rack end, and did not touch the widow’s mark because a well is not an opening. On Account-day she set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carried him home without a word about the figure read over him. Each dusk she set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, and put the fold right without looking at his face. She stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote a fifth note and did not ask what was written, and said nothing about the payer of the milk, the payer of any warmth, or the crust that went out of the fold on Day 46. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 13: Days 55--60. On Ilmen 26 at the yard well told the fire it was the thaw when a man come downriver from Greybank spoke of a counting room shut in the last war with the damper closed and men dead of the breath, and did not connect it to the Vail kiln (T065); touched no mark, because a well and a story over a bucket are not openings. On Ilmen 27 carried the basket three doors down into House Silt, set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, opened no slate, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row, stood a half-pace off while Alda laid the slates writing-down and pressed the fold too long, and asked nothing (T058, T084). Through the days gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket, never to the basket, said the house, and kept the days to Silt in loaves, glances and an uncalled space at the shelf’s end. On Ilmen 29 laid one thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and brought the knowledge back without saying which was which and without fetching a broom (T013, T009). At the last market kept the half-pace and carried him home at dusk with one crust and an empty place in the fold. On Silt 1 stood over the new hairline of grey in the corner with a broom in her hand and did not sweep, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it goes; touched the widow’s mark before the opening and at no other hour; kept the carried fire under blind ash and broken pot at four, four and a gap; set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and said nothing about the river beginning to move under the ice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 14: Days 61–67. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and kept her half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the well. Told the fire it was the thaw when the brook came up clay-heavy and when the ice was honeyed all through; left the new finer grey beside the clean dark line unswept. No opening came in seven days and she did not touch the widow’s mark once. On Silt 5 carried the basket three doors down, set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote and asked nothing. Each dusk set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, and put the fold right without looking at his face, carrying one crust and an empty place through seven days unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 15: Days 68–74, Silt 9–15. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and kept the half-pace from every open slate at the Fishstairs, the Cross, the racks and three doors down. Carried him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back; told the fire it was the thaw when a neighbour said the house had been saved and did not say it herself. Stood over the clean dark line and the new finer grey with a broom and swept neither, and gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around}); went wide around the space under the lowest rack. Touched the widow’s mark at no hour in seven days, because no opening came at a rack, a shore, a step, a door or a bed. On Silt 13 carried him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and opened no slate, asking nothing about the sixth page or the tin. Did not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stayed cold, and the boy did not lay it beside the child of hers who cooled while everybody was kind. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one crust stiff in the fold with the empty place unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 16: Days 75–77, Silt 16–18. Kept the house through the mud the flood left: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the well, the Fishstairs and House Silt. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the finer grey and the space under the lowest rack with neither line swept; told the fire it was the thaw. Told a woman who wanted a figure to ask the pot what a wet thing costs, and did not say the house was saved. At the well went wide around a slate set out to dry, did not touch the widow’s mark, and did not look at the foundling in cast-offs, his green sliver or the warm loaf in his pocket, and did not connect the man from Slate Row with either. No opening came in three days and the mark was not touched. Carried him up at dusk each day, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one stiff crust and its unnamed empty place. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 17: Days 78–84, Silt 19–25. Kept the house through the lean week: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the Cross, House Silt and the racks. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them and telling the fire it was the thaw. At the yard well on Silt 25 heard the second man from Greybank tell the bucket-round of the counting room shut in the war with the damper closed and the men dead of the breath; told the fire it was the thaw, made nothing of it and did not join it to her roof. Carried the boy three doors down on Silt 21, set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from any open slate, opened none and turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid the slates down before the fold and wrote what she would not show. Let Jorra’s dust and his finger at the damper pass unasked, let Tarn’s six counted and seventh held stand as the house’s one unchecked entry. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark was not touched; the private roll stayed unshown. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped, one brown-edged crust with the empty place beside it still unnamed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 18: Days 85–90, Silt 26–30 and Seed 1. Kept the house through the turning of the month: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody on Silt 26 and Seed 1 and went around the boot-print in the brown skin, the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them and telling the fire it was the thaw. To the woman who asked what the month would cost moved her lips along the loaf shelf, glanced at the clay jar and said to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there; put no figure to the space at the row’s end and let a man say the strips east of town would want hands by the morrow without giving the hands or the strips a number. When the shut-room story went over the bucket again told the fire it was the thaw and joined nothing to her roof. Three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long and wrote what she would not show. On Silt 30 set him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr read one in twelve over fewer bodies, carried him home at dusk and said nothing about what had been read over him. Jorra’s dust and his damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Alda’s tin and Berr’s box all stayed as they were; no opening came in six days and a month’s turning was not one, so the widow’s mark was not touched. The private roll stayed unshown and the empty place at the row’s end stayed unnamed. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped, one crust and its unnamed empty place carried into Seed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 19: Days 91–93. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the strips east of Low Kiln, the Clay Yard, the yard well, the Fishstairs and House Silt, and set him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; gave the broom its instruction before anybody --- \emph{Round it. The month’s for planting and there’s nothing planted here. It cost enough to come in; it’ll cost more to take out} --- and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them. On Seed 2 told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and, to a woman who asked what the planting would cost, moved her lips along the loaf shelf, glanced at the clay jar, left the empty place at the row’s end with no figure and said \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there} and \emph{the house has said it}. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days; its payer had gone unnamed for ninety-three days and the coal the gull took was entered in no slate. Did not touch the widow’s mark at a strip, a broom, a well, a market, a door or a bed, because none was an opening. Three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the close put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; one brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold with the empty place unnamed and no third.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 20: Days 94–100, Seed 5–11, the planting become waiting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate in the strips, the Clay Yard, the yard well, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and under the roof, setting him on his bed each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket, the broom and the pot and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 5 told a woman at the well to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there because \emph{the house has said it}; on Seed 6 moved her lips along a loaf row that now stood with two empty places and said nothing about either, while a neighbour’s hand passed over the new gap and went on with her pot. Told the fire it was the thaw on all seven days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and kept its payer unnamed for a hundred days. Did not go down to the child below the sill whose foot stayed cold, though it is told of her in the yard that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everybody was kind; she has never told that story herself and would not describe it that way. At the close put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, and did not touch the widow’s mark because no opening came. The two shelf gaps and the empty place in the fold stayed in rooms that do not touch and were not named, joined or solved; the private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 21: Days 101–103, Seed 12–14, the third week of the planting become waiting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate in the Clay Yard, at the loaf shelf, at the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the pot, the fire, the broom, the wool and the water and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and three days. On Seed 12 moved her lips along a loaf row that stood with two empty places, glanced at the clay jar and left both gaps unfigured while a neighbour named them in one breath as a planting and an appetite; she did not join them. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 13 said \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying; stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote three doors down, and did not ask about the writing or the tin. On Seed 14 carried him down to the eels, set the basket where no slate lay, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down, away from every open slate, opening none. At dusk put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; touched the widow’s mark at no hour, because a shelf, a strip, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 22: Days 104–106, Seed 15–17, the hands at last going into the strips. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips east of Low Kiln, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at dusk each day. Gave the instruction to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out}) and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 15 moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour said the old space at the end came in with the planting and went off with her pot; she did not join the two tellings. Told the fire it was the thaw and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and four days; the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. On Seed 16 said \emph{Yes, house} to the early and late thaw and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, and gave the house no name for the men. On Seed 17 set the basket at the very end of the fish-trade shade, told the wool and the water and never the basket, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down away from every open slate, opening none and turning no errand into a walk to Slate Row; said nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. At dusk put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; touched the widow’s mark at no hour, because a strip, a shelf, a rack, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The private roll stayed unshown, the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed apart and unnamed with no third, and no bond changed hands, no tin or box opened and no new scar or possession.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 23: Days 107–109, Seed 18–20, the planting month entering its last tend. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the yard well, the wheel-shed, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at dusk each day. Gave the instruction to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gave the broom its instruction before she gave it to anybody (\emph{Over the road first, then the Clay Yard, and let the line lie where it lies}), and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 18 three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. At the loaf shelf that afternoon moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour called the old gap a thing the planting brought in and went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at his ear; did not join the two tellings. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and fed it, the fire answering four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; stood a moment at the fire with the back of the broken pot in her hand counting something under her breath, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 18 said \emph{Yes, house} to those who wanted the thaw early and those who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On Seed 19 stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, giving the house no name for them; told the fire it was the thaw and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a wheel-shed, a rack, a yard and a basket are not openings. On Seed 20 set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade before the crowd thickened, gave the instruction to the wool and the wind and never to the basket, kept her half-pace from every open slate and carried him home at dusk saying nothing about the figure read over the strips. Touched the widow’s mark at no hour and kept her private roll unshown; put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; one stiff crust and its unnamed empty place, the shelf’s two gaps in the other room, no third. No new scar or possession; the grey streak at her temple is more marked.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 24: Days 110–112, Seed 21–23, the last tend of the planting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each dusk. Gave the instruction to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, went around a slate set out to dry and the space under the lowest rack, and gave nobody a figure. At the loaf shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar cold under its glaze and let a neighbour reach past the bare board and go off naming the old gap a planting and the new one the price of a wet thing without joining the two sayings or touching the widow’s mark. At the well on Seed 22 sent a woman who asked what the planting cost to the pot: \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}; stood a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting something under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn, the grey streak pale at her temple, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 22 gave the broom its instruction before anybody and Tarn took it up; men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, the household straightening around his silence, and she gave the end of it to the pot. His broom checked half a beat behind the standing finger and went on, and she asked nothing about either. At the Fishstairs and three doors down set the basket where no slate lay and opened none, standing a half-pace off; said nothing about the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. The carried fire kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twelve days. No opening came in three days, the widow’s mark hung where it hung and the private roll stayed unshown; one crust in the fold and two shelf gaps in another room were not named, joined or solved.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 25: Days 113–115, Seed 24–26, the last tend of the planting held with the seed up. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the loaf shelf, the worked strips, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs, the Cross and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light, putting the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed before it went away. Gave the instruction to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gave nobody a figure. At the shelf on Seed 24 sent a woman with wet sleeves to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and heard a neighbour call the old gap a planting and the child’s empty place an appetite in one breath without joining the two or touching the widow’s mark. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 25 stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and the household straightened around his silence. Tarn took the broom only after its instruction and his stroke went on without the half-check of the day before, the flagstones keeping the stopped place; she asked nothing about either. Three doors down at midday set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. At the Fishstairs and the Cross on Seed 26 set the basket where no slate lay and opened none. No opening came in three days and the widow’s mark stayed untouched; the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 26: Days 116–119, Seed 27–30, the planting month ending and Reed coming on. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the wheel-shed’s edge of light, the stalls beyond the Cross, the yard well, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light, putting the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed before it went away. Gave the instruction to the bucket, broom, pot, fire, wool, water and wind before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, held the basket level the way a woman carries a bowl filled to the lip, and went around the empty place in the returning line, the space beneath the lowest rack and the clean dark line as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering none of them. At the loaf shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf is not an opening; she heard neighbours on Seed 27 and Seed 29 lay two bare boards under one appetite in a single breath and did not join the sayings or the two absences. At the well on Seed 29 she sent a woman asking the planting’s cost to the pot: \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} Told the fire it was the thaw on all four days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the little-door burn, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 28 men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and asked nothing about the dust or the men. With Tarn the exact account held — six counted, the seventh nearly gone and held at the edge of the sill, the breath from Seed 16 unspent, the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat — and she asked about neither. Three doors down at midday she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. The carried fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nineteen days. No opening came in four days, the widow’s mark hung where it hung, the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 27: Days 120–122, Reed 1–3, the planting month going out and the reed work coming downriver. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the worked strips’ edge, the stalls beyond the Cross, the road downriver, the Weir and under the roof, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light, putting the fold right without looking at his face and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed. Gave every instruction to the bucket, broom, pot, fire, wool and river wind and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and sent a woman who asked what the reeds would cost to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it} (T058/T079) and a man who asked what the work would want to the river with \emph{Ask it. It’ll tell you when it’s had enough. The house has said it}. Went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw, the space under the lowest rack and the missing hand’s place in the strip as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering none of them (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). At the shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, gave nobody a figure and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a market and a bed are not openings (T060/T086). On all three days told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, standing a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed; its payer went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-two days (T088). On Reed 2 gave the men unnamed before first grey no name and let Jorra’s bent finger stand in the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, giving the end of it to the pot (T035/T031/T062), and let Tarn’s stroke go on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones kept the stopped place, asking about neither (T036/T076). No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown, the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed in rooms that do not touch, and she has still not said whose child he is.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 28: Days 123–125, Reed 4–6. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the yard, the strips’ edge, the Weir, the Cross and back under the roof, set him on his bed each dusk and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed. Gave the instruction to the wool, wind, bucket, broom, pot and fire and never the basket; said \emph{the house}; went wide around the rack space and the missing hand’s place; sent a woman asking the reeds’ cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it} and glanced once at the clay jar. Moved her lips along a shelf standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure. Told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, and set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand without looking toward the bed. Asked nothing about the men unnamed, Jorra’s finger in the damper, his dust, Tarn’s near-saying or his seventh year. Widow’s mark untouched; payer of the carried fire’s fifth breath unnamed for a hundred and twenty-five days. No new scar or possession.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 29: Days 126–128, Reed 7–9. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the stalls beyond the Cross, the Weir, House Silt three doors down and back under the roof, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each dusk, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting each night. Gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the bucket, the broom, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; said \emph{the house}; went around the clean dark line, the finer hairline called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates and the place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). A woman who asked what the reeds would cost was sent to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. At the Cross on Day 126 set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay and stood a half-pace off; kept half a pace from a woman come near with a slate under her arm. Three doors down on Day 128 set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, opened no slate, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid her birth-slates before the fold, asked nothing about the sign, the date, the tin or the six pages. At the fire on all three days told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and did not look toward the bed; the payer went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-eight days (T088). Within hearing of Tarn’s second stopping she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; she did not ask Jorra about the men, his dust or his finger in the damper, and neither man named the other’s silence. Widow’s mark untouched at a rack, a strip, a well, a yard, a market, a road, a basket, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening. Instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket; \emph{the house} where another woman says \emph{I}. At the fire on all three days told it it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand two inches beyond it and did not look toward the bed; the payer went unnamed for one hundred and thirty-two, one hundred and thirty-three and one hundred and thirty-four days (T088). Widow’s mark untouched at a shelf, an afternoon, a strip, a rack, a basket, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and nothing was explained.

On Day 141 a neighbour reached past the bare board with her hand before her eyes and named the old shelf-gap and the empty place at the boy’s ear under one appetite in a single breath; Sella heard and did not join either, sent her to the pot, moved her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and, standing with her back to the basket, reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies without looking and without a word, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread; T097 advanced, not paid). \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 35: Days 144–146, Reed 25–27, the reed month going out. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the loaf shelf and hearth, the wheel-shed’s edge, the Weir and House Silt three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof each going of the light and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, leaving the thread of drool frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it went away. Gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and sent a woman who asked what the hands would be paid to the weather and the river with no figure. On Day 144 stood with her back to the basket, moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread). Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, and set the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand. On Day 145 gave the house no name to the men who came low into the back room before first grey, did not say the room was cold, and did not ask Jorra about his dust or the damper; within hearing of Tarn’s \textbf{eighth} stopping she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing, and neither man named the other’s silence. On Day 146 set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid her birth-slates before the fold, crossed the flower unknowing, covered it with \emph{Stone seven. The account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, said \emph{Warm and breathing} exact and not true and touched her tin unopened; she asked nothing about the writing, the tin, the sign or the date. At the close she went around the pan set out to dry and the iced trough, left the widow’s mark untouched because a dusk is not an opening, and went to her own bed without explaining the count. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 36: Days 147–149, Reed 28–30, on stage all three days. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the reed beds, the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed’s edge, the Weir and the last market at the Cross, and up the clay road at the going of the light, giving the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and telling the fire it was the thaw. To a girl with a creel and to a man who asked what the hands would be paid she gave the weather and the river, never a figure; to the recurring woman who came up from the strips with a wet pot and asked what the row would want she gave \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level so nothing slopped (T058/T079, T077). Went wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates and the empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). On Day 147, standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, she glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies without looking and without a word, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread). On Day 148, before first grey, men unnamed went low into the room off the shed; she carried him past at the half-pace, turned no head toward the door, gave the house no name for them and did not say the room was cold, and within hearing of Tarn’s \textbf{ninth} stopping gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing (T035/T031, T036/T076). On all three days she turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, and set the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand; neither looked toward the bed nor touched the widow’s mark at a shelf, an afternoon, a market or a dusk, because none was an opening. At the last market she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and kept the half-pace from every open slate while the square sold over the clerk and a sixth green and a sixth half-turn stood unread; she made nothing of either and joined nothing. At the going of the light on Day 149 she carried him up the clay road around the pan and the trough with its skin of ice, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face, left the thread of drool frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it went away, told the fire it was the thaw, said \emph{The house will keep it} and went to her own bed without explaining the count; the two rooms did not touch. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 37: Days 150–152, Tallow 1–3, Firstday to Thirdday, on stage all three days. On Day 150 at the kiln mouth she performed the chapter’s one meaningful change --- the first opening of the month --- touching the widow’s mark before the kiln, holding it one breath and letting go, then tipping the coal under a broken pot and going back to setting pots, with the rule holding exactly at every shelf, well, afternoon and dusk that followed (T058/T079). Through the three days she carried the boy at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to wool, fire, pot, broom and running water and never to the basket, went around the pan’s gone place, the trough without its ice and wide around the rack space with the broken birth-slates, told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, set the pot handle two inches beyond the hand that could not close on it and left the mark hanging where it hung at a dusk. On Day 151 at the Weir she gave a cost asked as a direction back as a direction (T077), and at the shelf, standing with her back to the basket, reached a finger beneath the board where the charcoal tally lies without looking or a word (T100 carried, unread). On Day 152, with men unnamed in the back room and Jorra’s finger leading at the damper, she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing while Tarn’s ear-sentence stopped short of the threshold with no tenth standing (T035/T031, T036/T076, T065/T095); the fire’s payer was unnamed for a hundred and fifty-two days (T088). No bond changed hands, no tin or box opened, no secret entered.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

At the going of the light on all three days she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke going before her and the river wind behind, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, let her hand rest a half-beat longer than the setting needed, and went to her own bed; the two rooms did not touch. The two rooms did not touch. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no secret entered.

Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate; gave the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}; set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting; and kept the widow’s mark where it hung at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon and dusk, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour (T058/T079). The house has said it}, and the woman carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, paid small and non-fatally:} on Day 188 a rack-worker’s pot gave its high thin note before its time and then sang itself out early, and the woman went on with her hands and made no lesson of it; two men then carried a glaze-room hand out of the kiln and across the yard toward the clay road, alive and breathing, sweet-sickness on his breath, the pale line at his gum, his own hand limp with fingers the colour of old rope and pewter-pale nails, one carrier’s thumb hooked under his arm to keep the head from lopping. She set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned his face as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it, went wide around the place the carriers crossed with a look that asked for nothing and found nothing, and gave the yard no name for what ailed him; no collector called, no figure given, no payer named and no slate opened, and the cost stayed entered nowhere (T077 advanced, not paid as a thread). At the going of the light each day she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before and river wind behind, going wide around the pan’s gone place, the bare dark trough, the rack space and the field’s empty place, and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled as a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and the thread frozen and unwiped (T058/T079). She moved her lips along the loaf row with its two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, kept her finger from beneath the front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100 carried), and glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without a touch. When her instruction went low and unfinished at the hearth on all three days Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper until the sentence reached the pot; the fraction stayed held and unspoken, a remembered holding on the second and third days and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 beat or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T062). While the finger stood Tarn’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check and neither man named the other’s silence (T036/T076). Three or four unnamed men went low into the back room before first grey on Day 187 and she gave them no name and did not say the room was cold; the two shut-room tellings stayed two with no third (T035/T031, T065/T095). No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no opening and no bond paid.

\end{itemize}

\item Ch 55: Through Days 216–218, Grain 7–9, the house keeps the second working week of Grain the way it keeps the fire: without an entry, without correcting either of the district’s two month-names, and with no market and no Account-day until Grain 10 (Day 219). She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings and afternoons, gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, moves her lips along a row standing with two unnamed gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, uncounted and uncopied, tells the fire it is the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot and stands with the back of the pot counting under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go. She sets the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and lets her hand rest a half-beat longer at the setting, and does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and sixteen, seventeen and eighteen days, while the river’s note comes through the finger’s-width door and the boards keep four nails, four and a thumb-width knot: three counts in three places that do not become one (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since — no opening in thirty-six, thirty-seven and thirty-eight days — and the private roll stays unshown while Dessa’s cost stays unentered. She sends a neighbour’s cost-question at the door and a rack woman’s at the well to the pot and the weather, nothing priced, refused or entered, and goes wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the pan’s gone round ring, the bare trough, the rack space with its broken birth-slates and the field’s empty place with a look and a wide step and no number (T077, T009/T013/T092/T098). She hears the wrong-wind saying take a third shape — a pot gone quiet on every row come the thaw — and gives the pot no story; she hears the burned-slate word go around a fourth time and makes nothing of it. Jorra’s quiet goes before him into the shed the way cold air goes before a door and the household straightens around it without an order from her; her unfinished sentence still arrives at the pot behind his remembered finger (T035/T031/T065/T095, T062). With Tarn she gives the broom its instruction and asks nothing about the ear or his seventh year, and no collector comes on any morning. She carries him home at the going of the light at the half-pace and sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen and unwiped, and goes to her own bed before the small hours of Day 218, the two rooms not touching. No new scar or possession, no opening, no bond paid or spoken; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 64: Days 243, 244 and 245, Smoke 4–6, Fourthday to Sixthday, on stage on all three days at the fire, the hearth, the loaf shelf with its two unnamed gaps, the bed, the drying racks, the Clay Yard, the yard well, the boards and the terrace, carrying him home each evening at the half-pace from every open slate and going wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number. Came to the fire before the basket on all three mornings; gave every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; said \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}; told the fire the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, counted under her breath toward no opening (small intake, hold, letting-go), pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale off the coals, moved her lips along the two-gapped row without giving a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shut her hand half over nothing without a touch, kept her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and sent cost-questions to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T058/T079, T100, T077). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 4, 5 or 6, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; the one opening stayed behind the household, not recalled as a sign, a lesson, a mending or a payment and with no payer named (T058/T079). The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp on all three mornings, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changed in state and given no figure, counted in glances, handfuls and the carrying arm’s weight that knows weight and not cost, entered on no slate and laid across none of the absences (T077). The fire answered four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty-three, forty-four and forty-five days, while the river’s note through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept three counts in three places that did not become one (T088, T061/T082). On Smoke 5 a woman of the firing work at the yard well, Ilva, passed a thumb-nail over notched birch bark before her eyes went to the woman who asked and before her mouth answered; Sella had no part in it and did not join the order of reaching to anything under her roof. On Smoke 6 a wrong wind off High Kiln brought the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touched the fold where the dressed grain lay and went out on the wind that brought it — a direction arrived nowhere and not a second edge paid — and she let one of the three pot sayings stand again as a saying with no fourth likeness made a cause (T064 held). At the hearth on all three days her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot behind Jorra’s remembered finger; with Tarn the two silences stayed unjoined and no collector came up or went down the clay road; Garl was kept in objects with his name unspoken two hundred and forty-five days. She set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, and went to her own bed before the small hours, leaving the coals to keep themselves. No new scar, possession or change of voice; no bond changed hands, the private roll stayed unshown and Dessa’s cost unentered.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 65: Days 246, 247 and 248, Smoke 7–9, Seventhday to Ninthday, on stage on all three days at the fire, the hearth, the loaf shelf with its two unnamed gaps, the bed, the drying racks, the Clay Yard, the yard well, the boards and the terrace, carrying him home each evening at the half-pace from every open slate and going wide around the walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number. Came to the fire before the basket on all three mornings; gave every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; told the fire the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening (small intake, hold, letting-go), pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale off the coals, moved her lips along the two-gapped row without giving a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shut her hand half over nothing without a touch, kept her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal tally stayed unread, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and sent cost-questions to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T058/T079, T100, T077). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 7, 8 or 9, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; the one opening was behind the household, not looked at again as sign, lesson, mending or payment and with no payer named (T058/T079). The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp on all three mornings, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changed state and gained no figure, counted in glances and handfuls and by an arm that knew weight and not cost, entered on no slate and laid across no absence (T077). \textbf{The question over the boards:} on the afternoon of Smoke 8 a voice with no owner, room, hand at the kiln or cause asked over the boards a fifth time which row the pot went quiet on; she answered it as she answered everything that wanted a number — the weather first, with the sweet edge of lead glaze on a wrong wind off High Kiln touching the fold and going out on the wind that brought it, and the price of barley after it — and the voice went up the terrace while the row stood where it stood with nobody leaning in to take the answer down. Five askings are not one witness and no row was named (T101 advanced, unpaid). At the yard well on Smoke 8 she saw Ilva draw water with her hand in her sleeve and give the answer to the question put; no figure came off the stick and the ninth hand stayed nine (T080 held). A man come down the clay road brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back into his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere (T015/T041/T047 held). The fire answered four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should be, its payer unnamed two hundred and forty-six, forty-seven and forty-eight days (T088). With Jorra her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot behind his remembered finger and she gave the men who went low into the back room no name; with Tarn the two silences stayed unjoined and his ear-sentence stopped short of the calling word with no tenth standing. Garl was kept in objects, his name unspoken two hundred and forty-eight days, no collector coming up or down the clay road on Smoke 7, 8 or 9 (T009/T013/T092). No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first and no ending.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 66: Days 249, 250 and 251, Smoke 10–12, Tenthday to Secondday, on stage on all three days at the hearth, the kiln mouth, the loaf shelf with its two unnamed gaps, the bed, the drying racks, the Clay Yard, the yard well, the boards, the terrace and the Cross with the moot-post’s thin shade, carrying him home each evening at the half-pace from every open slate and going wide around the walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number. Came to the fire before the basket on all three mornings; gave every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; said \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}; told the fire the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, counted under her breath toward no opening (small intake, hold, letting-go), pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale off the coals, moved her lips along the two-gapped row without giving a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shut her hand half over nothing without a touch, kept her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal tally stayed unread, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and sent cost-questions to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T058/T079, T100, T077). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 10, 11 or 12, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; the one opening before the kiln stayed behind the household, not looked at again as sign, lesson, mending or payment and with no payer named (T058/T079). The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp on all three mornings, spread thin, gathered back by the handful and the fold set flat, changed in state and given no figure, counted in glances, handfuls and by an arm that knew weight and not cost, entered on no slate and laid across no absence (T077). The fire answered four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty-nine, fifty and fifty-one days, while the river’s note through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept three counts in three places that do not become one (T088, T061/T082). \textbf{On Smoke 10, the first Account-day and market of the second firing,} she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction and no reason to the basket; she heard the levy called and denied with \emph{your house}, saw two hundred lean in and eight pigs go over the wet boards, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him (T015/T041/T047, T077, T058/T079). She gave nothing to the reading: the figure read stayed beside the figure paid with no signature between them and the grain stayed covered and unfigured under this roof. Garl was kept in objects with his name unspoken two hundred and fifty-one days and no collector on the clay road (T009/T013/T092). At dusk each day she put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped; no opening came after Smoke 1 and the private roll stayed unshown. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no lesson made, nothing explained.

\end{itemize}

The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin, gathered by the handful and laid flat under the fold on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure, counted in glances and handfuls and by an arm that knew weight and not cost, entered on no slate and laid across no absence (T077). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 13, 14 or 15, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; the one opening before the kiln stayed behind the household, not recalled as a sign, lesson, mending or payment and with no payer named, and the first firing of Frost (Day 271) stayed far off and unbrought (T058/T079). At the going of the light on Smoke 15 she carried him up the clay road, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right, left the thread frozen and unwiped, fed the fire and went to her own bed before the small hours. A man come down the clay road with a number in his fist brought it up toward the well, looked at it and put it back into his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere and was not a missing figure (T015/T041/T047 held). On Smoke 14 a pot set down wrong at the racks gave its high thin note before its time and a woman swept around it with a practical word about the slip; Sella made no lesson of the sound and no fourth likeness of the three sayings, and a wrong wind off High Kiln carried the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touched the fold and went out on the wind that brought it (T064). The fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and fifty-two, fifty-three and fifty-four days (T088).
