\textbf{Ch 102.} Ash’s third and last reading goes up the clay road in his locked box on the thirtieth of the dark month, earned by that morning’s own light, and with the three of Frost and the first, second and third of Bone and Ash’s first and second it makes \textbf{nine arithmetics of the year standing behind one unsigned figure}; nine readings are nine and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid and no signature stands on the space between. He comes up short off the clay road with the red cord folded square under his coat and the sweet green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, reads \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, calls the levy, denies it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never I, says something low to the block about kindness being entered and goes off up the road with the box locked and the third subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. The boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer and no doctrine stood up out of nine; nothing in it answered for the hand that went in on Seed 15 or the man carried out on Day 188. Sella’s widow’s mark, Garl’s uncalled debt, Jorra’s dust, Alda’s pages and Dessa’s name stayed untouched; he did not look into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 99.} Ash’s second reading goes up the clay road in his locked box on the twentieth of the dark month, earned by its own morning, and \textbf{eight arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure}: the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, and Ash’s first and second. Eight are eight and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature on the space, and a rule made from eight would want a payer put under all eight where none stood. He is unchanged in himself — the local face of the Court, a man with a clean slate and a good reason who wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over the figure, sends the figure twice over the basket once for the moot and once for the late households, and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, going off believing he has done a kindness. He said something low to the block about kindness being entered and the block answered nothing; there was no anger and no triumph in it. The boy keeps the finding on a place of its own with no payer under it, not a lesson, grievance, mending, doctrine or rule, and does not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the hand-at-the-sill breath, the Ash 5 joining, the Ash 17 direction or his own gaps — the edges came near to touching and the finger went between. No doctrine stood up out of eight, and the reading answered none of the held questions. Ash 19 and 21 were ordinary tending days with no market, Cross or bell and no collector on the road; Ash 30 (Day 359) stands nine mornings ahead and is named only as a date. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 96.} Ash’s first reading goes up the clay road in his locked box on the tenth of the dark month, earned by its own morning, and \textbf{seven arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure}: the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, and Ash’s first. Seven are seven and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space, and a rule made from seven would want a payer put under all seven where none stood. He is unchanged in himself — the local face of the Court, a man with a clean slate and a good reason who wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over the figure, sends the figure twice over the basket once for the moot and once for the late households, and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, going off believing he has done a kindness. He said something low to the block about kindness being entered and the block answered nothing. The boy keeps the finding on a place of its own with no payer under it, not a lesson, grievance, mending, doctrine or rule, and does not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the dressed grain under wool, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the handful, the thumb’s resting, the two small objects of the hand or his own gaps — the edges came near to touching and the finger went between. The reading answers nothing for the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188, the dressed grain read over by a number that did not know its cost or the carried fire’s missing fifth. Ash 11 and 12 were ordinary days with no market, Cross or bell and no collector on the road; no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 92.} Bone’s third and last reading goes up the clay road in his locked box on the thirtieth beside Frost’s three and Bone’s first two, and \textbf{six arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure}: six are six and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space between and a rule made from six would want a payer put under all six where none stood. He is unchanged in himself — the local face of the Court, a man with a clean slate and a good reason who wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over the figure, sends the figure twice over the basket once for the moot and once for the late households, and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, going off believing he has done a kindness. He said something low to the block about kindness being entered. The change was done to the square and not to the basket; the boy keeps the finding on a place of its own with no payer under it, not a lesson, grievance, mending, doctrine or rule, and does not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the four held changes, the handful, the thumb’s resting, the two small objects of the hand or his own gaps. The reading answers nothing for the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188, the dressed grain read over by a number that did not know its cost or the carried fire’s missing fifth. No collector comes up or goes down the clay road on Bone 28, 29 or 30 and Bone goes out without a boundary drawn; no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 89.} Bone’s second reading goes up the clay road in his locked box on the twentieth beside Frost’s three and Bone’s first, and \textbf{five arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure}: five are five and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space between and a rule made from five would want a payer put under all five where none stood. He is unchanged in himself — the local face of the Court, a man with a clean slate and a good reason who wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over the figure, sends the figure twice over the basket once for the moot and once for the late households, and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, going off believing he has done a kindness. The change was done to the square and not to the basket; the boy keeps the finding on a place of its own with no payer under it, not a lesson, grievance, mending, doctrine or rule, and does not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the four held changes, the two small objects of the hand or his own gaps. The reading answers nothing for the hare gone into the weather, the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188 or the dressed grain read over by a number that did not know its cost. No collector comes up or goes down the clay road on Bone 19, 20 or 21; no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 86.} Bone’s first reading goes up the clay road in his locked box beside Frost’s three, and four arithmetics now stand behind one printed figure: four are four and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid and a rule made from the four would want a payer where none stood. He is still the local face of the Court — a man with a clean slate and a good reason who wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over the figure and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes off believing he has done a kindness. The change is done to the square and not to the basket; the boy keeps the finding on a place of its own with no payer under it, not a lesson, grievance, mending, doctrine or rule, and does not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the four held changes or his own gaps. No collector comes up or goes down the clay road on Bone 11 or 12; the printed figure stands unchallenged and the space between figure and price stays unsigned.

\textbf{Ch 79.} Frost’s second reading goes up the clay road in his locked box with the true subtraction inside and cannot be changed back, while the figure read stays not the figure paid and the grain’s price stays unsigned. He is still the local face of the Court: a man with a clean slate and a good reason who takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes home believing he has done a kindness. Two arithmetics of Frost now stand behind and the third waits on Frost 30; he has entered none of it, and has never looked into the basket.

\textbf{Ch 72.} Smoke’s third and last reading goes up the clay road in his locked box with the true subtraction inside and cannot be changed back, while the figure read stays not the figure paid and the grain’s price stays unsigned. He is still the local face of the Court: a man with a clean slate and a good reason who takes himself out of his own sentence and goes home believing he has done a kindness.

He enters at the Account-day moot of Stone 10, Y.H. 812, wiping his thumb on his apron before touching the slate, and says \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} in a low voice that makes the shouting stop because the crowd has to lean in. He never says \emph{I}; he says the district, the account and the notice, and apologises in the form of an instruction. He sets the slate down twice and twice it answers flat, and he does not hear what the boy hears. Later, at the Slate Row end of the Cross, he confirms Sella’s widow’s mark as a kindness that is entered, leaves Garl’s debt against the tiles uncalled, and goes back to the moot with the red cord folded square. The locked box in his house has not been shown or named. He has been on the page for one chapter and is already the local face of the Court: reasonable, clean-handed, with a good reason for every cruelty and no idea that he has given any.

On Stone 14 the Thane comes down to the eel trade and is the same man in a market that he was at the Cross: the clean thumb, the passive grammar that takes the speaker out of his own sentence, the hand that counts a figure before he lets it go. He calls the levy for the feast and says it is not called by him, and takes four eels where six should go and does not seem to notice, which is how a man can be short and kind and reasonable in the same breath. The number of days to the Five is let out into the market air and is still nothing anybody can spend.

On Stone 20 he is the same man at the Cross that he was at the eel trade: the thumb wiped clean before the slate, the passive grammar that takes the speaker out of his own sentence, the figure passed over with a finger to make sure it is still where he put it. Two hundred people lean in because they have to; he reads one in twelve as the notice says, calls the levy for the feast and says it is not called by him, and goes around the uncalled debt against the tiles as carefully as Sella goes around Ash in a corner. He confirms the mark and the fire and sets the printed figure down where everyone can see it. The boy lies in the post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek and hears a number he cannot spend, and Berr never once looks into the basket or enters what he has left lying where it lay. He goes home by dusk believing he has done the district a kindness.

On Days 15 through 24 the same arithmetic is done at a remove. He is not on the page until Stone 30, when he reads the figure again at the last market of the year and says the levy was called for the feast and not by him, the grammar that takes the speaker out of his own sentence now ordinary market speech in every mouth around him. He goes around Garl’s uncalled debt without naming it, sets the printed figure where everyone can see it, and gives out that the Five are three days off while the district gives out three and then two and then whatever it has already decided to pay. The boy lies in the moot-post’s shade with cold iron at his cheek, and Berr never looks into the basket or enters what he has left lying where it lay. He goes home believing his own sentences and the box stays locked.

On Days 25 through 30 the same arithmetic is done at a remove and then begins a new year. He is glimpsed once, at the Weighing, with the red cord folded under his coat and the green at one corner of his mouth, wiping his thumb before he touches his slate and passing a finger over the figure; he reads a name the household will not repeat and goes off explaining nothing, the box still locked. The officer’s clean voice wears his grammar in a temple’s clothes, and a whole return is announced for somebody absent --- the district’s ordinary kindness, now in an institution’s mouth. At the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1 one in twelve is still printed and unchallenged, the true deduction is spoken by nobody, and Garl’s uncalled debt is left where it lay through the turn of the year. He goes on believing his own sentences and the box stays locked.

On Days 31 through 37 the same arithmetic is done at a remove and the withholding becomes a district habit. On Ilmen 7 Berr comes back from the river with the red cord folded under his coat, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, keeps a number he does not care to give and tells a neighbour there will be a slate at the watch; one in twelve stays printed and unchallenged and the true subtraction is spoken by nobody. He never looks into the basket. The boy files the twice-wiped thumb beside the other record-first hands without joining it to any of them, and watches the green at the corner of the mouth. The box stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

On Days 38 through 44 the same arithmetic goes on over a body entered nowhere, and the withholding becomes ordinary market speech. On Ilmen 10 he came to the Cross with the red wool cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} into the top of the leaning crowd, passed a finger over the figure and put himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}. The true subtraction went over the basket unspoken, the number for the thaw went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and was never given, and Garl’s uncalled debt lay in the space where a name might have stood. He looked nowhere near the basket in the moot-post’s shade and went home believing his own sentences. He was not at the Weir on Ilmen 14 or 15. The clerk he keeps at the Court’s table and the clerk set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody called both reached for the slate before the person; the boy kept the three record-first orders on separate trays and did not join them. The box in his house stayed locked and the true deduction stayed in it.

On Days 45 through 47 the same arithmetic is done at the remove of a yard and the withholding becomes the district’s ordinary speech. On Day 47 he comes up from the road with the red cord folded under his coat and the green at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a slate he will not open and says a number goes into a slate and not into a well. He takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}, never looks into the basket and goes off with the box still locked; the number for the thaw passes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere. The clerk at the Fishstairs still sits for a measure nobody called and the woman in the brook is still uncollected, and Berr’s twice-wiped thumb stays on the boy’s tray of record-first hands, not joined to the midwife’s, the neighbour’s at this well, the clerk’s behind the Court table or the man who priced the basket. He goes on believing his own sentences and the true deduction stays in the box.

On Days 48 through 54 the same arithmetic is done once more over a body the Court has not entered and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Account-day at the Cross he comes to the block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket; the true subtraction goes over it unspoken and the crowd goes back to the pigs. To a neighbour who begins to ask he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well; there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence; the number for the thaw goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and is given to nobody. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself. He goes off toward High Kiln believing his own sentences, never looking into the basket, with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside.

On Days 55 through 60 the same arithmetic is done once more over a body the Court has not entered and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Ilmen 30, the last Account-day and market before Silt, he comes to the block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket. He calls the levy for Silt and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}; the true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the number for the thaw goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and is given to nobody. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself. Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles goes around the space where a name might have stood and is not called. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs is glimpsed hand-to-slate-before-eyes and silent, filed apart from Marra, the Drawing collector and the Court-table clerk; Berr does not look into the basket and goes off toward High Kiln believing his own sentences. The box in his house stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

On Days 61 through 67 the same arithmetic is done at the remove of a market edge and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Silt 2 Berr comes up short below the north bridge with the red cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened and passes a finger over what is written. He says a number goes into a slate and not into a well and that there will be a slate at the watch, taking himself out of his own sentence and never saying \emph{I}; the green at his mouth and the twice-wiped thumb are the same tells the boy has kept for years. He does not look into the basket, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The soft-cuffed clerk sits silent at the landing with his hand to his slate before his eyes to the stalls, and the boy keeps the two orders of reaching apart. Nothing is called, paid or explained, and the figure the buyer gave for the pair goes into the noise of the stalls and is gone.

On Days 68 through 74 the same arithmetic is done over a district under water and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. On Silt 10, Account-day, he comes up short at the dry step with the water sitting on the one below, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened, passes a finger over the figure, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the water and the basket and takes himself out of his own sentence, never saying \emph{I} and never looking into the basket. The true subtraction goes over it unspoken, the number for the flood’s cost goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrives nowhere, and the bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. He goes off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness; the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the Fishstairs and the boy keeps Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or to any other record-first hand. Nothing is called, paid or explained, and the figure over the basket goes into the noise of the stalls and is gone.

On Days 78 through 84 the same arithmetic is done over a thinner district and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Silt 20 he comes to the block with the red cord folded under his coat, green glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads one in twelve over fewer bodies than stood at the flood’s Account-day. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the printed figure stands unchallenged; a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. He takes himself out of his own sentence and goes off believing he has done a kindness, with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. Garl’s debt against the tiles is left where it lay, neither paid nor settled, never done with. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself; the clerk at the Fishstairs still sits for an uncalled measure. The boy files the twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own and does not join it to any other hand. Nothing is called, paid or explained.

On Days 85 through 90 the same arithmetic is done over the last market of Silt and goes over the turn of the month unchanged. On Silt 30, the tenth day of the tend and the last market of Silt, he comes up to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before he touches nothing, reads one in twelve twice over the basket, passes a finger over the figure and says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}. To a man who brings a number in a fist and asks what the thaw will cost he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If the house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} --- and the number goes from the fist to his mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrives nowhere. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the printed figure stands unchallenged; a man can stand under it all morning and go home with the number still in his fist and never have entered it. He takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on and goes off toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself; across the market a woman stands with green at one corner of her mouth and the boy files it in silence without a name for the mouth or the woman. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs is still set for a measure nobody called. On Seed 1 a month turns over the arithmetic without noticing and he is not on the page; Garl’s debt against the tiles is neither paid nor settled and the box stays locked. The boy keeps the twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own and does not join it to any other hand, and no figure read aloud is the figure paid.

On Day 91 the same arithmetic is done over worked ground instead of a market, and the withholding stays the district’s ordinary speech. He comes down from the north road to look at the strips east of Low Kiln, short, with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it, the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm. To the man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting will cost now that seed has gone into the ground he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip. If the house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, and to the yard says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}. He never says \emph{I}; he takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and the true subtraction goes over the strips unspoken. A figure read aloud is not the figure paid and nothing in the strip changes its figure because a man has looked at it. He does not look into the basket, files his twice-wiped thumb on its own tray beside the other record-first hands, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The uncalled debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled.

On Days 94 through 100 the same arithmetic is done over the worked strips and then over a planting month that has become waiting, and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Seed 10, Tenthday and the second Account-day of Seed, he comes to the reading block at the Cross with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it; his hands are large and clean and he wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, passes a finger over the figure, calls the levy for Seed and says \emph{It is not called by me}, and says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the number for what the planting will cost goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrives nowhere; a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. The bell goes four, four and a gap over the market and nobody crosses himself; he keeps the heard bell beside the told bell in two places. At the Slate Row fringe a man whose name is on no roll, with soft hands and a patient face, hands a figure to a slate and holds it at the edge where nobody else can see; the boy files the soft hands apart from Marra, the Drawing collector with grey fingertips, the Court-table clerk and the Fishstairs clerk, apart from the child and the loaf, and does not call it a sale. Berr goes off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. He has not looked into the basket, has never said \emph{I}, and no new scar, possession or change of voice is recorded.

On Days 101 through 103 the same arithmetic is done from the clay road rather than the block and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He comes up the clay road on Seed 13 from the Cross with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, calls the levy and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{There’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The true subtraction goes over the basket unspoken and the number for the planting goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrives nowhere, a figure read aloud that is not the figure paid; nothing in the strip changes its figure because a man has looked at it. He does not look into the basket, files his twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own beside the other record-first hands, and goes off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The uncalled debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled and the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody called.

On Days 104 through 106 the same arithmetic is done over worked ground with hands in it and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Seed 15 he comes down off the north road at midday with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest a breath longer than the writing required. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the work, calls the levy and says it is not called by him. To a man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting will cost now that hands have gone into it he says a number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The figure read aloud is not the figure paid and the true subtraction sits in the locked box in his house up the road; nothing in the strip changes its figure because a man has looked at it. He never looks into the basket and goes off toward High Kiln believing he has done the district a kindness. Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles stays neither paid nor settled and the boy files his twice-wiped thumb on its own tray beside the other record-first hands, not joined to any of them. Offstage on Seed 16 and 17.

On Days 107 through 109 the same arithmetic is done over the planting month’s last tend and its Account-day, and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. On Seed 20, Tenthday and Account-day, he comes up to the reading block at the Cross short, with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and, under it, nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before he touches nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest a breath longer than the writing required, the way a man checks a dish he has already set down to be sure it will not slop. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd over the worked ground where the hands went in on Seed 15, calls the levy and says \emph{It is not called by me}. To a man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting cost now that hands have been in it, he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The sentence passes around the square like a bucket passed from hand to hand and nobody thinks to ask who is carrying it. The figure read aloud is not the figure paid; the true subtraction goes over the strips unspoken and sits in the locked box in his house up the road, and nothing in the ground changes its figure because a man has looked at it. The bell at the Cross goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself; word comes up that the soft-cuffed clerk is still set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody called. Garl’s uncalled debt against the firing of tiles goes around the space where a name might have stood and is not called. He never looks into the basket and goes off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness.

On Days 110 through 112 the same arithmetic is done over the planting month’s last tend and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He appears once, on Seed 22 in the afternoon at the outer edge of the yard well, and is offstage for the other two days. He comes up short off the north road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath; his hands are large and clean and he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, holding a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the leaning yard and says \emph{A number goes into a slate and not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. A man brings a number up out of a fist toward the well, looks at it, thinks better of giving it, puts the fist back in his sleeve and goes off, so the figure arrives nowhere; the district’s whole arithmetic is done in the open air, from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and nowhere, and a figure let fall is still a figure carried. The boy files Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to the neighbour’s reaching hand at the shelf or to any other record-first hand. Berr does not look into the basket and goes off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box in his house locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness; Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles goes around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with, and a thing kept is a thing that will one day be asked for.

On Days 113 through 115 the same arithmetic is done offstage and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He does not appear; on Seed 26 the boy sets the twice-wiped thumb and the finger over a figure on a place of its own among the record-first hands, beside the midwife’s reaching hand, the neighbour’s at the well, the Court-table clerk’s, the man who priced him, the wheel-keeper’s, the woman who keeps the fire’s and the midwife’s again — all kept apart and none joined. At the Cross a man whose name is on no roll holds a figure to a slate at the edge with a thumb resting on the corner afterward, without wiping twice and passing a finger over the number as Berr would have done, and the boy files the soft hands apart from him and from every other tray: no wiped thumb, no sentence with the speaker taken out of it, no sale. A number brought up out of a fist toward the well on Seed 24 is looked at and put back in the sleeve, arriving nowhere, the district’s arithmetic done in the open air without him. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled, never done with; Sella’s mark is untouched, Jorra’s dust unspoken, Alda’s notes where they belonged. He is off up the clay road with the box locked in his house and the true deduction inside, and nobody under the Vail roof has called him or thanked him or asked him for the figure.

On Days 116 through 119 the same arithmetic is done over the planting month’s last market and goes over the turn into Reed unchanged, and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He appears once, on Seed 30 at the reading block at the Cross, and is offstage on the other three days. He comes up short off the north road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and, under it, nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before he touches nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that will be on it, and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm while he passes a finger over what is written and lets his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required — the check of a man setting down a dish already sure it will not slop. He reads \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the two hundred and says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me.} To a man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the planting cost now the hands have been in it he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, leaving the field open and clean and nobody’s. The number goes from the fist to his mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrives nowhere. The figure read aloud is not the figure paid; the true subtraction sits in the locked box in his house up the road; and the figure that goes into the slate does not know the hand that did not come back out of the strip, does not know there had been a hand, does not know there had been a strip. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself, and the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the out-of-line Fishstairs landing for a measure nobody called. He has not looked into the basket, has never said \emph{I}, and enters none of it. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled; he goes off up the clay road believing he has done the district a kindness, the box still locked and the true deduction inside. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

Through Reed 1–3 the same arithmetic is done offstage and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He does not appear; on Reed 3 the boy passes over his twice-wiped thumb and his finger laid on a figure that was not the figure paid as one shape among the record-first hands on their separate trays, not joined to the soft-cuffed clerk’s order of reaching, the neighbour’s hand at the shelf, the midwife’s reaching for a slate before a child, the wheel-keeper’s, the woman who keeps the fire’s or the foundling’s late turning. The direction the planting withheld no longer has hands in it and the reed work is a going-downriver judged by the arm that carries it; no figure goes with either, and the hand that did not come back out of the strip still has no figure, no name and no body. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of; Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. He is off up the clay road with the box locked in his house and the true deduction inside, and nobody under the Vail roof has called him or thanked him or asked him for the figure. Never said \emph{I}, never looked into the basket; no new scar, possession or change of voice.

On Day 125 the same arithmetic is done over the first reed bundles of the year and the withholding stays ordinary market speech. He comes up short off the clay road with the red cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and nothing under it, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required, the way a man checks a dish he has set down to be sure it will not slop. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, calls the levy and says it is not called by him, and to a man who brings a number up out of a fist and asks what the reeds cost now the hands are out of them says a number goes into a slate, not into a bundle, and that there will be a slate at the watch — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. The number arrives nowhere, the true subtraction stays in the locked box in his house up the road, and a figure read aloud is not the figure paid; a number put into a slate is not a number put into a strip. The boy keeps the cord in the man’s coat, the tally in the slate and the figure that went nowhere on three places, and no hand of his could lay one across another. Berr does not look into the basket and goes off believing he has done a kindness; Garl’s uncalled debt goes around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with.

On Days 126 through 128 he is offstage on Reed 7 and 9 and comes up short off the clay road on Reed 8, late in the day, with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passes a finger over a figure and lets his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a bundle}, he says; to a man who brings a number up out of a fist he says there will be a slate at the watch — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. He reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, calls the levy and says it is not called by him; the figure arrives nowhere, the true subtraction stays in the locked box and the number read aloud does not know the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back out of the strips. He never looks into the basket. His green is filed apart from the third green glimpsed at the market’s edge the day before, and his twice-wiped thumb goes on a tray of its own among the record-first hands, not joined to the soft-cuffed clerk’s order of reaching, the midwife’s reaching hand, the wheel-keeper’s or the woman who keeps the fire. The boy reads the self-removal as the oldest grammar he knows, a chart that says one thing and a room that has done another, and puts it where it belongs. Sella’s mark and Garl’s debt are untouched, Jorra’s dust unasked about, Alda’s pages unread, Dessa dead and unnamed. The box stays locked, the good reason stays good, and he goes up the clay road believing he has done a kindness.

One in twelve is printed and unchallenged over the first Account-day of Reed, and the true subtraction stays in the locked box up the clay road. A figure read over a crowd is not the figure paid, and does not know the hand that did not come back out of the strips. The twice-wiped thumb stays on its own tray among the record-first hands; his green stays a colour on its own place and is not Fenna. The good reason is intact.

One in twelve is still the printed figure and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid. On Reed 15 he added the bundle to the strip and the well in the saying \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle}, paid two marks short for two pair of eels, and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. His green is one of five shapes of the colour and stays on its own place, not the silent woman’s green and not Fenna; the twice-wiped thumb stays on its own tray among the record-first hands. The box stays locked, the good reason stays good, and he goes up the clay road believing he has done a kindness.

On Day 137 the arithmetic of the market stays separate from the rest. He comes up short with the red cord folded under his coat and glaze green at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds the narrow slate unopened to his forearm and passes a finger over the figure; he buys two pair of eels and pays two marks short, and the stall-keeper puts the marks in her palm without counting them aloud. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle}; if the house wants it again there will be a slate at the watch, and the house is never I. The low sentence about the levy and one in twelve goes into the boards, read and not paid, while the true subtraction sits in the locked box up the clay road. A figure read aloud is not the figure paid, and nothing in the ground changed its figure because he looked at it. He goes off believing he has done a kindness, his twice-wiped thumb on its own tray. The second Account-day of Reed stands two days off, when he will read one in twelve again over the last bundles.

On Days 138 through 140 the performance of arithmetic goes on with the speaker taken neatly out of it. On Day 139, the second Account-day of Reed, he comes up short to the reading block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and glaze at one mouth-corner, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passes a finger over the figure and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the last bundles of the reed month; he calls the levy and denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, so the figure goes into the air and the true subtraction stays in the locked box. The heard bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself and the clerk below the bridge stays set for a measure nobody called. A fifth green comes to a silent woman’s mouth across the square, a colour and not a name, held on a place of its own beside his glaze and the four earlier greens. At the stalls he takes two pair of eels and pays two marks short, the stall-keeper putting the marks in her palm without counting them where anyone can hear, says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle} and lets the low voice about the levy fall on the boards with nobody leaning in; then he goes up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box locked, believing he has done a kindness. On Day 140 he is offstage, and the reed month enters its last week with the figure he read still not knowing the hand that did not come back. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, and the box stayed shut.

Through Reed 23 the box stays locked and the subtraction stays true. He comes up short off the clay road in the afternoon with the red cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of glaze at one mouth-corner, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds the narrow slate unopened and reads the printed figure as the notice says it, calls the levy and denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sending a man with a number to a slate at the watch. At the stalls a number goes into a slate and not a bundle; he pays two marks short into a palm that does not count where anyone can hear, believes he has done the district a kindness and goes up the road with the box still locked. The figure read aloud does not know the hand that did not come back out of the strip, and a figure read is not a figure paid. He takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on, and the grammar he speaks is the same one that will one day be heard in the Keeping; he is offstage on Day 141 and Day 143 and no new possession or change of voice came to him.

On Day 149, the third Account-day and the last market of Reed, the good reason is intact and the arithmetic stays in the slate and not in the hand. He comes up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passes a finger over the figure and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by over the last bundles. He calls the levy and denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, says a number goes into a slate and not a bundle and that there will be a slate at the watch, takes two pair of eels and pays two marks short into a palm that does not count them aloud, and goes off up the clay road with the box locked behind him and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done the district a kindness. The figure read aloud is not the figure paid, and the figure that goes into the slate does not know the hand that did not come back out of the strips; his green stays on its own tray, a colour joined to no ear, and the twice-wiped thumb is one more record-first hand filed apart.

\textbf{Ch 38.} On Day 158 the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat was spoken of as a direction up the clay road toward High Kiln, not as a place anybody meant to go that day, and a number came up from the road in a man’s fist and went from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrived nowhere while the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged; his cord, green at the mouth spoken of but not seen, was a direction and no more. On Day 159, the first Account-day and market-day of Tallow, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, his hands large and clean, wiping his thumb twice before touching nothing. He held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. A figure read aloud was not a figure paid. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the bridge at the out-of-line landing with his slate turned inward for a measure nobody called, hand to slate before eyes to stalls. His narrow slate went up the clay road edge-on toward Greybank in the hands of Hessa Rale of Slate Row, who carried it and did not read it and let nobody read it; the boy filed her order of reaching as an eighth record-first hand apart from his twice-wiped thumb. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and carried it home at the going of the light saying nothing. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; box locked, good reason intact. \textbf{Ch 49 (bonds).} On Day 199, Ember 20, the second Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. The reading did not answer the man carried out on Day 188: no figure, collector or slate knew what he cost, no collector was called and no cause was named in Grathic. Hessa carried his slate up the road unread; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the landing for his uncalled measure. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s debt were neither touched nor named, and he did not look into the basket. No bond paid, no new scar or possession, no change of voice; the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

On the month’s second Account-day the same arithmetic is done in the same reasonable voice. He comes up to the block under the moot-post with the red cord folded square, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, reads one in twelve as the notice says and denies the levy with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sending a man with a number in his fist to a slate at the watch. The crowd leans in and goes back to the pigs; the printed figure stands unchallenged and the true subtraction goes home in the locked box. The heard bell stands beside the told bell and his slate goes up the road in the hands of a woman who carries without reading. He goes off believing he has done the district a kindness, and nothing in his account has changed.

On Days 173 through 179 the same arithmetic is done at the remove of a month’s end, and on Day 179, the third Account-day and last market of Tallow, he comes up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord folded square under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one mouth-corner. He wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passes a finger over the figure, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid; the bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. His slate goes up the road in Hessa Rale’s hands, edge-on and unread. He has never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind.

On Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day of the kiln month, he comes up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red office cord folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner. He wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passes a finger over the figure, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid; the bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. His slate goes up the clay road in Hessa Rale’s hands, edge-on and unread. He was not called for the glaze-room hand carried out on Day 188, and never once looks into the basket or enters any of this in his own mind. The box stays locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 52.} The kiln month goes out with its third and last reading, and the arc’s great subject becomes a figure changed for the third time in one month and still not paid. Berr comes up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth; he wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passes a finger over the figure and reads \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that come late. He says \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changes for the third time and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid, and the reading answers nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 — no figure, collector, slate, cause or offstage death, and no name for what ailed him. The bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, heard beside told; Hessa carries the slate up the road unread and the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the landing for his uncalled measure. The boy reads the twice-told figure and the speaker’s taking himself out of his own sentence as the grammar of charts and signatures, and a crowd sorted in ninety seconds by a man with no hand to carry any of it. Forward, not closed.

On Grain 10 he reads Grain’s first figure as he has read every figure: twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, with the thumb wiped twice before touching nothing and the speaker taken neatly out of his own sentence. He calls the levy, denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes up the road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness; the district’s arithmetic changes for Grain and cannot be changed back, while a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid and the reading answers nothing for the man carried out on Day 188. Offstage through the two tending days, he is present only as a shape in the boy’s file and a subtraction nobody can reach.

Grain’s second Account-day on Day 229 is his third reading in the harvest month and the second of Grain, and it changes the district’s arithmetic where two hundred people stood and cannot be changed back: he reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, calls the levy and takes himself out of his own sentence with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sends a man’s number from fist to mouth to shoulder into a slate at the watch, and goes off up the clay road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid; the dressed grain under the Vail roof is read over by a number that does not know what it cost, and the true subtraction answers nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that did not come back out of the strip. He is the most frightening thing in Sarn — not a dark lord but a reasonable man with a ledger and a good reason — and the reason is the part that will be remembered against him. Nothing he has kept has been opened or paid.

Through Smoke 10–12 (Days 249–251) he comes up short off the clay road on the first Account-day and market of the second firing and reads Smoke’s first arithmetic over the basket, changing the district’s numbers for the month in a way that cannot be changed back while his own box goes up the road locked with the true subtraction inside and he believes he has done a kindness. He is offstage on Smoke 11 and 12; the arithmetic stands behind and is not brought early, and nothing under the Vail roof is settled by it. His large clean hands, twice-wiped thumb, narrow slate held unopened to the forearm, finger passed over the figure, eyes resting a breath longer than the writing required, red wool cord folded square and green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner are as they have been for a dozen markets; the figure read aloud is still not the figure paid and the space between the figure read over the covered grain and its cost has no signature. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

Through Smoke 19–21 he is seen once, on Smoke 20, the second Account-day and market of the second firing, and does what he did at the first: comes up short off the clay road with the red cord folded square, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over a narrow slate and reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, calls the levy, denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and goes off up the clay road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changes a second time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stands unchallenged and the figure read is still not the figure paid, and the figure read over the dressed grain covered at home does not know what it cost, the space between the two figures having no signature. Hessa carries the slate up the road unread; the bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the landing for a measure nobody called. Sella sets the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade and stands half a pace off, giving the house no reason and saying nothing on the walk home. The reading answers nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15; Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt stay untouched and unnamed, and the boy is not looked into (T015/T041/T047, T077, T078, T080, T090).

On Frost 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 279), the first Account-day and market of the month, he comes up short off the clay road as he came up short on Smoke 10, 20 and 30, with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay the smell of nothing at all. His large clean hands wipe the thumb twice before touching nothing, hold a narrow slate unopened to the forearm, pass a finger over the figure and let the eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing requires; he reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the two hundred, calls the levy and denies it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and goes off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the first true subtraction of Frost inside, believing he has done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changes for the new month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid. The reading answers nothing for the man carried out on Day 188, the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, or the dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end, which is read over by a number that does not know what it cost. Hessa carries the narrow slate up the road unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stays set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and the bell goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself (T080, T090, T078). He never looks into the basket and has entered that nowhere nowhere. Offstage on Frost 11 and 12; the arithmetic stands behind and is not brought early (T015/T041/T047, T077 advanced, unpaid).

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 121: On Ilmen 20 (Day 414), the month’s second Account-day and market, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm with the writing inward, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve, let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, sending it twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sent a man with a number in a shut fist to a slate at the watch, said something low to the block about kindness being entered with no anger and no triumph, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Ilmen’s second true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. \textbf{Two readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure} — two and not one account, the first not made a thirteenth by the second, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space and no doctrine out of two; the twelve old arithmetics were not laid across the two new ones, for paper is not a payer and the key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. The boy filed the order of his reaching on its own tray and kept his low saying about kindness on a place of its own with no payer standing. Hessa carried the slate up the road before noon unread and was not made a reader by a second figure; Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge for a measure nobody called; the bell went four, four and a gap and the green and the shape stayed sightings with no eighth. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 117: On Ilmen 10 (Day 404), the new year’s first Account-day and market, came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve, read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by and sent it twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the late households; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, said something low to the block about kindness being entered with no anger and no triumph, sent a number from a shut fist to a slate at the watch and went off up the road with the box locked and the year’s first true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. Something low he said to the block about kindness being entered, in the tone of a man setting a cup where a cup belongs, and the block answered nothing. He went off up the clay road with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked, Stone’s second true subtraction riding inside beside the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone and the first, second and third of Ash, believing he had done a kindness with no anger and no triumph. \textbf{Eleven arithmetics of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — eleven are eleven and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid and no doctrine out of eleven; the boy kept the twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own and joined it to none.
