Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him (T058/T079). The reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back (T064, T098 carried). No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid or repaired: box locked, good reason intact.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 62: Day 239, Grain 30, Tenthday, the third and last Account-day and market of Grain, morning at the reading block under the moot-post and going off up the clay road toward High Kiln; offstage on Grain 28 and 29. Came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all; his hands were large and clean and he wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required (T015/T041/T047). He read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, and said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon withdraws a hand before the dressing goes on. The district’s arithmetic changed for the third time in Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. The reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back; no figure, collector, slate, cause or name stood to either absence and no offstage death was invented (T077, T098 carried). The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told (T078); Hessa Rale took his narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and no figure came off it (T080 advanced, not paid); below the north bridge the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called (T090). Across the square at the pot board the seventh green stayed a colour at a silent woman’s mouth and at the market’s edge the seventh shape stayed a shape in cast-offs, with no eighth of either, no name and no joining (T050/T051, T033/T034 held). He never looked into the basket and went off with the cord folded square, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked, believing he had done a kindness. The boy kept his twice-wiped thumb and finger over the figure on their own tray and did not let the old shape stand up beside Hessa’s inward slate, the clerk’s inward slate or any other record-first hand and call itself a rule (T080). No new scar or possession, no change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 59: On Day 229, Grain 20, Tenthday, the second Account-day and market of Grain, morning at the reading block under the moot-post and going off up the clay road toward High Kiln; offstage on Grain 19 and 21. Came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, smelling of hot clay and, under that, of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands were large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm with the writing turned inward, passed a finger over the figure and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, then raised them to the crowd. The order of reaching — thumb, slate, finger, eyes — went down into the private file as an old shape on an old place; he did not file it twice and did not let it stand up beside the other record-first hands and call itself a rule (T080). He read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, and said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}. To a man at the rail who brought a number up out of a fist and wanted to know what the month’s firing would want now the harvest had been dressed and stored he said a number goes into a slate and not into a bundle, and that if \emph{your house} wanted it again there would be a slate at the watch — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes his hand out of a field before the dressing goes on; the number went from the fist to his mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrived nowhere. He never looked into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the cord folded square and the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked with the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the second time in Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid, and the true subtraction answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or for the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, heard beside told (T078); Hessa Rale took his slate up the road unread and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge for a measure nobody called (T080/T090). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off, giving no reason to the basket, and carried him home at midday saying nothing of what had been read over him. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were neither touched nor named; Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of; Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged; Dessa is dead and unnamed and the figure read over the boy did not know her name or his. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid or repaired; box locked, good reason intact.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 56: Day 219, Grain 10, Tenthday, the first Account-day and market of Grain, morning at the reading block under the moot-post; offstage on Days 220 and 221. Came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, smelling of hot clay and of nothing at all. His hands were large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm with the writing turned inward, passed a finger over the figure, let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, and only then raised them to the crowd. He read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for those who came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. To a man at the rail who brought a number up out of a fist he said a number goes into a slate and not into a bundle and that if \emph{your house} wanted it again there would be a slate at the watch; the number went from the fist to his mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrived nowhere. The true subtraction went back up the road in the locked box and the printed figure stood where it had always stood. He never looked into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the cord folded square and the narrow slate under his arm, believing he had done the district a kindness. The boy kept his twice-wiped thumb and finger over the figure on their own tray and did not join them to Hessa’s runner’s hand, the clerk’s hand at the landing or any of the other record-first hands (T015/T041/T047, T080). The figure read was still not the figure paid and did not know what the man carried out on Day 188 had cost (T077). Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt were neither touched nor named; Dessa stayed dead and unnamed. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. At the Cross, before two hundred people and eight pigs, wiped his thumb on his apron before touching the clean slate and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} in the voice that stops the roar; added that a household which has heard otherwise has heard wrong, that the account stands as read, and that there will be a slate at the watch for any household that wants the figure again. Read it a second time in the afternoon for the households that came late. Set the slate down twice; both times it gave its small flat answer, unremarked. Wore the red wool cord of his office folded square and tasted his own glaze without appearing to. At the Slate Row end confirmed Sella’s widow’s mark as a kindness entered by the factor at Greybank, spoke around the uncalled debt against the firing of tiles, did not ask to see the mark, and left the debt as he found it. Did not look into the basket and never addressed the boy.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Day 8, at the Fishstairs. Came down the steps with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, hands large and clean, thumb wiped on his apron before he touched his slate, lead-glaze green at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing. Said \emph{the levy is called for the feast; it is not called by me} to the eels, accepted four eels where six should go, and gave out \emph{three days to the Five} from the top of the steps with a finger passed over the figure. Did not acknowledge the two eels short against his two marks short of six years and did not look into the basket.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Day 14, Stone 20, Account-day, at the Cross. Came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, hands large and clean and lead-glaze green at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching the slate. Read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of a crowd of two hundred, added that a household which has heard otherwise has heard wrong, passed a finger over the figure and said \emph{The figure stands as read. There’ll be a slate at the watch if the house wants it again.} Said \emph{the levy is called for the feast; it is not called by me.} Spoke of the kiln-house, the mark confirmed by the factor at Greybank and the fire kept under the roof, and went around a consignment of tiles where a debt might have stood, never naming it. Did not look into the basket and went home by dusk believing his own sentences. The box in his house stayed locked.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Day 24, Stone 30, Account-day and the year’s last market. Came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and lead-glaze green at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching the slate and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, passed a finger over the figure, and said the levy was called for the feast and was not called by him. Went around the uncalled debt against the firing of tiles without naming it, set the printed figure where everyone could see it, and did not look into the basket. The household’s stores went into the last tend and the Five were spoken of as three days off; the district argued three, two and whatever the moot had already decided to give out. Went back to the pigs by dusk believing he had done the district a kindness. The box in his house stayed locked and the true deduction stayed in it.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Day 26, Weighing. Glimpsed at the edge of the reading with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb before touching his slate and passed a finger over the figure. An officer in a clean voice wearing a temple’s clothes read the measures --- his Cross grammar in an institution’s mouth --- announced a whole return for a person not in the room and read a name the household would not afterward repeat; he explained nothing, looked nowhere near the basket and went off with the box in his house still locked. On Ilmen 1 one in twelve stayed printed and unchallenged at the Opening of the Slates and the true deduction was spoken by nobody. The box stayed locked and the uncalled debt against the tiles stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Day 36, Ilmen 7, came back from looking at the ice with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth; wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, passed a finger across the figure on a narrow slate he held, and had a number he did not care to give. To a neighbour at the well who started to ask said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If your house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, saying \emph{your house} and not \emph{my account}, and took himself out of his own sentence. Went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and looked nowhere near the basket. One in twelve stood printed and unchallenged and the true subtraction was spoken by nobody.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Day 39, Ilmen 10, Account-day. Came to the Cross with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} into the crowd, called the levy for the thaw and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}. To a neighbour who started to ask said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well}; the true subtraction went over the basket and the number for the thaw went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and was never given. Went around Garl’s uncalled debt without naming it, did not look into the basket and went off with the box in his house still locked. Not at the Weir on Ilmen 14 or 15.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

Wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened, passing a finger over it and letting his eyes rest longer than the writing required. Said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. The house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence; never said I. Did not look into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. The figure that had gone from fist to mouth to shoulder went with him into a slate and stayed there.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\end{itemize}

Said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well; there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence, never saying \emph{I}. Did not look into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside. \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

On Silt 10, Account-day, came up short at the dry step with the water sitting on the one below, red cord folded under his coat, green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay under the smell of nothing at all. Wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passed a finger over what was written and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the water and the basket, taking himself out of his own sentence, never saying \emph{I} and never looking in. The true subtraction went over the basket unspoken; the number for the flood’s cost went from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrived nowhere; the bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. Word came up that the soft-cuffed clerk was still set at the Fishstairs, and the boy put Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or any other record-first hand. Went off toward High Kiln with the box still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

Passed a finger over the figure, took himself out of his own sentence and went off toward High Kiln believing he had done a kindness. The true subtraction went over the basket unspoken and the printed figure stood unchallenged over fewer bodies: a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself; the soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs was still set for a measure nobody called, hand to slate before eyes to stalls. Did not look into the basket, left Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles neither paid nor settled, and went away with the box in his house locked and the true deduction inside. Offstage for the rest of the week.

\end{itemize}

\item Ch 24: Day 111, Seed 22, afternoon, at the outer edge of the yard well, offstage on Seed 21 and 23. Came up short off the north road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all; hands large and clean, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest a breath longer than the writing required, the way a man checks a dish already set down to be sure it will not slop. Read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the leaning yard, said \emph{A number goes into a slate and not into a strip. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. A man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it, thought better of giving it, put the fist in his sleeve and went off, so the figure arrived nowhere; nothing in the strip’s account changed its figure because a man had looked at it. Never said \emph{I} and did not look into the basket; the boy put his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to the neighbour’s reaching hand at the shelf or to any other record-first hand. Tarn said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. Went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the narrow slate under his coat and the box locked in his house behind him and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness; Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 25: Offstage on Days 113–115, Seed 24–26, present only as a filed shape. On Seed 26 at the Fishstairs the boy set his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over a figure on a place of its own among the record-first hands — a midwife reaching for a slate before a child, a neighbour at a well, a clerk behind a Court table, a man who priced him, Jorra speaking to the wheel before the pots, Sella giving the instruction to the wool before anybody, Alda laying her birth-slates down before the fold — and did not join any of them. At the Cross a man from Slate Row whose name was on no roll held a figure to a slate at the edge where nobody else could see it and rested his thumb on the corner afterward without wiping twice and passing a finger over the number as Berr would have done; the boy filed the soft hands apart from him and from Marra, the Drawing collector, the Court-table clerk and the Fishstairs clerk, a sixth shape on no tray, with no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand and no sale. A man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well on Seed 24, looked at it, thought better of giving it and put the fist back in his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with; Sella’s widow’s mark stayed untouched, Jorra’s dust and the back room unspoken, Alda’s second notes where they belonged. Never said \emph{I} and never looked into the basket; the box stayed locked in his house up the clay road and the true deduction inside, and he believed he had done the district a kindness. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\item Ch 26: Day 119, Seed 30, Tenthday, Account-day and the last market of Seed, at the reading block at the Cross; offstage on Seed 27–29. Came up short off the north road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, smelling of hot clay and, under it, nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands were large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice on his apron before he touched anything, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it, and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm while he passed a finger over what was written and let his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required, the check of a man setting down a dish already sure it will not slop. He read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the two hundred and said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me.} A man come up from the strips brought a number up out of a fist and asked what the planting cost now the hands had been in it; Berr did not look at the palm, passed his finger over the figure again the way a surgeon goes back to the chart before the patient, and said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. The man shut his fist and put it back in his sleeve and the number went from the fist to Berr’s mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrived nowhere. A figure read aloud was not the figure paid, the true subtraction sat in the locked box in his house up the road and had not been shown to anybody, and the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself, and the soft-cuffed clerk was still set at the out-of-line Fishstairs landing with his slate to his forearm for a measure nobody called. He never looked into the basket; the boy kept his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to any other record-first hand. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with. He went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box locked in his house behind him and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\end{itemize}

The sixth green stayed a colour at the pot board and the foundling a shape at the market’s edge, no seventh of either (T050/T051, T033/T034 held). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood a half-pace off, giving no instruction or reason to the basket. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 66: Day 249, Smoke 10, Tenthday, the first Account-day and market of the second firing, morning at the reading block under the moot-post and going off up the clay road toward High Kiln; offstage on Smoke 11 and 12. Came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, hot clay under the smell of nothing at all, his hands large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it (T015/T041/T047). Held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, then read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes his hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness (T077). The district’s arithmetic changed for the first time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, answering nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15, and the figure read over the dressed grain lying covered under wool at home did not know what that grain had cost — the space between the two figures had no signature. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told (T078). Hessa Rale carried his narrow slate up the clay road edge-on and unread, and to a woman who asked what she carried said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} (T080 advanced, not paid); below the north bridge the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called (T090). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off, giving no instruction or reason to the basket, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him (T058/T079). No new scar or possession, no change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

\end{itemize}

He said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the third true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness (T015/T041/T047). The district’s arithmetic changed for the third time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, answering nothing for the man carried out on Day 188, the hand that went in on Seed 15 or the dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end, whose price stayed unsigned (T077, T098 carried). Two hundred leaned over the reading block and eight pigs went over the wet boards; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told (T078). I’ve got a road to walk}; no figure came off the slate and the eight record-first hand stayed on a place of its own, advanced and not paid; offstage on Grain 19 and 21; earlier on Day 219 (Grain 10, the first Account-day and market of Grain) and on Day 209 (Ember 30, the third and last Account-day of the kiln month) she carried the same slate up the same road in the same manner, edge-on, writing inward and unread}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 38}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
A woman of thirty-odd years with the drained, level face of somebody who has walked the same road too often to measure it any more. Nothing about her is arranged for looking at: her coat is shortened at the skirt for the road’s mud, and the mud has dried on it in a pale scurf which she does not brush off, because a runner’s coat is a tool and nobody scours a tool for its own sake. A strap crosses her chest and a second, shorter strap has been let out to take the weight when the road is long; she settles both without seeming to, the way a person settles a burden that has become part of the walk. Her hands are the hands of a woman who carries and does not open. The fingers close on a slate’s edge with a working looseness, the thumb lies along the grain of the frame, and nothing presses where the writing is. She holds the slate edge-on to her own forearm so that the face of it turns toward her sleeve and the writing looks at nobody. That is not concealment: it is the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. She moves at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. What people notice first is the slate; what they notice last, if they notice at all, is that her hand went to it before her eyes went to them.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Clipped, practical, the grammar of the road rather than the Court. She answers the question actually put and not the one behind it, and she is done with a conversation when the road is done with it, without rudeness and without apology. She never pronounces, never reads aloud, never says \emph{the account} or \emph{the figure} where \emph{the slate} will do. Her sentences are short and complete; what she will not carry she leaves standing where it was set down, the way a man leaves a pot where there is no hand to carry it. A slight dry amusement goes with the road and not with people.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which.”

\item “Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk.”

\item “Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She comes out of Slate Row, where the Court’s tables and the Waiting Room stand and where a person can be made answerable for a thing merely by having touched it. She took up running because it was work that could be measured in the legs and kept in the hands: a slate goes from the Cross to Greybank and back, and what is written on it belongs to the person who set it down. Over the years she has carried slates for the assessor’s house, for the collector’s table at the Cross, and for Berr Clay the Thane, whose narrow slate goes up the clay road ahead of the reading and comes back with the true subtraction nobody in Sill has been shown. She has never been asked to read one and has never offered. The district is full of people who put a hand to a record before they put an eye to a person; she is one of them and does not know it, or does not think about it, which amounts to the same thing from the outside. She knows the road in all weathers, knows which ruts hold water and which stretch of the clay road dries pale in scurf, and has made a bargain with distance that she keeps without thinking. Nothing in her history has yet made her a reader of anyone’s private keeping, and she is careful that nothing does.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
No wound is spoken of. Her hands carry the small wear of a working person who grips an edge and not a face: nails short, thumb callused along one side from the frame of a slate, the skin at the wrist hardened by a strap. She fears a slate rubbed blank in a coat, a strap parting on the road, and being made answerable for a figure she did not set down; these are the fears of a carrier, not of a clerk. She has seen what happens to a person in Slate Row who is caught between a figure and the person it is about, and she keeps her own face turned toward the sleeve.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the road kept, the slates delivered whole, and to be paid for carrying and never for knowing. She thinks she wants nobody to take an interest in what she carries. What she needs, years from now, is harder: to understand that a figure is not a thing that travels by itself, and that the hand which lays the district’s separate keepings together will one day be a hand like hers — a carrier’s hand that has learned, too late, what it has been carrying. That day is far off and she is not yet part of it.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 121 (bonds).} On Ilmen 20, the month’s second Account-day and market, she went up the clay road toward Greybank before noon carrying Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, her hand to the slate before her eyes went up to the crowd, giving no figure and not made a reader by the carrying; asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it. Offstage as a sighting on Ilmen 21 and 22 and not on any road; no slate of hers was opened within reach of the basket and no figure came off any wood. She is not the second man from Slate Row who went down the north bridge road on Ilmen 21 with his own narrow slate turned to his sleeve — his slate and direction are his own shape on a place of its own, filed beside the first man’s face, the clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping with a finger between every pair (T102 opened, advanced and not paid) — and she is not the soft-cuffed clerk whose entered figure stayed a report at the landing, not a reader made of the softening at the river’s skin and not the speaker of any word that came up at the well. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stays eight and joined to none, with a finger between it and the fifth shaping, the entered figure, Ilva’s ninth staying nine and the faces filed and not counted. The first and second arithmetics of the year have gone up the clay road in Berr Clay’s locked box and she did not read either; her going up the road unread on the Account-days behind goes on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together, advanced and not paid. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 120 (bonds).} Not on stage as a sighting on Ilmen 17, 18 or 19 and not on any road; no slate of hers is opened within reach of the basket and no figure comes off any wood. When the softening at the river’s skin came on the nineteenth and the yard called it weather, she is expressly not a reader made of that change and no figure came off either her slate or the river; Tarn’s sentence withheld on the eighteenth and said again on the nineteenth is not hers and buys no figure on her wood. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stays eight and joined to none, with a finger between it and the fifth shaping of the well-saying found where put, the clerk’s entered figure on its own place, Ilva’s ninth staying nine, and the man from Slate Row’s face filed and not counted. The first arithmetic of the year has gone up the clay road in Berr Clay’s locked box and she did not read that either; her going up the road unread on the Account-days behind goes on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together, advanced and not paid. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 119 (bonds).} Not on stage as a sighting on Ilmen 14, 15 or 16 and not on any road; no slate of hers is opened within reach of the basket and no figure comes off any wood. When word came up the yard on Ilmen 15 that the soft-cuffed clerk set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing had entered a figure on his inward slate before he looked up to find the man who gave it, she is expressly not that clerk and not the speaker, not a sighting and not a reader made of the report. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stays eight and joined to none, with a finger between it and the fifth shaping of the well-saying found where put, the clerk’s entered figure on its own place, Ilva’s ninth staying nine and the man from Slate Row’s face filed and not counted. The first arithmetic of the year has gone up the clay road in Berr Clay’s locked box and she did not read that either; her going up the road unread on the Account-days behind goes on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together, advanced and not paid. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 118 (bonds).} Not on stage as a sighting on any of the three days; on Ilmen 12 (Day 406) she is present only as the unnamed subject of a word at the yard well: one of the bucket-round said low, into the space between her pot and the next woman’s shoulder, that the woman who carries the slate had once carried a figure that named a person she knew. No owner stood under the word, no room came with it, no hand at a slate, no name for the person, no figure, no date and nobody to ask; it stopped on the stone lip and went off into the yard’s ordinary talk. The boy took it apart as a surgeon takes a field apart and filed it as the \textbf{fifth shaping} of the well-saying on a place of its own with a finger between it and her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand and another between it and the Cross-to-Greybank road saying and a third between it and the four ownerless directions — expressly not a witness (no owner standing to be asked), not a confession (no mouth owned the figure), not a reader made (no slate opened within reach of the basket) and not a sixth shaping, with no sixth made due. Her eighth hand stays eight and joined to none; she is neither made a reader by the word nor joined to Ilva’s count in wood, which stayed on its own place with a finger between. The word buys no figure and no payer; her going up the road unread on the Account-days behind goes on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together. No new scar or possession, no change of voice. \textbf{Ch 117 (bonds).} On Ilmen 10, the year’s first Account-day and market, she went up the clay road toward Greybank before noon carrying Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm, the writing turned to her sleeve, her hand to the slate before her eyes went up to the crowd. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and was not made a reader by the carrying; asked what she carried, she answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} — so that the runner’s saying went on a place of its own beside the other unread things. The boy filed the order of her reaching as the eighth record-first hand-shape joined to none, her eighth hand staying eight with no ninth made of the carrying and no reader, witness or payer standing. The first arithmetic of the year went up the road in Berr’s locked box while hers went unread; the two went on separate places and were not joined. No new scar or possession, no change of voice. \textbf{Ch 112 (bonds).} On Stone 30 (Day 389), the year’s third and last Account-day and market, she goes up the clay road toward Greybank before noon with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned to her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing is — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. Her hand goes to the slate before her eyes go to the crowd, and the reaching comes before the word; no figure comes off the face of it and she is not made a reader by the year’s last figure. The boy files no tenth hand: her \textbf{eighth} stays eight on a place of its own, joined neither to Ilva’s ninth at the well, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the charcoal under the loaf shelf, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping. She was offstage on Stone 28 and 29. No new scar or possession and no change of voice; the carrying goes on gathering interest toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries, and nothing on this last market made the choice for her.

\textbf{Ch 110 (bonds).} On Stone 23 (Day 382), before noon, she goes up the clay road toward Greybank with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned toward her sleeve; the thumb lies along the grain of the frame and nothing presses where the writing is — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. The second strap is let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stands unbrushed on the shortened skirt; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist come first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the yard, and no figure comes off the face of it. To the woman who asks what she carries she answers the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to the woman who wants more, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She settles the second strap again, not for the women and not for the road, reads nothing aloud, gives no figure and does not look into the basket, and goes on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy files the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own beside the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself is not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled; no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no reader, no witness and no payment, and he joins her neither to Ilva’s strip in its sleeve, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the charcoal under the loaf shelf, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stays eight with no tenth, and \textbf{eleven arithmetics behind one unsigned figure do not make her a reader}. She was offstage on Stone 22 and 24; nothing from the keeping at the fold or the fourth direction over the boards came to her road as sign, lesson, mending, cause or payment, and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 109 (bonds).} On Stone 20 (Day 379), the month’s second Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, held edge-on to her own forearm with the writing turned toward her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand going to the slate before her eyes went to the crowd, and no figure came off the face of it. To the woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}. To the woman who wanted more she said, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She settled the second strap again, not for the women and not for the square, gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own beside the Ash 6 sighting, with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself was not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled. He made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no witness, no reader and no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip in its sleeve, to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, to the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf, to the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor to any other private keeping. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth; she was a runner and not a reader, and \textbf{eleven arithmetics going up the road behind her did not make her one}. She was offstage on Stone 19 and 21; nothing from the keeping at the fold or the eleven readings came to her road as figure, lesson or payment, and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 108 (bonds).} On Stone 17 (Day 376), in the afternoon, she went \textbf{up} the clay road in the boy’s sight out of Low Kiln with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned toward her own sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand going to the slate before her eyes went to the yard. To the woman who asked what she carried she said \emph{A slate. I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}, and to one who wanted more, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself is not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled. He made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no witness, no reader and no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s thumb, the charcoal, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping; her eighth record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth. She is a runner and not a reader and the road does not care which. Offstage on Stone 16 and 18; Ilva’s ninth at the well, the keeping at the fold found where put and ten arithmetics behind one unsigned figure brought no figure to her road. She was not made a reader early and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 107 (bonds).} On Stone 14 (Day 373), in the afternoon, she came \textbf{down} the clay road in the boy’s sight out of the direction of Greybank, with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her own forearm and the writing turned toward her sleeve. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap came first and the turn of the wrist after it, bringing the edge round, and only then did her eyes go to the yard, her hand having gone to the slate before either. The thumb lay along the grain of the frame and nothing pressed where the writing was — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it — and she went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner coming back down the road with the writing toward herself was not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled. He made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no witness, no reader and no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s thumb, the charcoal, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping; her eighth record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth. She is a runner and not a reader and the road does not care which. Offstage on Stone 13 and 15; no runner was seen on those days, the ten arithmetics behind one unsigned figure brought no figure to her road, and Sella’s small keeping at the fold on the fifteenth evening was neither sign nor payment to her. She was not made a reader early and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 106 (bonds).} On Stone 10 (Day 369), the deep-winter month’s first Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, making the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd and nothing pressing where the writing was; no figure came off it. To a woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, without rudeness and without apology and with the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance. Berr read one in twelve twice over the basket below her — once for the moot, once for the late households — called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and Stone’s first true subtraction inside; \textbf{ten arithmetics now stand behind one unsigned figure, ten are ten and not one account}, and they did not make her a reader of what she carried. She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The Frost 14 well-saying stands at one saying and four shapings beside her eighth hand with a finger between, not a witness, not a confession, not a joining and not paid; the collector’s ordinary hand on its own tray at the Drawing two mornings later is not joined to hers. Offstage on Stone 11 and 12; no runner was seen on either day and no figure came off any slate. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and gave the runner no name. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 102 (bonds).} On Ash 30 (Day 359), the dark month’s third and last Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon with the second strap let out and dried pale scurf of road-mud unbrushed on the shortened skirt, the small flat correction of the strap first and the turn of the wrist bringing the edge round, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd and nothing pressing where the writing was. To a woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}, and to one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}. No figure came off the slate. Nine arithmetics of the year went up the road in Berr’s locked box below her and stood behind one unsigned figure — nine are nine and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space — and did not make her a reader of what she carried; the runner went up before noon and was offstage on Ash 28 and 29. She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The Frost 14 well-saying stands at one saying and four shapings beside her eighth hand with a finger between, not a witness, not a confession, not a joining and not paid (T080 advanced, not paid). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off and gave the runner no name; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge for a measure nobody called. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 99 (bonds).} On Ash 20 (Day 349), the dark month’s second Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon with the second strap let out, dried pale scurf of road-mud unbrushed on the shortened skirt, the writing turned to her sleeve and her hand arriving at the slate before her eyes arrived at the crowd; nothing pressed where the writing was and no figure came off it. To a woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}, and to one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, without rudeness and without apology and with the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance. Eight arithmetics of the year went up the clay road in Berr’s locked box below her and stood behind one printed figure — eight are eight and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space — and did not make her a reader of what she carried. She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching stays the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The Frost 14 well-saying stands at one saying and four shapings, held on a place of its own beside her eighth hand with a finger between, not a witness, not a cause, not a confession, not a joining, not a prophecy, not a payment and not made due by the reading (T080 advanced, not paid). Offstage on Ash 19 and 21; no runner was seen on those two days. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 96 (bonds).} On Ash 10 (Day 339), the dark month’s first Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd, the writing turned to her sleeve and the slate’s face edge-on, the second strap let out for the long stretch and the dried pale scurf of road-mud unbrushed on the shortened skirt; nothing pressed where the writing was and no figure came off the slate. To a woman waiting by the path who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} — without rudeness, without apology, and with the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching stays the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, and she is joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The boy did not make her a reader of a figure that named a person she knew, did not join the Ash 6 turning of her writing to the Ash 5 fourth shaping of the well-saying, and made neither a prophecy nor a payment (T080 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Offstage on Ash 11 and 12; no runner was seen on any road after Ash 10 and no figure came off any slate. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 94 (bonds).} Offstage on Ash 4 and 5, she was glimpsed once on Ash 6 (Day 335) coming \textbf{down} the clay road in the afternoon with the writing of Berr Clay’s narrow slate turned toward herself for the first time in the boy’s knowing of her. On Account-days she takes that road up toward Greybank before noon with the writing to her sleeve and the slate’s face turned away from everybody; here she came down it and the face stayed turned toward her own forearm, still edge-on, the writing looking at her sleeve and at nobody, the thumb along the grain of the frame with nothing pressing where the writing was and no figure coming off it. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the shortened skirt; her hand went to the slate before her eyes went to the yard. To a woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows.} She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching stays the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, and she is joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 5 fourth shaping of the well-saying with a finger between: a voice said the runner had come back down the road and here she comes, but a voice standing in no doorway is not a prophecy fulfilled, and he refused to join saying to sighting, make a fifth shaping, make her a reader, make the sighting a payment or pay the claim (T080 advanced, not paid). The far-off day she must choose whether to read what she has carried is not brought nearer. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 92 (bonds).} On Bone 30, the month’s third and last Account-day and market, she carried Berr’s slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, the second strap let out for the long stretch and the dried pale scurf of road-mud standing unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it. Her hand arrived at the slate before her eyes arrived at the crowd, and nothing pressed where the writing was. To two women by the rail who asked what she carried she said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and, to the one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, answering the question put and not the one behind it and going on with the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. No figure came off the slate. The sixth arithmetic had changed the district’s figures below her on the square — six arithmetics now standing behind one printed figure, six readings six and not one account — and had not made her a reader of what she carried; her order of reaching stayed the eighth record-first hand in the district, eight and not a rule, kept on a place of its own and joined to none, and the three shapings of the Frost 14 well-saying stood beside it with a finger between every pair and did not make her a witness, a cause or a confession. She was not the soft-handed man from Slate Row, not the clerk at the Court’s table, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the woman who had carried the saying at the well and not the green-mouthed woman at the pot board or the foundling at the market’s edge, which stayed a colour and a shape with no eighth; Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and stood half a pace off and gave the runner no name. She was offstage on Bone 28 and 29 and Bone went out without a boundary drawn. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

No figure came off the slate. The fifth arithmetic had changed the district’s figures below her on the square and had not made her a reader of what she carried; her order of reaching stayed the eighth record-first hand in the district, eight and not a rule, kept on a place of its own and joined to none, and the three shapings of the Frost 14 well-saying stood beside it with a finger between every pair and did not make her a witness, a cause or a confession. She was not the soft-handed man from Slate Row, not the clerk at the Court’s table, not Ilva with her count in wood, and not the woman who had carried the saying at the well. \textbf{Ch 86 (bonds).} On Bone 10 she carried Berr’s slate up the road before noon, edge-on and unread, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd, answering the question put with \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}. No figure came off it; her eighth hand stayed on its own place joined to none, and the three shapings of the Frost 14 well-saying were not joined to her slate and did not make a reader, a witness, a cause or a confession. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and stood half a pace off and gave the runner no name; the clerk stayed set at the landing for a measure nobody called, and the green and the shape stayed sightings with no eighth. Bone’s arithmetic rode unread in the box behind Frost’s three and made four readings four and not one account. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — she carries his narrow slate between the Cross and Greybank and does not read it. He is a good reason in a neat hand; she is the road under it. On Day 158 his cord was spoken of as a direction up the clay road, and on Day 159 she took the slate up that road ahead of the reading, after he had called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. No loyalty is spoken and no figure passes between them.

\textbf{The Cross and Greybank} — the two ends of her road. At the Cross the reading goes up before noon; at Greybank the factor and the bank are. She joins the two places without ever joining what is written at either.

\textbf{Sella Vail and the Vail basket} — on Day 158 she came through the Clay Yard and Sella carried the boy past at the half-pace, gave the house no name for the slate and did not say whose it was. Neither woman asked the other anything. At the Cross on Day 159 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay.

\textbf{The boy under the Vail roof} — he does not know her name and she has not looked into the basket. He saw the order of her reaching and filed it as the eighth record-first hand in the district, on a place of its own, joined to none. She has no idea she has been filed.

\textbf{Ch 40 (bonds).} On the second Account-day of Tallow she is seen again going up the clay road with Berr’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm, her hand to it before her eyes go to the crowd, the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist bringing the edge round; her coat is shortened at the skirt for the road’s mud with the dried pale scurf unbrushed, two straps settled, thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing is. To a woman who asks what she carries: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to the woman who wants more: \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk.} No figure comes off the slate and no joining is made to Marra, the clerks, the reed-cutter’s cord, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the finger beneath the loaf shelf or the soft-cuffed clerk at the landing. She is a runner and not a reader; the order of her reaching remains the eighth record-first hand on a place of its own (T080 advanced, not paid).

\textbf{Ch 42 (bonds).} On the third Account-day of Tallow she went up the clay road to Greybank before noon with Berr’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm, the writing turned to her sleeve and her hand arriving before her eyes. To a woman who asked what she carried she said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference}; to the next question, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, answering the question put and not the one behind it. No figure came off the slate. She was not joined to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate, Marra, the other record-first hands or any keeping; what she carries stays a thing somebody else set down. No bond paid, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 46 (bonds).} On Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, she went up the clay road to Greybank before noon with Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned to her sleeve, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd; the second strap was let out for the long road and the dried pale scurf of the mud stood unbrushed on the shortened skirt. To two women who asked what she carried she said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, answering the question put and not the one behind it. No figure came off the slate. She was not joined to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate at the out-of-line landing, Marra, the other record-first hands or any keeping; her order of reaching stayed the eighth such hand on a place of its own, advanced and not paid (T080). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off, gave the runner no name and asked nothing about the slate. No bond paid, no new scar or possession, no change of voice; she is a runner and not a reader.

She enters in the firing month of Y.H. 813, on the eve of the first Account-day of Tallow, and is seen twice: once coming through the Clay Yard from the direction of the Cross with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm, and once the next morning taking it up the clay road toward Greybank. In the yard a woman asked what the levy would take now the kilns had been brought up and hands were in the month; Hessa answered that she did not read it, she carried it, that there was a difference and the road did not care which; when the woman wanted more she said \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk} and went on through the yard, leaving the question standing where it had been set down. Her hand went to the slate before her eyes went to the people, the small flat correction of the strap and a turn of the wrist to bring the edge round. To the boy that order of reaching is an eighth such hand-shape in the district, kept on its own place beside Marra’s pause, the neat dark hand, the Court-table clerk, the soft-cuffed clerk at the landing, the soft hands at Slate Row, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and the finger that goes beneath the Vail loaf shelf. He does not let eight likenesses trouble him into a rule, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them. At the Cross on the Account-day she came through again with the slate edge-on, hand to slate before eye to the crowd, and went up the clay road with the writing turned to her sleeve; no figure came off it under any roof in Sill. She is a runner and not a reader of anyone’s private keeping, and the figure on the slate remained what figures on carried slates remained in this district: a thing somebody else had set down and nobody here had read.

She enters the second Account-day of the firing month as she entered the first: a figure going up the road in a narrow slate held edge-on, the writing turned toward a sleeve and the hand arriving before the eyes. The road between Cross and Greybank is the whole of her account, and she joins the two ends without joining what is written at either. The district is full of hands that put a record before a person; hers is one more such hand and she has made a manner of it, so that a slate is carried and no figure is read and nothing in it becomes hers to answer for. The boy has filed the order once and does not file it twice; eight likenesses must still be held apart by hand, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them.

She enters Smoke’s first market as she entered every other Account-day: a figure going up the clay road in a narrow slate held edge-on, the writing toward the sleeve, the hand arriving before the eyes, and the road’s pace kept without thinking. She joins the procession of carriers whose kept records wait for the far-off hand that will lay them together and call the joining an account; her order of reaching remains the eighth record-first hand on a place of its own, advanced and not paid (T080). Offstage on Frost 11 and 12; Frost’s arithmetic changed the district below her on the square and did not change her road.

Went up the road with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned to her sleeve, the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist bringing the edge round, the second strap let out for the long road and the dried pale scurf of mud unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; her hand arrived at the slate before her eyes arrived at the crowd and nothing pressed where the writing was. Her order of reaching stayed the eighth record-first hand in the district on a place of its own, not joined to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate at the out-of-line landing, Ilva’s strip in her sleeve, the charcoal under the shelf or any other record, and eight were eight and not a rule. Bone’s first arithmetic went up the road in Berr’s locked box behind Frost’s three and made four readings standing behind one printed figure; the printed figure stood unchallenged, the figure read was still not the figure paid and no signature stood on the space between, and nothing of the reading made her a reader or a party to it. The three shapings of the Frost 14 well-saying stood beside her eighth hand with a finger between every pair, not a witness, not a cause, not a confession, not a joining and not paid. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and stood half a pace off and gave the runner no name; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid; she is a runner and not a reader.

\CRcharacter{Ilva}{the woman who keeps the month’s firings in a strip of birch bark}{build/portraits/ilva.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Ilva of the firing work, the woman at the yard well}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 780s, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath — the year was never entered on any slate she keeps}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; of the yard’s firing work, not of a kiln-house}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the firing work of the Clay Yard, Low Kiln}\CRfield{Status}{alive; seen once on Ilmen 26 at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in her nail crescents and finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb she does not scrub out, her hand going flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would have put an intention. A woman waiting her turn brought a number up out of a shut fist, held it toward the light and put the fist toward the strip in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings; Ilva answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and the figure went from the fist toward the wood, looked at the light and went back into the sleeve, arriving nowhere, the stick keeping its notch and learning no name and the woman going back to the round with \emph{Then it’s a stick}. No slate was opened within reach of the basket, no figure came off the wood, no reader was made and no name was spoken over the notches; the boy filed the \textbf{offer and its return} on a place of its own beside her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair, a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together and not that hand.
