A woman of the firing work in Low Kiln, past her first youth and not old enough to be spoken of as old, with the yard’s pale clay dried in the crescents of her nails and the finer grey dust of the racks worked into the seam of one thumb. She does not scrub the seam out. Her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board, and are not soft. She draws water at the yard well with the pail against her knee and goes on with her work without looking to see who has noticed her. The district would not turn its head twice for her; she is of the yard in the way the rack and the trough are of the yard. What she carries that nobody sees is a short strip of birch bark notched along one edge, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, kept in her sleeve and put back with the flat of a hand. People notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Plain, short, and exact in the way a tally is exact. She answers the question put and not the one behind it, and she never volunteers a figure for the work. She gives no name to the thing she keeps and has never been asked for one. There is no proverb in her, no instruction addressed to a pot or a fire; that belongs to the houses. When she is asked how many firings a month has taken, her hand goes to the record, her thumb passes over it, her eyes go to the person who asked, and only then does her mouth open. She does not explain the order and would not know what there was to explain.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Five to this morning.”

\item “If it went on a slate it would want a figure put on it. It’s a firing. Ask the pot what it cost.”

\item “I keep the count of the fires. I don’t keep the account.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in Low Kiln into the firing work and has never left it for a house. The work is the racks, the pails, the carrying, the counting of how many times the kilns have been lit since the month came in; it is done in glances and hands and the weight of the thing carried, and nobody in the yard gives it a figure aloud. A slate would want a figure put on it, and the yard has no wish to give the slate one, so Ilva keeps the month’s firings in wood. The strip is hers; she puts it in her sleeve with the flat of her hand and takes it out when a question is asked that wants an answer. She is not a reader of private keepings. She is not the woman in the grey coat at the flare, not Hessa Rale with her edge-on slate between the Cross and Greybank, not the soft-cuffed clerk set below the north bridge for a measure nobody called, and not an officer with a reason. She is a woman who keeps a count in wood and draws water in a yard.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
The sweet edge of lead glaze comes up off High Kiln on a wrong wind and goes over the boards and out again; she has learned to know it on the air and to make nothing of it, as the yard makes nothing of it. The yard goes around the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, and she goes around it with a look and a wide step like everybody else, and does not count it among the firings or give it a name. Her fear is small and practical: that one day a slate will be put to her stick and a figure taken off it, and the count of firings will become an account with a payer standing under it. She has no wish to be the woman who explains what the notches mean.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the firings to go on and the count to stay true in wood, where no clerk’s thumb can read it. She thinks she wants nothing beyond keeping her place in the yard. What she needs, though she is far from it, is to be one of the hands that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together — the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord, the knot-string, the six pages, the tins, the pewter tin, the inward slates and this strip of notched birch — and to find that a count kept from a slate was still a record all along.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 123 (bonds).} On Ilmen 26 she stands once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board and have never been soft, and people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. A woman waiting her turn shifts a pot from one hip to the other, brings a number up out of a shut fist, holds it toward the light and puts the fist toward the strip in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings. Ilva’s hand goes flat over the fold before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would have put an intention; the short strip of notched birch lies in its fold, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and it is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined, and no figure comes off the wood. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve. The woman holds the figure out a breath longer, then shuts her fist upon it and puts it back into her sleeve, where it arrives nowhere; \emph{Then it’s a stick}, she says, and goes back to the round, and nobody turns twice. \textbf{The boy files the offer and its return}, advanced and not paid, on a place of its own beside Ilva’s \textbf{ninth} record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair: not a sale, a reader made, a tenth hand, a payer, an account or a sixth shaping, not the calling of the loan and not joined to the well-asking, the clerk’s entered figure, the second man’s turned slate or the face at the yard’s edge. It is a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, and is not that hand; her fear is advanced and left unpaid — the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it — and she is expressly not the speaker of the well-asking, which came up once on the twenty-third and was not told again. Offstage on Ilmen 27 and 28 with her keeping where she left it: no figure was offered twice, no reader was made of her keeping and the ninth stays nine with no tenth. No new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 122 (bonds).} On Ilmen 23 she stands once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. Word comes up once at the bucket-round, from mouth to mouth with no body standing under it, that a man with a narrow slate under his arm had asked after a house-name under this roof and been answered with the weather. Her hand goes toward her sleeve before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention; the short strip of notched birch lies in its fold, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and it is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the asking, and no figure comes off the wood. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and goes back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The boy takes the order of reaching apart as a surgeon takes a field apart and files it as her \textbf{ninth} record-first hand on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth; he files no tenth, makes no reader of her keeping and no figure of the word’s nearness. \textbf{She is expressly not the speaker of the asking:} nobody saw the asking, no voice carried into the yard, no slate was opened within reach of the basket, no room entered and no name spoken, and she is not made a reader by its nearness. The boy files the asking on its own place beside the second man’s direction down the north bridge road and his narrow slate turned to the sleeve, the first man’s face, the clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair, and joins it to none. Offstage on Ilmen 24 and 25 with her keeping where she left it; the softening at the river’s skin, the two readings up the road and the fifth shaping found where put buy no figure for her wood and stand on separate places with a finger between. The ninth stays nine with no tenth and no reader made of her keeping. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

I keep the count, not the account} — puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and goes back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The softening at the river’s skin, the clerk’s entered figure, the two readings up the road and the fifth shaping found where put buy no figure for her wood and stand on separate places with a finger between; the ninth stays nine with no tenth and no reader made of her keeping. \textbf{Ch 120 (bonds).} Offstage on all three days — Ilmen 17, 18 and 19 — with her keeping where she left it: the short strip of notched birch lies in its fold in her sleeve, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and nobody takes it out, reads it, copies it or takes a figure off the wood. Her count of the month’s firings stays in wood and her answer stays the answer behind every question about what a thing cost: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}. Her \textbf{ninth} record-first hand stays nine with no tenth made of it. On the nineteenth the yard said the air had turned and a man said it would be back before morning, and the river’s skin softened at one edge where the low note ran nearer under it; she is expressly \textbf{not} the speaker of either saying and the softening is not made a figure for her count — the softening and her strip go on separate places with a finger between, a change called weather arriving nowhere and a count kept in wood refusing to become an account. The clerk’s entered figure on its own place at the landing and the first arithmetic up the road are not joined to her wood, and the fifth shaping found where put at the well is not made a sixth and buys no figure for her count. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

Offstage on Ilmen 11 and 13; no figure from the clay road came to her well and the ninth hand stayed nine. To the woman waiting her turn who asks what Stone’s firings have taken, her hand goes toward her sleeve before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, with the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention. The short strip of notched birch bark lies in the fold where it always lies, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between; it is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the open slate a pace away on the stone lip, to the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf, to the cord or the knot-string, and no figure comes off the wood. She answers the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and goes back to the pail, and nobody turns twice. The boy takes the order of reaching apart as a surgeon takes a field apart and files it as her \textbf{ninth} record-first hand on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth; he files no tenth, makes no reader of her keeping and makes no figure of the slate’s nearness. \textbf{She is expressly not the speaker of any voice that came over the boards} — the Frost 14 well-saying stays at one saying and four shapings with no fifth, the burned-slate word at five, the shut-room tellings at two and the row at five askings with no witness, and no ownerless voice came over the boards on Stone 28 or on the morning of the twenty-ninth. The boy filed the order of reaching as the ninth record-first hand on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth, filed no tenth, made no figure of the slate’s nearness and did not make her a reader of her own keeping (T080 advanced, not paid). She does not know she was read. She is not Marra, not the soft-handed man, not the soft-cuffed clerk, not Hessa, not the green-mouthed woman at the pot board and not the woman whose voice came over the boards, and is joined to none of them. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and no change of voice.

\textbf{Corin (the boy in the basket).} He was set down at the edge of the work where no slate lay while she answered a woman with a pot. She did not look at him, did not know he was reading her, and went on with her water. He took the order of her reaching and nothing else; he did not read the stick, ask her about it or take a figure off it. To her he is a child at the edge of the work. In his private file she is the ninth record-first hand, joined to none.

\textbf{The neighbour with the pot} — asked how many firings the month had taken, got \emph{Five to this morning}, and went off with her answer level. The exchange is the whole of their connection.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — keeper of the house whose kiln the firings count. Ilva is of the yard and not of the house; there is no argument between them because there is no occasion for one.

\textbf{Hessa Rale} — a fellow keeper of a record that no figure comes off, but a runner with a slate on the road to Greybank. The two are filed far apart and must not be joined.

\textbf{Berr Clay} — his slate would want a figure off the stick. Ilva has never handed him the stick and never will; there is no quarrel, only the distance between wood and slate.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
\textbf{Ch 123 (Days 420–422, Ilmen 26–28).} Seen once on Ilmen 26 at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold, clay pale in her nail crescents and rack dust in one thumb seam she does not scrub out, her hand flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap. A woman waiting her turn offered a figure for the month’s firings and put it toward the strip in her sleeve; Ilva answered the question put and not the one behind it, \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, and the figure went from the fist toward the wood, looked at the light and went back into the sleeve, arriving nowhere, the stick keeping its notch and learning no name and the woman going back to the round with \emph{Then it’s a stick}. The boy filed the \textbf{offer and its return} on a place of its own beside her ninth hand and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair — a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together and not that hand (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, not paid). She is expressly not the speaker of the well-asking and is not made a reader by the figure’s nearness; the ninth stays nine with no tenth, the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and her fear is advanced and left unpaid. Offstage on the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth, not offered a figure twice. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 122 (Days 417–419, Ilmen 23–25).} Seen once on Ilmen 23 at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, her hand to her sleeve before her eyes to the asker and her mouth after both, the notched birch strip unread in its fold; she answers the question put and not the one behind it, \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, and the ninth stays nine with no tenth. She is expressly not the speaker of the word that came up at the well — a man with a narrow slate had asked after a house-name under this roof and been answered with the weather, with nobody standing under the asking — and is not made a reader by its nearness; her wood and the asking stand on separate places with a finger between. Offstage on Ilmen 24 and 25; the softening at the river’s skin, the two readings up the road, the clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping buy no figure for her count and go on separate places with a finger between. Forward, not closed.

I keep the count, not the account}, and the ninth stays nine with no tenth. Offstage on Ilmen 20 and 22; the softening at the river’s skin, the clerk’s entered figure, the two readings up the road and the fifth shaping buy no figure for her count and go on separate places with a finger between. Forward, not closed.

On Bone 22–24, Days 321–323, she is a woman of the yard and not of a house, and keeps the month’s firings in wood where no slate can take a figure off them. On Bone 23 she is seen once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb; asked what the firings of Bone had taken, her hand goes toward her sleeve and stays, the short notched birch strip is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf, the cord, the open slate a pace away, the knot-string or the ownerless saying, and no figure comes off the wood. Her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both with a half-beat, and she answers the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account.} The boy files the order of reaching as the ninth record-first hand on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth, files no tenth, and does not join her strip to the handful Sella let fall at the rack end the day before or to the charcoal under the shelf, for testing and keeping are two acts and neither pays for the other. She is offstage on Bone 22 and 24; the twice-mended pot with its crack showing, the dressed grain turned under wool and given no figure, the three coverings called weather and the five arithmetics going up the road in a locked box bring no figure to her well as sign, lesson, mending, cause or payment. Nine are nine and not a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to this one. She does not know she was read; no new scar or possession came and no bond changed hands.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 123: On Ilmen 26 she stands once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board and have never been soft, and people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. A woman waiting her turn shifts a pot from one hip to the other, brings a number up out of a shut fist, holds it toward the light and puts the fist toward the strip in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings. Ilva draws with the pail against her knee; the rope is stiff in the dry cold and gives its small rasp; clay is dried pale in her nail crescents and the finer rack dust is worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out. Her hand goes flat over the fold before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would have put an intention. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve. The woman holds the figure out a breath longer, then shuts her fist upon it and puts it back into her sleeve, where it arrives nowhere; \emph{Then it’s a stick}, she says, and goes back to the round, and nobody turns twice. No slate is opened within reach of the basket, no figure comes off the wood, no reader is made and no name is spoken over the notches. \textbf{The boy takes the offer apart by the place of each part — fist, eye, mouth, the half-beat in the gap — and files the offer and its return on a place of its own beside her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, not paid).} It is not a sale, a reader made, a tenth hand, a payer, an account or a sixth shaping, not the calling of the loan and not joined to the well-asking, the clerk’s entered figure, the second man’s turned slate or the face at the yard’s edge, but a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, and is not that hand. Her fear is advanced and left unpaid: the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and the figure that looked at the light went home with the woman. She is expressly not the speaker of the well-asking, which came up once on the twenty-third and was not told again. Offstage on Ilmen 27 and 28 with her keeping where she left it, not made a reader and offered no figure twice; the ninth stays nine with no tenth. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

The boy filed no tenth record-first hand: the ninth stayed on its own tray with a finger between it and the eighth, nine objects and not a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to this one (T080 held at nine, not paid). \item Ch 64: At the yard well on Smoke 5 (Day 244) she answered a woman who asked how many firings the month had taken. Her hand went into her sleeve for a short strip of birch bark notched along one edge, the nail of her thumb passed across the notches (pale where rubbed, dark in the uncut grain), her eyes went to the asker, and only then did her mouth answer \emph{Five to this morning}. She put the strip back inside her sleeve with the flat of her hand and went on with her water. Clay was dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the grey rack dust was worked into the seam of one thumb; she was of the yard and not of the house, and nobody turned to look at her twice. The boy did not read the notches, ask her about them or take a figure off the stick, and did not join the order of reaching to the cord, the knots, the pages, the tins, the missing hand or the pale line. Twenty-two and bent at the shoulders from six years in the slip pit, which makes him look older than his term. He has grey Ash in the creases of his knuckles that no amount of scrubbing lifts, and a pale ring round his left wrist where an iron clip sat in Y.H. 806, when he was bound. He is a narrow man with a narrow face and the habit of putting the smallest tool on the bench into his pocket when he thinks nobody is looking, because a man who owns nothing should know where the small things are. He sleeps in the Debt Loft above the wheel-shed and keeps his few possessions in a clay pot with no mark on it. He smells of wet wool, tallow and the sour tang of a corner that has not been swept. The thing people notice first is how quickly he moves; the thing they notice last is that he stops moving altogether when he is told he is doing well.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Deferential with a nail in it. He calls everyone \emph{house}, including Sella, and says \emph{I owe} where another man would say \emph{I am}. He never argues; he agrees so thoroughly that the argument has nowhere to go. When he is frightened he becomes helpful, which in a kiln-house means doing three things at once and quietly putting the fourth right. His jokes are not jokes; they are statements of fact made in a tone that invites someone else to laugh so that he does not have to.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Yes, house. I’ll sweep it. I swept it this morning. I’ll sweep it again.”

\item “Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.”

\item “He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.”

\item “You can’t return a man to himself. They tried with my mother. She came back with somebody else’s hands.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.” --- said of his own accord, to nobody, in the tone of a man stating the weather.

\item “Six counted. The next I don’t count.” --- to the kindling at the going of the light, with the knife set back where it can be checked; the sentence about the ear under this roof came a sixth time on Reed 20 to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the breath drawn and not spent.

\item “Yes, house.” --- said on Day 140 to an early thaw and a late, wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
His mother was banked in Y.H. 792 and came back thin to the district’s name-pot, with fragments of a life she could not name and hands that frightened him because they were not her hands. He was born of that return, which means he carries a little of somebody else’s interest in a life he cannot place, and has been told all his life that this makes him useful. In Y.H. 806, at sixteen, his mother’s account was entered against him and he was bound to House Vail for seven years, a term he did not choose and has counted every day of. He has worked the slip pits, swept the yard, banked the fire and carried the household’s small accounts in his head for six years.

He was sent to fetch a collector for Garl Vail in the Long Cold and turned back at the frozen ford. Sella never asked whether he had gone. Jorra, who was thirteen, never asked either, which Tarn has decided is worse. He was in the house when Corin arrived and watched the boy be given a bed while he slept in the loft, and he has never said the thing he thinks about it, because a clay-bound hand who complains about beds is a clay-bound hand who can be returned to the slate.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He is a debt with a body, and one year of a seven-year term left. He fears that when the term ends there will be no house to take him and he will be entered again for vagrancy, which is how the district keeps people. He fears the Second Want in himself — the shape that comes over him some nights and leaves him reaching for a tool he has never used. He fears Sella’s kindness more than Jorra’s command, because the kindness is the thing he cannot enter in any account and therefore cannot pay back. His contradiction: the man who owns nothing is the one who notices when a tool is missing and the one who keeps the house’s accounts most exactly.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a slate with his own name on it and no mark against it. He wants to be called by something that is not a house’s possession. He thinks he wants freedom; what he needs is to learn that freedom in Sarn is another category of account, and that a man can be unowned and still be cold, and that the thing to want is not an empty column but a way to keep warm without being spent.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 123 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed across Ilmen 26, 27 and 28 and nothing from the offered figure at the well, the well-asking answered with the weather, the second man’s turned slate and direction, the clerk’s entered figure or the softening at the river’s skin came to the kindling as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer; he takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has not asked about his term or his ear. At the kindling on the afternoons of all three days six pieces stood in the worn thumb-mark where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the debt, the small knife at the very edge of its sill; his hand went over blade and sill as a man passes a hand over a tool put back where it belongs and came away with no breath held at the top of the reach, the coming away the whole of the checking. In the tone of a man stating the weather he told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} on all three days; the sentence was found where put and not made a habit, not a tenth stopping, payment, hearing or rule, and was not turned into a custom on a day that had earned only its twenty-seventh or twenty-eighth, for a second silence would be a way and a way wants a payer where none stands. The boy filed it on a place of its own beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence and Jorra’s silence and did not lay it across the clerk’s entered figure, the offered figure and its return, the well-asking, the second man’s direction and slate, the first man’s face, Tarn’s degree toward the landing or the fifth shaping, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood. The ear-sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it stayed stopped at the word that would call the loan, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth, at the very end of a term already ended; the Seed 16 breath stayed unspent, the loan uncalled, the fear of being entered again for vagrancy still his without a figure and the want he did not voice still there for a slate with his own name and no mark against it. He did not turn his head toward the landing; the degree stayed a shape found where put and was not repeated. The Ash 14 held breath and the Bone 26 thumb’s resting were found where put and not made again, the warm loft stone stayed unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiving; chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist catching what little light there was, his stroke over the flagstones going without the half-check. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 122 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed across Ilmen 23, 24 and 25 and nothing from the asking at the well, the second man’s turned slate and direction, the clerk’s entered figure or the softening at the river’s skin came to the kindling as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer; he takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has not asked about his term or his ear. At the kindling on the afternoons of all three days six pieces stood in the worn thumb-mark where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the debt, the small knife at the very edge of its sill; his hand went over blade and sill and away with no breath held at the top of the reach, the coming away the whole of the checking, and in the tone of a man stating the weather he told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}. The sentence was found where put on all three days and not made a habit, not a tenth stopping, a payment, a hearing or a rule; it did not gather a second silence on an unearned day, for a second silence would be a custom and a third a way and both want a payer where none stands. The boy filed it on a place of its own beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence and Jorra’s silence and laid none of them across the clerk’s entered figure, the well-asking, the degree toward the landing or the fifth shaping, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood. He kept the six where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, told the wood \emph{Six counted. His stroke went over the shallow bright patch without the half-check, and the Bone 8 returned half-check stayed on its own place as the fourth of four held changes and not a rule. The warm loft stone stayed cold and unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiveness. Sella’s reading-day went past without a number spoken to him and Jorra’s standing finger was not made a cause of anything. No name given, no debt paid, no bond paid, sold, named or spoken.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — she holds his debt and once, in the winter Garl died, gave him a warm stone for the loft which he has kept in his clay pot for two years. He cannot reconcile the stone with the debt, and has stopped trying, which is not the same as forgiving it. \emph{Ch 2:} he calls her \emph{house}, says \emph{I owe} where another man says \emph{I am}, and agreed with everything so thoroughly that there was nowhere for an argument to go. She gave the foundling a bed and him the loft, and he put the one sentence into the room that nobody had asked for.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — son of the house, who treats him as a brother when the wheel needs him and as a servant when it does not. Tarn has decided to hate him for it and keeps failing, because Jorra once sat up all night with him through a fever and has never mentioned it. \emph{Ch 2:} Jorra noticed a rasp left out of its place and Tarn answered him; the kindness and the command arrived in the same voice and Tarn did not separate them.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling who arrived and was given a bed in the house. Tarn was the first to notice that the boy turns his head toward a pot before anyone taps it, and has told nobody, because a clay-bound hand who can hear the full note is worth more than his debt and he does not want to be bought. \emph{Ch 2:} he said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} His resentment is not envy of the bed; it is a man keeping the one thing he owns, which is the exact account of what he is owed and what he owes.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he has carried messages between her and the house, and barley from her to Sella, and has hated being the thin part of that chain. He knows her cough is not the pits and has never said so.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she has suspected for a year that he is more than he says, and has not asked. He has noticed her noticing, and has answered her with the weather every time.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — he was sent for a collector and turned back. The dead man’s coat still hangs behind the door and Tarn has never once touched it.

\textbf{Ch 4.} He called Sella \emph{house} and put the knife back twice where it could be checked; his broom stopped two strokes at the Vail pot’s note without a turn of the head, and the boy watched and kept the silence as carefully as he did. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not. Jorra came in from the back room with slate dust and said the back room was cold; Tarn said nothing about that either. Dessa’s cough went by him as weather, as it always did. The one thing he owns stays kept.

\textbf{Ch 5.} On Stone 13 he came up the yard with the knife already back on its sill, went through the motion of checking it with his eyes, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot \emph{before} it was set down. His broom stopped half a stroke at the soft set-down that gave nothing, and he said nothing about either thing, as he has said nothing about the pot’s note through the wall. He counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back; when Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then began again. At dusk he set the knife back where it could be checked and told the yard he had done so, unasked. He wants his exact account and grudges the house the loan of a bed; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and he has said neither sentence.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 he measured the kindling stack with his eyes --- four, four, a space where the fifth should be --- and told the stack six were counted and the seventh held back. On Stone 17 the knife went back on the sill and was announced to the empty yard, and when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} the broom stopped altogether for two breaths before he said \emph{Yes, house} and went on; he scraped Ash from his knuckles, held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist up to the light, and put the knife back, this time without announcing it. He named the kiln’s breath as the thing that takes a man in his sleep and told of the man in Mud End the district called merciful; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. His broom stopped half a stroke at the bench where no note came. On Stone 20 he told the yard again that the knife was back where it could be checked; six of seven years counted, the seventh held back, and he offered to check the ridge. He said nothing about the boy’s ear and the boy said nothing about his.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 22 his head turned a degree when a vessel carried past the door gave its flat note, and he went back to the broom without looking at the basket or calling the sound a sound; he had been sent for the collector who came with grey fingertips, and the boy put that grey on a tray of its own. On Stone 25 his broom checked half a stroke at the place in the yard where a pot cracked all the way through, and again at the place on the bench where no note had come, and he said nothing about either. He set the small knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was on Stone 22, Stone 23 and Stone 30; counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back every day; held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light; and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Stone 29 he offered to check the width of the ridge with his thumb and took his eyes off it as a man takes his eyes off a woman who has been crying. The two silences under one roof kept their usual shape, and the loan that could hear went on being worth more than the debt that held him.

\textbf{Ch 8.} Through the Five the knife went back to its sill and the seventh year was held back every day; he announced the knife to the empty yard and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count. The Ash in the creases of his knuckles was the colour of the ridge no scrubbing lifted, and he kept the silence about the flat note all five days, as he kept the silence about the boy’s ear. On the Long Night he said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark and he let the proverb go to the pot. He wanted the late thaw still, because a late thaw puts off the paying, and on Ilmen 1 he swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife on its sill and the seventh year held back again.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the knife went back to its sill and he announced it to the empty yard, six years counted and the seventh held back, Ash worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifted. He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound or looking at the basket; the boy kept the turning beside his own hearing and did not join them. On Ilmen 7 he was with the yard at the well when the Singing Sill gave its note early and did not say what it was. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the sentence was not said under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 10.} The small knife goes back to its sill before light and is announced to the empty yard --- \emph{It’s back. You can check} --- with six years of the seven counted and the seventh held where he always holds it; Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring catches what light there is. He sweeps around the place where the clay-heavy water came up behind the racks and sweeps the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once looking along it, which is the road a man goes down when a house wants a collector. No collector comes for the woman in the brook and he does not go for one, and he does not say the omission has a name. He still wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off the paying; he agrees with the early and the late without taking either side. The loan that can hear is still uncalled and the sentence is still unsaid under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 11.} The small knife went back to its sill before the light was gone on Days 45 and 46 and he told the empty yard where it was, unasked; on Day 47 he put it back and told nobody, because the yard had already been told and a man does not say the same thing twice to a house that does not answer. Six years of the seven were counted and the seventh held back on all three mornings, the one entry in this house the house cannot check. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning to look along it, and no collector went down it for the woman the brook took nine mornings ago; he did not say the thing which had not happened had a name. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring caught the light. He agreed with the ones who wanted the thaw early and the ones who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. When Sella said he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths before saying \emph{Yes, house}.

\textbf{Ch 12.} He kept Sella’s house in its exact account and kept his own seventh year out of it; he said house to the yard and counted six where the house could check and the seventh where it could not. With the boy he kept the older equality: a vessel gave its note past the door on Day 50 and a pot answered nearly full on Day 52, and his head did not turn at either and he said nothing about either. Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked and Mira passed without a question. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled, and he still wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying.

\textbf{Ch 13.} He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, saying \emph{Yes, house} to both, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. The small knife was back on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the light and gave it back. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook. A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Ilmen 28 and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply a Grathic word for it, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. Sella told him he had done well and he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Before light on Silt 3 the small knife went back to its sill and was announced to the empty yard — \emph{It’s back. You can check} — and he told the kindling six were counted and the next he did not count; six years stood, and the seventh was nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house could not check. Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the little light and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the water came with the paying. His broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked on Stone 25 and went on without a turn of the head or a name for the sound. When a vessel gave its note past the yard door he did not turn. On Silt 6 his head went a degree toward a pot that answered nearly full under nobody’s knuckle, and then went back to the broom; he said nothing and did not look toward the basket. The boy kept his turning beside his own hearing and did not join them, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 15.} Through Silt 9–15 the seventh year presses against the rising water and is still held back. The small knife went back to its sill before light and was announced to the empty yard, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house could not check; Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the paying came with the water. His broom checked at the cracked-pot place and went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gave its note past the yard door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head did not turn and he did not name the sound or look toward the basket. He does not say that an ear which can hear is worth more than the debt that holds him, and the sentence that would call the loan lies under the roof as it has for six years.

\textbf{Ch 16.} Through Days 75–77 the seventh year presses against the mud the flood left and is still held back. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to both sides of the thaw argument, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts all week and goes over the boundary into Seed unchanged. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector comes. He has been sent for one once, in the Long Cold, and come back at the frozen ford and told the house it had been done; he keeps that sentence where he keeps the seventh year and neither is entered. A vessel gives its note past the door on Silt 27 and again on Seed 1 and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound; the boy does not call either a seventh hearing. He takes the broom from Sella’s hands on Seed 1 only after she has given it its instruction, and the first work of the planting month is sweeping. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof; the loan that can hear stays uncalled. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the count crosses into Seed with the seventh still held.

The change made on Seed 22 is held and not repeated: while Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence his bristles go on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the place where the stroke stopped that day, and the stones keep that place as a shallow bright patch worn into the stone, a thing nobody will enter. Neither man names the other’s silence; the ear worth more than the debt is unsafe, and the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has not been said under this roof in six years and is not said today. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and it did not give here; the count goes into Reed with the seventh still held.

On Days 120 through 122 the seventh year is pressed past the end of the planting and still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. On Reed 2, the only day he is on stage, he takes the broom only after Sella has given it its instruction (\emph{Go around, it cost enough to come in, it will cost more to take out}) and says \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument can find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. The small bench knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; the unforged collector sentence stays beside it where he has kept it since the frozen ford, and neither is entered. The next I don’t count.} The change made on Seed 22 stays held and not repeated: while Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence his bristles go on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the shallow bright patch the stones keep where the stroke stopped, and neither man turns or speaks. The boy files the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray, two objects and not a rule. On Days 123 through 125 the seventh year presses past the third tend of the planting and is still held. The small bench knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years standing in a thumb-mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; the unforged collector sentence lies beside it where he has kept it since the frozen ford, and he enters neither. Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to the woman who wants the thaw early and the man who wants it late, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. His chest is tight and the breath from Seed 16 is still unspent, a small interval at the top of each reach where it should have gone in, a breath stopped against iron and never let through. On Reed 5 he puts his hand to the knife on its sill, moves it a hair’s breadth and sets it back where it can be checked, and tells the sill where it is; behind Jorra’s standing finger his bristles go on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the shallow bright patch the stones keep where the stroke stopped, and neither man names the other’s silence. On Reed 5 night, crouched to the kindling that smells of straw and tallow, he brings the sentence about the ear and the debt to the threshold of the word that would call the loan and stops there; the wood takes it as wood takes everything, without answer and without keeping, and the boy files the stopped sentence on the interval tray beside the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and his own held breath. Something must give at the end of the seventh year and has not given yet; the loan that can hear stays uncalled.

On Days 126 through 128 the seventh year is pressed further past its third tend and still held, and the thing that must give at its end has not given. Reed has come on and the reeds stand in the yard in armfuls judged by the arm that carries them; he takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. His knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years in the worn thumb-mark and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the unforged collector sentence beside it, his chest tight with the breath from Seed 16 still unspent and a small interval at the top of each reach where it should have gone in. On Day 127, with the coals banked and the knife set back where it can be checked, he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, and the sentence about the ear under this roof worth more than the debt that holds it comes a second time to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name; he draws the breath and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} and goes on with the broom. The boy files the second stopping beside the first on the interval tray as two intervals and not two payments, and the loan stays uncalled. Under the wheel-shed Jorra’s bent finger leads at the damper ahead of an unfinished sentence and the dust comes out of the back room from men unnamed; Tarn’s stroke goes on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones keep the shallow bright patch where it stopped, neither man naming the other’s silence. He never looks toward the bed or the basket and says nothing of the ear; Sella asks nothing within hearing. The silver clip-ring at his wrist holds what light there is and Ash stays worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line. Nothing is spent, called, named or joined, and the seventh year goes into the next days still held.

Three stoppings now stand on the interval tray and none of them is a payment. The seventh year is pressed past another tend of Reed, the knife back on its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh held where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 still unspent. A thing stopped three times is not settled; the loan that can hear waits for the word that has not been said.

\textbf{Four stoppings now stand on the interval tray and none of them is a payment.} The seventh year is pressed past the middle tend of Reed, the knife back on its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh held where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 still unspent. A thing stopped four times is not settled; a held word is a debt and a debt that can hear can be called, and the loan waits for the word that has not been said. The stroke goes on over the flagstones without the half-check and the two silences stay unjoined.

On Days 135 through 137 the seventh year presses nearer its end and is still held; the boy is carried past him at the half-pace and the day’s arithmetic goes on in loaves and weather. On Day 136 he takes the broom after its instruction, agrees with an early thaw and a late and wants the late because it puts off the paying; men unnamed go into the room off the shed and he does not ask about it, just as Jorra does not ask about the ear. With the coals banked and the knife set back where it can be checked he measures the kindling four, four and an empty fifth and tells it \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Then the sentence about the ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes the fifth time to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name; he draws the breath and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} and goes on with the broom over the bright patch without the half-check. The boy files the fifth stopping beside the first four on the interval tray as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and refuses to let five likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine. A thing stopped five times is a thing held, not settled; something must give at the end of the seventh year and has not given yet. The loan stays uncalled and the two silences stay unjoined.

On Days 138 through 140 the seventh year presses nearer its end than it has ever stood and is still held; the boy is carried past him at the half-pace and the yard’s arithmetic goes on in loaves and weather. The next I don’t count} and then the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes a sixth time --- after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14 and 17 --- all the way to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name; he draws the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and goes on with the broom. The boy files a sixth stopping on the interval tray beside five as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and refuses to let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer has been named to any of the six. On Day 140 he takes the broom only after its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and keeps the late because it puts off the paying; the knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 unspent with a small interval at the top of each reach. Men unnamed go into the back room before first grey and he does not ask about them, just as Jorra does not ask about the ear; his stroke goes on over the shallow bright patch without the half-check and neither man names the other’s silence. Through Reed 22–24 the seventh year presses from nearer its end to one tend from it and still does not give. His stroke goes on past the shallow bright patch without even the half-check it had made once on Seed 22, and the equality under the roof holds at that place: Jorra’s finger leads at the damper, Tarn does not ask about the room and Jorra does not ask about the ear, and the two silences are not joined. No collector comes, the loan stays uncalled, and something must still give at the end of the seventh year and has not given here. Ash stays worked into the knuckle creases and his chest has been tight since the dark.

On Day 145 the seventh year stands one tend from its end and still does not give. The knife is at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach; Ash is worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is. On Days 147 through 149 the seventh year stands one tend from its end and has still not given. The next I don’t count} and brings the ear-sentence a ninth time to the word that would call the loan, stopping with no figure and no name; he draws the breath he does not spend, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and goes on with the broom. The loan that can hear is still uncalled and something must give at the end of the seventh year, but nothing gave here.

\textbf{Ch 37.} The firing month finds his seventh year still one tend from its end and held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check, the seventh at the lip of the sill where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge with the unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, his chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into his knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holding what light there is. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed and says \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late, wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On all three days his stroke goes on over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without even the half-check; he does not turn along the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, and no collector comes. The equality with the boy has stood a hundred and fifty-two days: his ear for a pot before a knuckle touches it, the boy’s turn toward the note before anybody makes it, two silences of one shape and a loan that can hear never called. At the going of the light on Day 152, with the coals banked, he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}; the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes up as it had come up nine times before, but on this day it is \textbf{not} brought to the word that would call the loan --- it stops short of the threshold, no tenth stopping stands up to join the nine, and he draws the breath that should have gone in and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and goes back to the broom. Sella, within hearing, gives the end of her instruction to the pot and asks nothing; Jorra does not ask about the ear and he does not ask about the room. The nine stoppings stay nine objects with no payer named to any, a tenth before the seventh year is earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill, and the absence of a tenth is a keeping and not a payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; the loan uncalled and something still to give at the end of the seventh year.

\textbf{Ch 38.} Tallow 4–10 finds his seventh year pressed nearer its end than it has ever stood and still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check, the seventh at the very edge of the sill where it cannot, the small knife set back at the lip with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, Ash worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there is, his chest tight since the dark. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed and says \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late, going on all the while wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On Days 153 and 156 his stroke goes on over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check while the stones keep the place where it stopped; he does not turn along the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, and no collector comes. On Day 158 the seventh year is pressed still nearer and still held, and he takes the broom only after the instruction, \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late. The sentence about an ear worth more than the debt that holds it does not come up in these seven days: no tenth stopping stands up to join the nine, and the boy files no new interval, for a tenth before the seventh year is earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill. The warm stone stays cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, the burned-slate word comes a fourth time and arrives nowhere, and the pot sayings stay sayings with no pot lost; the two silences under the roof stay unjoined. Forward, not closed.

Through Grain 10–12 the exact account under the roof goes on without a tenth standing up. The seventh year stands at its very end and has not given; the small knife stays at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it and the Seed 16 breath still unspent. The sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it still comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there, nine stoppings with no tenth, a remembered interval and not a payment; no collector comes on Grain 10, 11 or 12. Offstage at the market, he keeps the bright patch and the collector’s road unturned and lets the day’s new colours and shapes stay outside the house.

Through Grain 13–18 the exact account under the Vail roof goes on without a tenth standing up. The seventh year stands at its very end and has not given: the knife at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn and not spent, nine stoppings nine objects with no tenth and the loan uncalled. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed, tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, brings the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name as a remembered stopping and not a new one, and no collector comes up or down the clay road on any of the six days. His stroke goes past the shallow bright patch and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without the half-check and without a turn, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat. Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist; the warm stone lies cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft. The dressed grain under the fold gains no number, the yard goes around the returning-line place with a look and no number, and the boy’s thirtieth answer is filed on its sixth place and not stood up beside his nine stoppings. Forward into Grain 19, not closed.

Through Grain 19–21 his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn and not spent, nine stoppings with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled with no collector up or down the clay road on any of the three mornings. He brings the ear-sentence all the way to the word that would call the loan three more times and stops each time with no figure and no name, a remembered stopping and not a new one, and he wants the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. The warm stone lies cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving. His stroke goes past the bright patch without the half-check, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction and the Day 166 beat. He is a debt with a body, one year from the end of his term, valuable because he can hear and therefore unsafe, and the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Nothing paid, called, spent or forgiven.

Through Grain 22–24 (Days 231–233) his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled with no collector up or down the clay road on any of the three days. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument can find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifting it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back; the warm stone Sella gave him in the winter Garl died lies cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving. His stroke goes over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf. Nothing paid, called, spent or forgiven.

The next I don’t count} in the tone of a man stating the weather, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, and sweeps the collector’s road without once turning along it; no collector comes up or goes down the clay road on Smoke 10, 11 or 12. Through Smoke 16–18 his seventh year stands at its very end and still held, and the sentence about the ear under this roof comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there on all three days, a remembered stopping with no figure and no name. Six are counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh is at the lip where it cannot; the knife lies at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath is drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, and nine stoppings stand with no tenth. His stroke goes over the bright patch and the collector’s road without the half-check or a turn, and no collector comes up or down the clay road. The warm stone stays cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, not tried and not forgiven; Ash is worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holds what light there is, and his chest has been tight since the dark. He does not ask about the room and Jorra does not ask about the ear, and something must still give at the end of the seventh year.

Through Smoke 19–21 the seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given. He takes the broom only after its instruction, tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late while wanting the late because it puts off the paying, sets six where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, and brings the sentence about an ear under this roof worth more than the debt that holds it to the calling word on the 19th and 21st, stopping there with no figure and no name as a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven; the Seed 16 breath stays unspent, the loan uncalled, no collector coming up or down the clay road on any of the three days. Chest tight since the dark, Ash in the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holding what light there is, the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its unmarked loft pot, and his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check (T036/T076, T009/T013/T092, T006). Smoke’s second arithmetic goes up the road in Berr’s locked box on the 20th and changes nothing at the kindling; the boy’s six answers stay objects on a sixth place, never joined to the ear-sentence (T061/T082).

Through Smoke 22–24 the seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given. The next I don’t count}, sets six in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the very lip of the sill where it cannot, and keeps Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside the knife with no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the debt. On all three days the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven; he would not stand one up to make the nine into a rule. The Seed 16 breath is drawn and unspent, the loan uncalled, no collector coming up or down the clay road, chest tight, Ash in the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holding what light there is, his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check, and the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its unmarked loft pot, not tried and not forgiven (T036/T076, T006, T009/T013/T092). Smoke’s second arithmetic stays behind and unread up the road; the boy’s six answers stay objects on a sixth place, never joined to the ear-sentence, and the finding that a house keeps by not-doings is held on a place apart from the debt’s own omissions (T061/T082). Something must still give at the end of the seventh year, and did not give here.

Through Bone 10–12, Days 309–311, his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given. The knife lies at the very edge of its sill where it can be checked and where it can slip, six in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it with no name and no figure. On all three days he takes the broom only after its instruction, tells the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and keeps the late because it puts off the paying, and brings the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name — a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven. His stroke goes over the shallow bright patch without the half-check; the fourth held change stays on the flagstones with three older ones and four are four and not a rule. The loan is uncalled, no collector comes up or down the clay road, and Bone 20 stands five mornings ahead. Nothing is joined, named, opened, called, paid or ended.

Through Bone 22–24, Days 321–323, the exact account holds at the kindling and on the flagstones and nothing is spent. Six years stand in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, the knife at the very edge of its sill where it can be checked and where it can slip; he told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} on all three days and put the knife back where it could be checked, announcing it to nobody because the yard had already been told. He brought the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven; the breath he drew did not go in, the Seed 16 breath stayed unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, his chest tight since the dark, Ash in the knuckle creases the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding the little light and giving it back. His stroke went over the shallow bright patch without the half-check on all three days, and the returned half-check of Bone 8 stayed on the flagstones as the fourth of four held changes on four places, not a rule and with no payer named; Sella’s handful at the rack end was not made a fifth of them, and the boy’s staying and early letting-go stayed two objects with a finger between. The warm stone lay cold in its unmarked loft pot, unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiveness. He said nothing to an early thaw and a late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying; no collector came up or went down the clay road on any of the three days, and the five arithmetics going up in Berr’s locked box did not call the loan. Jorra did not ask about the ear and he did not ask about the room; the two silences stayed unjoined. No bond paid or spoken, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

Kept six years in the worn thumb-mark where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beyond it where it could not, with the small knife laid at the very edge of its sill where it could be checked and where it could slip and Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the debt. Told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} in the tone of a man stating the weather and put the knife back where it could be checked, announcing it to nobody because the yard had already been told. The sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that held it came to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name — a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist, in place since Y.H. 806, held what little light there was and gave it back, and he held the wrist up a moment to the grey as though to see whether the light had come to anything. His chest had been tight since the dark and the Seed 16 breath stayed unspent, a small empty place at the top of each reach where the breath should have gone in. He said \emph{Yes, house} to one who wanted the thaw early and to another who wanted it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and went on wanting the late because it puts off the paying though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. His stroke went over the shallow bright patch on the flagstones without the half-check on the eleventh and twelfth; the returned half-check of Bone 8 stayed on the flagstone’s own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction, the Day 166 shelf beat and the Frost 5 returned beat — four held changes on four places, four and not a rule, no fifth likeness made a cause and no payer named. Up in the Debt Loft, which reached the boy only as a sound with a direction, the warm stone she had given him in the winter Garl died lay cold in its unmarked pot and he did not reconcile it with the debt and did not try, which is not forgiveness. The loan stayed uncalled and no collector came up the clay road or went down it on any of these three days. No new scar, possession or change of voice; no bond paid or spoken.
