\item Ch 1: Does not appear; the broom, the knife and the loft are held for Chapter 2.

\item Ch 2: Swept the kiln-house before anyone woke and stopped for two strokes at a pot’s flat note without turning his head or naming the sound. Put the small bench knife in his pocket, then took it out and put it back where it could be checked and said so unasked. Told Sella \emph{Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.} Carried up from the Debt Loft with a broom on the third day, banked the coals, and said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} when the boy was given a bed. Heard the second flat note of the three days from a pot set down on the bench and did not say what it was.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. Swept before light on Stone 11 and again at dusk on Stone 12, with Ash in his knuckles and the pale ring at his left wrist. Took the small bench knife out and put it back where it could be checked, saying so unasked both times. His broom stopped for two strokes at the flat note of a pot through the shed wall and he did not turn his head, name the sound or say that it was a sound at all --- the second ear in the house, witnessed only by the reader. Said \emph{yes, house; I’ll sweep it; I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again} to the ground and kept his head down over the broom. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not counted. He said nothing about the note all day, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. On Stone 13 came up the yard with the small knife already back on its sill, checked it with his eyes only, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot before Jorra set it down; his broom stopped half a stroke at the set-down that gave nothing and he said nothing about either. Counted six years of seven and held the seventh back, and stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then swept again. At dusk put the knife back where it could be checked and announced it unasked, and kept his head down over the broom while Sella counted loaves and bits. Said nothing all three days about the note that did not come, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 measured the kindling stack with his eyes, four, four and a space at the end, and said to the stack \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} On Stone 17 set the small knife on its sill and told the yard to check, stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} and said \emph{Yes, house} before going on; his broom checked half a stroke when a pot turned toward on the bench gave nothing. Scraped Ash from his knuckles with the knife, held the pale ring at his left wrist up to the light and put the knife back without announcing it this time. Named the kiln’s breath as the danger and said a man in Mud End who slept before a kiln with the damper shut was called a merciful death; said he would take the late thaw, a longer week before the paying. On Stone 18 said he had swept and would sweep again; on Stone 19 agreed a late thaw was a longer week before the paying and offered to check the ridge; on Stone 20, Account-day, told the yard again the knife was back on its sill and let his broom stop half a stroke at the place where no note had come. Six of seven years counted all five days, the seventh held back and never named.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

You can check}, and said to the kindling \emph{Six counted; the next I don’t count}; was sent for a collector for a neighbour two doors down and returned with a man whose cuff was soft from washing and fingertips the colour of skimmed milk gone off, who said \emph{the measure is taken and the account stands as entered} to a slate. On the way back his head turned a degree at a vessel’s flat note carried past the door and he did not name it or look at the basket. On Stone 23 swept around the place where a pot had given nothing and said \emph{I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again}; Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked by him. On Stone 25 and 26 his broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked in the yard with the flat knock and he said nothing about either; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. On Stone 29 held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light, said \emph{I can check the width, house. I’ve a thumb as good as any}, and took his eyes off the ridge. On Stone 30 the knife was back on its sill and announced once more, unasked. Six of the seven years counted every day, the seventh held back and never named; the ear kept silent and the loan uncalled.

Scrubbed at the Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts, and kept the silence about the flat note all five days and about the boy’s ear as before. On the Long Night said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark. Wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying; on Ilmen 1 swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife back on its sill and the seventh still held back, and did not touch the ridge or the mark.

Agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 3 set the small bench knife on its sill and announced it to the empty yard --- \emph{I put it back. You can check} --- and scraped at the Ash in his knuckles. On Ilmen 5 swept near the bench and did not say what the pot gave or look toward the basket. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound. On Ilmen 7 stood with the yard as the Singing Sill gave its low note early and the argument ended in weather, and said nothing about either. Through the seven days kept the silence about the flat note and about the boy’s ear, and carried the count into Ilmen 8 with the knife back on its sill and the seventh year held back.

\end{itemize}

Swept around the place where the clay-heavy water had come up behind the drying racks and swept the road toward the Fishstairs over and over without looking along it, the road a man goes down to fetch a collector; no collector came for the woman in the brook and he did not go for one. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. Said nothing about the sixth hearing the boy had heard out of a person on the bank, and did not look at the basket on the way back up the yard.

Swept the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once turning to look along it; no collector went down it and he did not go, and he did not say the omission had a name. Stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then said \emph{Yes, house} and went on. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. At the well on Day 47 went once over the collector’s road and again without turning. Said nothing about the boy’s ear or his own, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Day 50 and another pot answered nearly full on Day 52 and his head did not turn at either; he did not call either a seventh hearing or name the sound. He agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying; his broom went over the collector’s road on Days 50 and 53 without once turning along it and no collector came. On Silt 1 he kept sweeping toward the thaw with the count unchanged; the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

Said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agreed with both so entirely no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying came with the water. His broom checked at the cracked-pot place and went over the collector’s road without once turning along it; when a vessel gave its note past the yard door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head did not turn and he did not name the sound or look toward the basket. Said \emph{Yes, house} to both sides of the thaw argument and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. His broom went over the collector’s road without once turning along it; a vessel gave its note past the door on Day 75 and a whole vessel did so on Day 77, and his head did not turn and he did not name either sound. He did not look toward the bed or the basket, said nothing about the foundling’s half-beat or the loaf, and kept the two ears and two silences under one roof as an equality neither named. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled; the seventh year pressed to its edge and was held.

\end{itemize}

Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. Said \emph{Yes, house} to the woman who wanted the thaw early and the man who wanted it late, agreed so entirely no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts all week. His broom went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector came; he kept the sentence about the frozen ford where he kept the seventh year. On Silt 26 and Seed 1 swept the yard around the boot-print, the clean dark line, the finer grey and the space under the lowest rack without touching any of them, and on Seed 1 took the broom only after Sella had given it its instruction. A vessel gave its note past the door on Silt 27 and again in the afternoon of Seed 1 and his head did not turn and he did not name the sound, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing; he did not turn toward the foundling’s half-beat at the market either and did not join the two turnings. At the going of the light set the knife back where it could be checked and told the yard so, unasked. The next I don’t count.} Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. A vessel gave its note past the door on Days 91 and 92 and his head did not turn and he did not name the sound; the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. No collector came, the loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the seventh year was held.

The small knife lay on its sill with six years in a mark his thumb had worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house cannot check, and he told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash was worked into his knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. Kept the sentence from the frozen ford with the seventh year and entered neither; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence that would call it was not said under the roof. A vessel gave its note past the door on Seed 13 and his head did not turn and he did not name it. The two ears kept their equality and the loan stayed uncalled; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here. No new scar or possession.

His chest had been tight since the dark. The small bench knife lay on its sill with six years in a mark his thumb had worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house cannot check, and he told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. He called everyone \emph{house}, said \emph{I owe the yard a sweep, house} to the trodden clay as a statement of fact, and said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreeing so entirely no argument could find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. He keeps the sentence from the frozen ford with the seventh year and enters neither; a loan that can hear can be called, and the sentence that would call it was not said under the roof. The two ears kept their equality and the loan stayed uncalled; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here, the breath pressed to its edge. Offstage on Seed 20. His seventh year was pressed past the end of the planting and still held; the small bench knife lay at the very edge of its sill with six years in a mark worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check, and the unforged collector sentence lay beside it where he has kept it since the frozen ford. His chest was tight and the breath from Seed 16 still unspent, a small interval at the top of each reach where it should have gone in; to the kindling he said \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. \textbf{The change of Seed 22 was held and not repeated:} while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence his bristles went on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the shallow bright patch the stones kept where the stroke had stopped, and neither man turned or spoke. The boy set the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray, two objects and not a rule. Two ears and two silences kept their equality under one roof, the loan that can hear was not called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market was not joined to his own turning. No new scar, possession or change of voice; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

\end{itemize}

The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, agrees with the early thaw and the late while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, sweeps the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and the collector’s road without once turning along it, and no collector came up or went down the clay road on Grain 7, 8 or 9 (T036/T076). Seventh year at its very end and still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn and unspent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled; chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was. On all three days he brought the ear-sentence all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, drew the breath he should have spent and did not spend it; at this late hour the stopping was a remembered interval and not a new one, and if the thing was paid at all it was paid as an interval and not as a calling (T036/T076, T061/T082). His stroke went over the bright patch without the half-check, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat, not repeated as a new change and not paired into a rule (T062, T100). While Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper he did not look toward the bed or ask about the room, and Jorra did not ask about the ear; the two silences stayed unjoined. Three or more unnamed men went low into the back room before first grey on all three mornings and neither man gave them a name, and the two shut-room tellings stayed two; the burned-slate word came over the boards a fourth time from Slate Row and arrived nowhere with no third telling (T035/T031, T065/T095). He heard the wrong-wind sayings about a pot gone quiet and gave no name to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188. The warm stone lay cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft and he did not go up to it, and not trying was not forgiving (T006). No new scar, possession or change of voice; the seventh year stands at its end and has still not given. Forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\chapter*{The Atlas}
\markboth{The Atlas}{The Atlas}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Atlas}
\CRmap*{The Bone Orchard — outside the north gate of Sill}{build/atlas/bone-orchard.jpg}{The burial ground a league north of the Cross, drawn at walking scale along the north gate road: the rough-staked ground of the thin-return children’s shallow graves, the east ground where pots are broken for the dead and left where they fell, the barrow of grey Ash that goes out through the north gate on every market-day and comes back empty, and the road running on through the gate to Cold Acre on the ridge with its six houses, its barley and turnips and its well that never freezes. The north bridge, the Ilm and Sill are drawn faint at the foot for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the barrow, the unslated graves, the pots broken for the house and the road that is clay to the ankle in Silt. An engraved broken pot in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Cold Acre — on the ridge two leagues north of Sill}{build/atlas/cold-acre.jpg}{The farm hamlet two leagues north of Sill, one league beyond the Bone Orchard by the north gate road, drawn at walking scale: six houses and a byre in their drift-stone wall, the barley strips and turnip ground, the bare ring of ground about the well where frost will not hold and the children leave the untaken turn standing, and the well itself with its stone lip, clay dish, well-rope, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand. The well-shrine and the children’s stone stand beside the curb; a red nought marks the place where the thirteenth would stand. The road runs south to the north gate, Sill and the Bone Orchard drawn faint below, and east to the Tallow Works two leagues off; the frozen Ilm and the Singing Sill lie at the foot. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the ninety-four days of ice, the bell that comes up the ridge four, four and a gap with the gap not ours to fill, the assessor’s column that has never held a figure, the barrow of grey Ash that goes past on market-days, and no Last Day on a ridge. An engraved clay dish set on a stone sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Cross and the Fishstairs — Sill’s market and the steps below the north bridge}{build/atlas/cross-and-fishstairs.jpg}{The ground the boy is carried over on every Account-day, drawn at the scale of the market: the market square with its stalls, the reading block under the moot-post and its finger’s width of shade, the eight pigs on the weighing rail and the turnips left standing with figures beside them, the Court’s table at the Slate Row fringe; below the north bridge the Fishstairs counting four steps, four, and the out-of-line landing, the edge of the fish-trade in the bridge’s shadow, Rusk’s room, the hard sill and the Singing Sill under the water, the dotted line of the Breaking, and the south bridge on the way to Low Kiln. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the reed month.}

\CRmap{Greybank, the Court’s gate}{build/atlas/greybank.jpg}{The Court’s granary town eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, drawn as its own surveyors would draw it: the Ilm and its quay, the factor’s house where the tally for Sill is kept, the Vhaleni Counting House with Veno Brine’s private drawer of dry documents, the Court’s granaries and banking hall, the winter ford, the burial grounds, and the ends of the Clay Road and the beginnings of the Salt and Hearth Roads. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{High Kiln — the glaze terrace above Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/high-kiln.jpg}{The other half of Sill, drawn at the scale a potter walks: the terrace two hundred paces above the low yard with its barley strip, House Clay and the folded red cord and locked box, the Glaze Room where lead is mixed and tasted, the master potters’ houses and their breathing kilns, the broken terrace lip, the steep street climbing from the north bridge and the Cross, the Ilm with its four-foot sill and Singing Sill, and Low Kiln below drawn faint for neighbourhood only. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{Sill and the Lower Ilm — the country of the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-region.jpg}{The clay country about Sill, drawn out a few days’ walking: the Ilm from Nine Pots and the Ferr to Greybank, the weir, the Old Kiln, Cold Acre, Mud End and the Reedholt marsh. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap{Sill and the Two Kilns — the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-settlement.jpg}{A detailed plan of Sill on the Ilm, drawn to the ground a child can walk: the four-foot fall and the Singing Sill, the two bridges, the Fishstairs and the Cross, Slate Row, Low Kiln with the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, High Kiln and the Glaze Room, the family houses, the smithy, the meal mill, the wells and fields, the Bone Orchard and the edge of the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{House Reed and the Birth-flower Shrine — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/house-reed.jpg}{The reed-cutter’s house east of the Clay Yard, Alda Reed’s dwelling, drawn close at the scale of a basket set just inside the finger’s-width-open door: the one room with its hearth and slip pot, the bench by the door with a birth-slate propped writing-down, the board-bed whose grey wool holds a warmed stone at the belly, the grey Ash ridge left where it lies, bundles of cut reeds inside and at the threshold, and the loose board lifted at one end under which six narrow pages lie face-down in a second hand with no seventh written. A few paces east stands the birth-flower shrine, the hearth-maids’ niche where the district’s birth-slates lie overnight: five slates on the flat stone, a candle end of beeswax, a curl of grey wool, the slate-box of answered slates at its foot, and the crossed mark cut into the stone above, drawn and not explained. Around both, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the Drawing house, House Silt, the smithy, the drying racks, the slip pits and the yard well; the Slip Brook clay-heavy along the north, the Ilm below, the walk the women take from the house to the niche, and the Clay Road west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the reedbeds going off toward Reedholt. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the hand that goes to the slate before the child, the mark for which a priest gave a date and did not look up, the six pages no Court physician has seen, and the date laid over a sign that no living person can take off. An engraved bundle of cut reeds sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{House Silt and the Birth Room — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/house-silt.jpg}{The house three doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail house, drawn at the scale at which a basket set just inside the door sees it: the front birth room with its bench by the door, hearth and slip pot, board-bed of grey wool with the hollow where the pale river stone lay, the round pewter tin above the bed with its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, the shelf’s chipped cup, the birth-slate and the six narrow pages turned face-down toward a floorboard, and the grey Ash ridge left where it lies along the skirting into the back room. There a neighbour scrubs at a board with lye water and a low song comes up through the floor. Around it, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the smithy, the Drawing house, the drying racks, the slip pits, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook where Dessa Silt was taken, and the nineteen counted steps. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.}

\CRmap{Keld Keep and the First Seam}{build/atlas/keld.jpg}{The Warden’s fortress city against the Rim and the deep survey cut into the stone beneath it, drawn cold and mineral as the Keep’s own survey-clerks would draw it: the walled Keep with the Warden’s hall and the mine-reeve’s room; the Rim Road coming up from Sill and going on ten leagues to the Cold Pass and its survey post; the Listening Stones five leagues higher in the Rim; and below, the timbered shaft of the First Seam with its galleries, the Descent, the Duelling Floor cut into the stone with nine clamps to the floor and the tenth behind the board, the survey room holding the crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 and its branching red mark, the Ninth Gallery with the tin lined with warm-stone, a seam-serpent’s passing entered only as a change in the numbers, and the hot-lead warning of the Sweating. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with a compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the measure before the name, the Warden’s claim, the once-a-year reading of the paper, and the insistence that no map is honest past the last pass.}

\CRmap*{The Meal Mill — below the south bridge, Sill}{build/atlas/meal-mill.jpg}{The water-mill under the south bridge, drawn at the scale of a sack set against the hopper: the Ilm coming down from the Cross with its silt shoals and tide ripples, the timber bridge, the race taking water from above the mill and the tail returning it below, the great wheel with its paddles and spokes, the two dressed millstones under the roof, the hopper with barley going in, the meal-book kept by the miller’s daughter with a barleycorn shut in its fold, the toll-bag, the sacks white with mill-dust, the grey print at the corner nobody will own, and the brown silt tideline the flood left along the foot of the leaf. The Cross and Slate Row stand faint on the north bank, High Kiln above them, Low Kiln with the Vail roof and the yard well across the water, the worked strips at the east edge. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ash, with compass, a scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the mill keeping one hour and the stone another, the figures that go into the meal and leave nothing on the leaf, the early note entered nil in a factor’s clerk’s narrow hand, the foundling left at the mill with a stone under him and no name, and the crust that travels two inches from a boy’s ear. An engraved barleycorn and an engraved dressing-pick sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Mud End — the peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill}{build/atlas/mud-end.jpg}{The peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale on the dry shelf above the marsh: nine houses and their peat stacks, the byre where the moot meets and its moot-post, sods set out to dry, the peat cuttings in the southern banks, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The Clay Road runs west to Sill and east the fifteen leagues on to Greybank, both drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only; the marsh drain comes down into the river, and Reedholt stands faint among the reeds to the south. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the winter peat that decides who stays warm, the man taken quiet in his sleep and called merciful, and the wolves of Reedholt. An engraved peat spade sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Nine Pots — the rival kiln hamlet west of Sill}{build/atlas/nine-pots.jpg}{The pottery hamlet eight leagues west of Sill, drawn at walking scale along the road of the old feud: four kilns and one shared clay pit, the potters’ houses and worked strips, the moot-post, and the road east forded over the Ferr toward Sill. Stonemouth stands three leagues east where the Ferr meets the Ilm, with its lime kilns and coarse sandstone workings; the blue-grey Lead Run comes in from the west, and the Rim Road passes north on its way to Keld Keep. Sill and Greybank are drawn faint at the east edge for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the feud, the lime and sandstone trade, the Lead Run that makes a man thin, and a cord from the Fishstairs never carried upriver. An engraved pot counted out at Nine Pots sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Reedholt — the reed-cutters’ hamlet in the east marsh}{build/atlas/reedholt.jpg}{The marsh hamlet four leagues east of Sill, drawn at walking scale: reed-cutters’ huts on posts on the dry hummock, the mud-wife’s hut with its grey-wool knot, the peat-dry with its drying sods and lifted tally board, peat stacks, the boardwalk over a cut with one plank gone, the peat-hut, the Reed Cut and its cut bundles, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The river road runs above the marsh toward Sill and Greybank; the marsh road comes down from Mud End, passes the hamlet and goes off toward the Quiet Acre and the Standing Post, both drawn faint or set down in notes. The black peat and the bog-cow are written in the surveyor’s margin and drawn nowhere, for a figure would make a thing stand that does not stand. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on going into the marsh in pairs, the reed-wolf’s five clicks and the man with two fingers gone, borrowed ground and standing reeves, peat and grey weighed under an apron and sealed under a Court name, and the child cutting a first bundle in the dark. An engraved reed-wolf and an engraved count-stick sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Rusk’s Room above the Fishstairs — Sill}{build/atlas/rusks-room.jpg}{The old man’s room above the Fishstairs and below the north bridge, drawn close at the scale of a hand laid on a drawer: the floorboards and their cold, the locked drawer with its small lock left shut, a bench and the stool nobody sees him use, the pot he taps for its note, the ice-mouse-fur coat and salt-stiff hat on their pegs, and the ash in the corners unswept; the window over the steps, the stair down, the four Fishstairs steps and the out-of-line landing where a fifth should stand, the bridge over the Ilm with the fish-trade shade beneath it, the Singing Sill and its four-foot fall, the river road upriver to the Weir and the Eel House and downriver to Greybank, with the Cross and its moot-post and Slate Row drawn faint at the edges. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ash, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the man who never sits down indoors and turns a question back on the asker, the paper read once a year on the Last Day that no surveyor has set down, and the boy who turned his head toward a pot before anybody tapped it. An engraved key with its small ward sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Bowl of Sere and the Ten Bowls}{build/atlas/sere.jpg}{The hot southern capital three hundred leagues south of Sill, drawn as a factor’s clerk at Greybank would copy a southern plan: no wall worth the name, but open courts each with a fire in the middle. The great Open Court holds the public bowl emptied at the third hour when an act of the Sun-Emperor is announced, and the fourth bowl that is set out at every feast and carried away full; nine other bowl-houses of the Ten Bowls stand about the courts. The Ember bowl-house is drawn with its fire-shrine fed with bought oil, its wine-press, its counting room no woman enters and a room with good light; Solene Ember was returned whole here in 799, 804 and 809. The grain mills stand on the cut to the south with their wheels and sacks, the grain strips and olive grounds beyond, the bond-quarters entered without a name, the trace of a broken wall, the burning winds and their yellow dust. The Peat Line runs along the north edge, where the southern advance stopped in Y.H. 634, with the road going on to Greybank and Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, a scale in leagues, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the announced act, the mercy of the Spending, the burning of the debt-slates, the two kinds of returned stranger, the clerk’s three times above the space and the Sere account with a place where a bowl should be emptied and is not.}

\CRmap*{Slate Row — the Court’s quarter in Sill}{build/atlas/slate-row.jpg}{The Court’s quarter, a quarter league east of the Cross, drawn at walking scale: the Clay Road passing through the Row to Greybank, the steep street climbing to High Kiln, the Ilm and its reedbeds along the south edge. The Court’s room with its bench by the door, pot, draught felt at the ankles and a place in the figures where a line should stand; the assessor’s narrow house of Y.H. 776; the collector’s table with its slate and cold-iron tube; the barred Waiting Room where the Forty of Low Kiln were held in Y.H. 812; the Court’s table at the market fringe and the printed one in twelve. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.}

\CRmap*{Stonemouth — where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm}{build/atlas/stonemouth.jpg}{The quarry village five leagues upriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm: the sandstone workings and the lime yard on the rising bank, the lime kilns with their smoke, the ale-room beside the kiln, the village houses, and the weigh-clerk’s bench by the landing with punts on the river. The river road runs east to Sill and west over the ford to Nine Pots three leagues away; the Lead Run comes in from the west stained blue-grey from an old working, and the Rim Road passes north-west toward Keld Keep. Sill and Nine Pots are drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the lime, sandstone and reed-wolf tooth that go out by water, the Ferr that makes a man thin with no figure set against it, the thirty-year habit of stopping at the end of the part when a clean coat comes up from Greybank, and the name kept in a room against the name kept on a slate. An engraved reed-wolf tooth sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Clay Yard and the Vail House — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-clay-yard.jpg}{The close ground of Low Kiln drawn at the scale a clay child walks: the Clay Yard with its slip pits and ruts, the Vail kiln-house with its hearth, loaf shelf and bed, the wheel-shed with the Debt Loft and the finger’s-width-open back room, the drying racks with the space beneath the lowest, the row of houses to House Silt, the smithy, the well and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook behind and the Ilm at the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Drawing House — the death-house two doors down the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-drawing-house.jpg}{The unnamed neighbour’s house two doors down the yard from Vail, drawn close at the scale of a basket set at the edge of the light: the bench by the door with its pot, the draught going along the floor before the cold is felt, four nails, four and a thumb’s-width knot overhead, the grey Ash ridge a finger’s width thicker than Vail’s and turning the corner by the door without a break. Inside, the drawing pallet against the far wall with the pale round place on the arm, the collector with the cold iron tube wrapped in wool and the slate face downward, a hearth, the folded quilt on the other side with the warmed stone at the belly and the pot set between child and door. The Vail kiln-house, wheel-shed, smithy, drying racks, House Silt, the birth-flower shrine, the yard well and the slip pits are drawn faint for neighbourhood; the Clay Yard and Clay Road run below, west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the room that bears no name, the knuckle set before the iron and the note before the figure, and the child who grew worse before the day was out. An engraved cold-iron tube in its wool sleeve sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Empty Cantons — the Quiet Acre}{build/atlas/the-empty-cantons.jpg}{The province sixty leagues south of Sill that the Court names the Empty Cantons and the Fen call the Quiet Acre: roads rutted under turf where no wheel has gone in eight hundred years, six wells dry with their stones laid in the old order, nine doorways standing where the walls have gone with bare squares above three of them and a slate unread in one, cold hearths with white ash unswept, dry cuts dug to drain, and a twelfth doorway left out of the count. Drawn from Gedde’s survey of Y.H. 812 and the Greybank annals, with the south road from Sill and Cold Acre, the way in from Greybank, the marsh road to Reedholt and the Standing Post, and the Peat Line and Sere beyond. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen.}

\CRmap{The Hearthseat on the Keel}{build/atlas/the-hearthseat.jpg}{The Court’s city, built over the Hearth a hundred and fifty leagues south-east of Sill, drawn cool and clean as its own surveyors would file it: the Weighing Hall with the grating of cold iron over the never-out fire and the Hearth shown in cut beneath the floor; Slate Row with the College of Assessors and its second file; the Steward’s room, the sealed files, the bank where measures are pressed into newborn vessels, the rooms of fewer than twenty Kept, the back rooms, the printed notice, the Hearth Road from Greybank and the way out to the Nine Wells. Surveyed and filed in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Old Kiln and the Ash Throat — one league south of Sill}{build/atlas/the-old-kiln.jpg}{The collapsed kiln in the grey clay a league south of Sill, drawn as its surveyor would draw it: the fallen crown and its broken brickwork, the fire mouth on the south-east flank, the flue broken at the top, the concentric throat where the ash runs deeper than a man, the hollow in its wall from which a slate was carried north to Low Kiln, the grey banks that will not take a glaze, the surveyor’s stakes and his cord, the track from Sill and the marsh way to Reedholt. A slow coil copied from the back of a slate is inked into the margin and left unread. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Smithy — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-smithy.jpg}{The forge east of the Clay Yard, drawn at the scale of a man standing at the bench: the long low shop with no kiln-mark over its door, the forge hearth and bellows, the anvil, the bench with its chisel notches that nobody has ever entered as a figure, the kiln behind the bench answering four pulls with the fifth missing, three collectors’ cold-iron tubes on their pegs with the grips polished grey to the thumb, Keldish bars with the blue bloom no potter will glaze over, the ash pit, the trough and the slate lying face down on a shop where no man would write a sentence. The yard well, the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed, the drying racks, House Silt, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine stand faint at the edges; the Clay Road runs west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the Slip Brook and the Ilm below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the tubes that take and do not give, the pale ring left at a wrist, the count kept in wood, the iron that comes down from Keld and the counting room shut in the last war eighteen leagues east. An engraved tube and an engraved anvil sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Standing Post and the Peat Paths — the Fenmarch}{build/atlas/the-standing-post.jpg}{The only Fen place a dry man is shown: the carved post and the dry boards where reeves settle fines standing up, the reeve’s stone with its peat-block niche, the loose board with the reed beneath, the huts on posts, the meres and black peat, the ways east to Mud End, south to the Peat Line and north-west toward the Quiet Acre, which is set down in words and drawn nowhere. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Bone.}

\CRmap*{The Tallow Works — the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill}{build/atlas/the-tallow-works.jpg}{The sheep-fat works known in Sill only by the smell on a north wind, drawn at walking scale: the rendering house or fat-house with its three vats, the hot flue and the thumb-wide warm crack where the wall meets it with grey paper nests hung behind, the lamp-room with its trimmed lamps and the leaf kept under a cracked saucer, the byre where the men sit at the turning of the year, the nest-fire at the shed door with the burnt paper beside it, the sheep-folds on the rise, and the sluice run carrying ash and wash-water away south-east. The ridge road comes in from the north gate past Cold Acre, both drawn faint, and the sweet smoke goes down on a north wind toward Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the fourth cup poured under the bench and the clerk who set it on the floor, the wasp that comes to the warmth and not the fat with twelve nests burnt and no value arising, fever first and the cold after with no figure asked for, the coal that comes up in clay on Kindling and the Long Night’s cost, the nought written where a name should stand, and the second warm crack in the cold north wall that has never held a nest and is set down in words but not marked on the wall. An engraved tallow lamp and an engraved tallow-wasp sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Waste beyond the Last Pass}{build/atlas/the-waste.jpg}{A chart of report and not of walking: the Rim and the Cold Pass at the east edge, the survey post, and beyond it the cold seams and the coastlines of cold, with the uncollected sitting upright facing the way they came. No distance past the post can be trusted. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813.}

\CRmap*{The Weir and the Eel Traps — one league upriver of Sill}{build/atlas/the-weir.jpg}{The eel weir on the Ilm a league upriver of Sill, drawn at the ground the trap-keepers walk: the V of stakes and its traps, the plank walk, Orra Weir’s hut and salting-racks, the hearth-maids’ blessing stone, the shoals and reeds, and the river road. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Worked Strips — the barley fields east of Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-worked-strips.jpg}{The ground east of Low Kiln drawn at walking scale, the chart the lived days have fallen on from the planting of Seed through the cutting and dressing of Grain to the wool-covered grain of Smoke: five long rutted plots with their furrows and a flood stone a woman swept around, the clay-heavy Slip Brook coming down behind the drying racks, the reedbeds standing grey in the ruts where the barley stood, the Ilm along the head of the chart with its landing and punt, and the river road above the strips. Low Kiln, the Vail roof and its smoke, the drying racks and the Cross are drawn faint at the western edge for neighbourhood only; the Weir lies a league upriver, Mud End and Greybank downriver, Reedholt away through the marsh. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the arm that knows a bundle’s weight and no slate its price, the clay-heavy rise that took a woman from the end of nineteen steps and was called weather, and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out — described in the margin and marked nowhere, for a mark would be a figure and no figure stands. An engraved ear of barley with its top grain gone sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Vail Kiln-house — the roof over the boy, Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/vail-house.jpg}{The house known by its objects before its people, drawn at the scale of a basket set just inside the door: the boy’s room with its bed, one crust in the fold and four nails, four and a knot overhead; the other room with the carried fire under ash at four and a gap, the loaf shelf with two unnamed gaps and the charcoal beneath unread, the clay jar, the charred slate and the clean dark line beside the finer grey called the thaw. Beyond it the kiln at its mouth, the wheel-shed with the cold damper of two bites, the Debt Loft and the finger’s-width-open back room, the drying racks, the flagstones with the bright patch, the yard well with its bare trough and the Clay Road going west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Ember.}

\CRmap*{Vhal and the Sallow coast}{build/atlas/vhal.jpg}{A salt-chart of the principal Vhaleni port and the five leagues of shore east of it, drawn in the tar-and-wet-rope manner of the Council’s own surveyors: the Quay with its piers, crane, moored salt boats and the pulled benches; the Council room that smells of tar and wet rope, the tide-tally house and the glass furnaces within the town; the Salt Pans outside it with their dippers at dawn and their drying salt-paper; the blue-green Glaze Cliffs stained by old lead workings, and the glass-sand pits behind them; the silt-mouthed Ilm entering from the west and the Salt Road coming up from Greybank by the coast pass. In the sea the Sallow draw runs seaward against the wind, with a brine-gull, a salt boat and a salt-thing by report, and a surveyor’s notes on boat-shares passing through mothers, contracts that rot in the damp, and children warned not to lick the cliffs. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, league scale and a convention of signs.}

\CRmap*{The War of Measures — the eastern border country}{build/atlas/war-of-measures.jpg}{A surveyor’s chart of the ground the measure-wars are fought over: the Ferr valley and the lower Ilm from Nine Pots and Stonemouth to Greybank and the Sallow shore. Burned kilns, a poisoned well, collectors’ boats on the Ilm and a district left cold for a season. The cold is drawn as the thing that advances. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 814.}

\CRmap*{Sarn — the bowl between Hearth and Waste}{build/atlas/world.jpg}{The known world as its own surveyors would draw it: the Rim and the cold beyond, the Sallow Sea, the Keel and the Hearth, and the nations between. Surveyed in Y.H. 812.}

\CRmap*{The Yard Well — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/yard-well.jpg}{The most-named uncharted stage of the daily round, drawn at the scale of a pail set down on the stone where a pail always stands: the shared well of the low houses with its little roof, uneven curb, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand; the white frost-bloom on the north lip where the Warm went out of the stone and the thawed edge where the sun took it off; the trough skinned bare and the silt-clouded plate of ice set on the flat stone out of the path of feet. At the bucket-round a woman draws with the pail against her knee and her hand toward her sleeve, the count kept in wood and unread, while a man brings a number up out of a shut fist toward the well and puts it back, so the figure arrives nowhere. The slate lies open on the lip with the writing turned toward its owner and nobody reading it aloud; the words spoken to the boards and the well-roof stand at five shapings with no owner standing under them, and the two tellings of the counting room shut in the last war do not touch. The Vail kiln-house, House Silt and the birth-flower shrine lie faint to the west, the drying racks to the east with the space under the lowest gone around, the Clay Road running west to the Cross and east the eighteen leagues to Greybank, High Kiln over the terrace above, the clay-heavy Slip Brook and the Ilm among the reedbeds below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the water that tasted different, the number that is kept back, the pail that goes down into weather and the plate of ice standing where the weather was told to stand. An engraved pail on a well-chain sits in the margin.}

\chapter*{The Reckoning of Days}
\markboth{The Reckoning of Days}{The Reckoning of Days}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Reckoning of Days}
\begin{CRtimeline}
\CRday{Day 414}{Ilmen 20, Y.H. 814, Tenthday, the month’s second Account-day and market  —  under the Vail kiln-house roof in the small hours at the bed, loaf shelf’s low angle, hearth, pot board with the twice-mended pot, rack end with dressed grain under wool, boards and towel, then down the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate and across to the Cross, the reading block under the moot-post and its finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, the market pot board where a silent woman turned a cup a quarter with the sweetish green at one mouth-corner, the market’s edge where a small shape in cast-offs caught light on a green sliver, the clay road up toward High Kiln, the out-of-line landing below the north bridge (reported, never entered), the road toward Greybank, the watch, and back under the roof at the going of the light, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  the twentieth came in the dark before first light earned by its own morning with nothing from the nineteenth crossing as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer and Ilmen 30 standing eight mornings off as a date, the count going 413 to 414 exact, six months and two hundred and thirty-three becoming two hundred and thirty-four days told by nobody, answers 403 and 404 entered on the sixth place, the carried fire’s fifth unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 414 days with their payer and their man unnamed, the crust gone leathery past the point where a child would still eat it with its corner a hair off the wool, the keeping at the fold found where put and still a finding, the thread frozen and unwiped, cold stopping at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint and the afterdrop waiting, the surgeon’s knowing checked by the infant’s three wants with both true, the second louder, neither winning; Sella setting the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay and standing half a pace off through the reading and the bell, saying nothing to the basket, the widow’s mark untouched because a market and a reading are not openings; Berr Clay coming up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat, the sweetish green of tasted glaze at one mouth-corner and the smell of nothing at all under the hot clay of him, wiping his thumb twice before touching nothing, holding the narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passing a finger over the figure through his sleeve, reading One in twelve, as the notice says low and twice over the basket once for the moot and once for the late households, calling the levy and denying it with your house never I as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing, sending a man’s number from a shut fist to a slate at the watch where it went from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrived nowhere, saying something low to the block about kindness being entered with no anger, no triumph and no payer, and going off up the road with the box locked and the second true subtraction of the month inside believing he had done a kindness; eight pigs going over the wet boards with no figure called, figures brought to a heap of turnips and left side by side without being made to agree, the bell going four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, Hessa Rale going up the clay road before noon with the narrow slate edge-on to her forearm and the writing to her sleeve, unread and not made a reader by a second figure, her eighth hand eight, the soft-cuffed clerk reported below the north bridge with his inward slate and his figure entered before a face was looked at still on a place of its own, the green at the pot board and the shape at the market’s edge sightings with no eighth; the boy filing two readings of the year behind one unsigned figure, two and not one account, the first not a thirteenth, the second supplying no signature, the figure read still not the figure paid, twelve old arithmetics not laid across two new ones to make a row come out even because paper is not a payer and the key went up a coat pocket that never comes back down, every kept thing advanced and not paid, nothing opened, joined, named, called, paid, forgiven or ended, the house going on as a house goes when a pot is set down in its place and the fire kept (T071/T072, T015/T041/T047 advanced NOT paid, T080/T090, T058/T079/T100, T060/T086/T097, T078, T061/T082, T088, T098)}
\CRday{Day 415}{Ilmen 21, Y.H. 814, Firstday  —  under the Vail kiln-house roof at the bed, loaf shelf’s low angle, hearth, pot board with the twice-mended pot, rack end with dressed grain under wool, boards and towel in the small hours and again at the going of the light, the nineteen steps down and up at the half-pace from every open slate, the Clay Yard with its seven walked-around places widest around the returning-line place, the yard well where Ilva drew with the pail against her knee and clay dried pale in her nail crescents, the Vail corner with the clean dark line, its finer grey called the thaw and the thinned sour tang of Ash, the bare trough and the gone pan’s round print, the worked strips with the field’s empty place, the kindling with the knife at its sill, the flagstones, the Vail wheel-shed edge and its cold damper, the north bridge road where a second man from Slate Row passed before first grey, the finger’s-width door and the river under its skin, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  the twenty-first came as an ordinary Firstday with no market, Cross, bell, reading or runner, no collector on the clay road and no ownerless voice over the boards, nothing from the twentieth crossing as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, the count going 414 to 415 exact, six months and two hundred and thirty-four becoming two hundred and thirty-five days told by nobody, answers 405 and 406 entered on the sixth place, the fire’s fifth unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 415 days with the two counts standing side by side, the crust leathery past a child’s eating and hardened into old horn, the keeping found where put, the thread unwiped, cold stopped at cheek, temple and wrist and the afterdrop waiting, Sella keeping the whole hearth grammar at both ends of the day and carrying him down and up without a word to the basket, Tarn’s hand over blade and sill and away with the sentence found where put and not made a habit, Jorra parting dusty forearms from clean as clot from vessel, speaking to the wheel before any person, withholding the pot’s full note three turns ahead and taking his finger from the cold damper without the extra holding of Ash 26; Ilva drawing at the well with her hand toward her sleeve before her eyes to the asker and her mouth after both, answering the question put and not the one behind it, Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account, her notched strip not taken out, read or counted, no figure coming off the wood, her ninth hand nine; before first grey a second man from Slate Row went down the north bridge road with a narrow slate under his arm and the writing turned toward his sleeve, a seen shape with no name, no loaf, no opened slate, no room entered, no threshold crossed and no word that carried, and the boy took the passing apart by the order of its parts the slate under the arm, the writing turned away, the direction down the bridge road, the word absent and the half-beat in the gap where an answer would have stood, filing the direction and the slate on places of their own beside the first man’s face, the clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping of the well-saying with a finger between every pair, giving the man no owner, errand, motive, interior, witness or tenth hand and joining none of them to Tarn’s valuable ear or ended term, Jorra’s ungiven promise or the clerk’s inward slate, a shape gathering interest toward a far-off calling and expressly not that calling, not a sale, not a rule and not a sixth shaping; in the afternoon neighbours at the well disagreed about the air and nobody owned the day, the softening at the Vail corner found where put and called weather, the direction not repeated, nothing opened, joined, named, called, paid or ended (T080/T090 and new T102 advanced NOT paid, T071/T072, T083/T085/T092, T009/T013/T092, T060/T086, T058/T079/T100, T036/T076/T006 held, T062/T035/T031 held)}
\CRday{Day 416}{Ilmen 22, Y.H. 814, Secondday  —  under the Vail kiln-house roof at the bed, loaf shelf’s low angle, hearth, pot board with the twice-mended pot and the hairline showing between old-brass staple and tighter wire, drying racks and rack end with dressed grain under wool, boards and towel in the small hours and again at the chapter’s close, the nineteen steps down and up at the half-pace from every open slate, the Clay Yard with its seven walked-around places widest around the returning-line place, the yard well where Ilva was seen and not asked with the strip in her sleeve, the trough bare and dark with the gone pan’s round print, the Vail corner with the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw and the thinned sour tang of Ash, the worked strips with the field’s empty place, the kindling with the knife at its sill and Garl’s unforged collector sentence, the flagstones, the Vail wheel-shed edge and the cold damper, the finger’s-width door and the river under its skin with the low note softer at one edge, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  the twenty-second came as an ordinary Secondday with no market, Cross, bell, reading, runner or collector, no second telling at the well, no sixth shaping, seventh hearing, tenth hand, eleventh arithmetic or eighth opening, nothing from the twenty-first crossing under the roof as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and Ilmen 30 standing eight mornings off as a date, the count going 415 to 416 exact, six months and two hundred and thirty-five becoming two hundred and thirty-six days told by nobody, a round-sounding number not stood up as a threshold, a doctrine or a figure, answers 407 and 408 entered on the sixth place so that six honest answers 403 through 408 stood there, worth nothing at two inches of air and not one a doctrine, the carried fire’s fifth unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 416 days with their payer and their man unnamed, the surgeon taking the body in its old order with the crust hardened through three dry nights into old horn two inches from the ear with its corner a hair off the wool, the keeping at the fold found where put and still a finding, the thread frozen and unwiped, cold stopping at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, the knowing that a basket set level out of the draught where the heat came sideways was the rewarming he would choose and could not ask for checked by the infant’s three wants with both true, the second louder, neither winning and the quarrel the work; Sella keeping the whole hearth grammar at both ends of the day with repair kept apart from restoration, grain covered and unfigured, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look, the widow’s mark untouched and no eighth opening due, Tarn’s six where the house can check and the seventh at the lip with the sentence found where put and the Seed 16 breath unspent at the end of a term already ended, Jorra’s dust and damper’s two bites with the extra holding not repeated and he’s not Vail sealed, Ilva seen and not asked; the afternoon going by small sounds with a pail on its stone, a rope in its knot, a loaf stopped short of a figure and a fist from the clay road bringing a number toward the well and taking it back into a sleeve, the softening at the river’s skin found where put and called weather with no hand or payer under it and no second look; in the small hours the towel came out as instruments come out when a case is done and every gap was left a gap, the clerk’s entered figure, degree and face on three places, the first man’s face and the second man’s slate and direction on their own places with a finger between them and every other kept thing, the fifth shaping on its own tray between Hessa’s eighth hand and the road saying, Berr’s low saying about kindness entered on a place of its own, twelve old arithmetics behind one unsigned figure beside the two readings payer and their man unnamed, the surgeon taking the field in its old order of stiff brown-edged crust gone into old horn two inches from the ear with its corner a hair off the wool, fold found where put and still a finding and not a placing, thread frozen and unwiped because nobody under any roof had ever given an instruction about the thread, cold stopping at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint as at the end of a line written out for it, Afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, the knowing that a basket set level out of the draught was the rewarming he would choose and could not ask for checked by the infant’s three wants, both true, the second louder, neither winning and the quarrel the work, Ilva offstage with her strip in her sleeve, her offered figure gone back into its fist and her ninth hand nine, and no figure offered a second time to a stick that had kept its notch, Sella keeping the whole hearth grammar at both ends of the day with the hairline showing between staple and wire, both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, repair kept apart from restoration, dressed grain turned under wool unfigured, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, nineteen steps at the half-pace, seven walked-around places once and not twice and the fold righted without a look at his face or a second fold, Tarn keeping six where the house could check and the seventh at the lip, telling the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} once and not twice and not turning his head toward the landing, the loan uncalled in a term already ended and the valuable ear exposure and not safety, Jorra parting dusty forearms from clean as clot from vessel, speaking to the wheel before any person, withholding the full note three turns ahead and keeping \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise neither given nor withdrawn, costs arriving as directions and going away as weather with the fist-to-nowhere number, the note not a price and no signature between figure and price, the offered figure kept where put beside the ninth hand and the fifth shaping and not spent, named, witnessed or joined, the clerk’s entered figure, the second man’s slate turned to the sleeve and his direction down the bridge road, the well-asking answered with the weather, Hessa’s unread slate, Berr’s locked box with two readings of the year inside and the softening at the river’s skin kept as weather all found where put with a finger between every pair, the called-gone grey kept beside the left-in-place ridge, six hearings standing beside and never among with the seventh place empty and the Drawing’s knock outside, nine record-first hands and nine stoppings with no tenth, no eighth opening, seventh hearing, sixth shaping, tenth hand, tenth stopping, eleventh arithmetic, signature, payer, witness or reader standing on any of the three days, and in the small hours the towel coming out as instruments come out when a case is done, the file set down where the next hand would find it without looking and there being no next hand in the room, four low pulls breathing under the floor with the fifth unsupplied, the figure gone back into the sleeve and the stick keeping its notch, the well giving back the weather, and the hand coming down flat on answer 420 as the house went on into a morning not yet lived and not brought.}
